The I ndian River County Sheriff's Office has located the vehicle allegedly involved in a deadly hit-and-run crash that killed a man riding an e-bike Sunday. According to IRCSO, its Real Time Crime Center has been working with the Florida Highway Patrol since the deadly crash to locate the vehicle involved. While reviewing leads, an IRCSO analyst located a vehicle matching the truck's description, including a key identifying characteristic: a missing passenger-side mirror. Deputies said they used Flock Safety technology and other investigative resources to identify the vehicle, its license plate and information about the driver. The information allowed FHP to locate the vehicle and confirm its connection to the crash. See also: Internal report details why PBSO deputy was reprimanded after ticketing one-armed driver CBS12 News reported Sunday that at about 8:57 p.m. , a 48-year-old Vero Beach man was riding an e-bike near 8th Street and 14th Avenue when he was struck by what investigators believed was a pickup truck. Investigators said a light-colored Ford F-150, believed to be a 2015 to 2020 model, was traveling behind the man in the same lane. As the pickup approached the bicyclist, the driver took evasive action, traveling southwest and partially entering the eastbound lane. However, troopers said the driver was unable to avoid the bicyclist, and the right side of the pickup struck him. The bicyclist was thrown onto the roadway and came to rest in the eastbound lane of 8th Street. FHP said the driver fled the scene without rendering aid or contacting law enforcement. The bicyclist was taken to Lawnwood Hospital, where he was pronounced dead. As of this writing, IRCSO has not identified the driver or released the identity of the bicyclist who was killed.

A Martin County senior citizen nearly lost $600,000 to a gold bar scam, but with the help of deputies, the crisis was averted. MCSO says that the victim was contacted by a fraudster claiming to be from his financial institution and was told that his bank account had been compromised. The scammer then convinced the senior citizen that he needed to protect his money by backing it up with gold. According to MCSO , the victim was then instructed to send $600,000 to a legitimate gold vendor. The scammer told the victim that the gold would then be picked up by a third-party driver and delivered to the bank. After going through with the transaction, the victim quickly realized something wasn’t right, and immediately went to his bank. The bank then recognized the situation as potential fraud and advised him to the sheriff's office. See also: Elderly woman accused of stealing nearly $2,000 worth of merchandise from Wellington Mall The responding deputy then spoke directly with the gold vendor and helped the victim stop the transaction from going through. MCSO says the victim confirmed he received a full refund of his $600,000.

The School District of Indian River County is looking to put around 10 properties on the market for potential buyers. WATCH WPTV's COVERAGE BELOW: William Dodds, CFO of the School District of Indian River County, said the properties are spread across the county and include 4 older schools, older office buildings, and district-owned land. "It's just the space is not needed," Dodds said. After consolidating multiple schools throughout the district, Dodds said some of the properties are no longer necessary. "That's not the best financial decision to try to maintain two buildings where we can do it in one," Dodds said. Money made from the sale of the properties would go back to the district's capital budget. "[It'll] help keep our buildings up, maybe enhance some buildings, do some things in capital that we wouldn't be able to do otherwise," Dodds said. No decisions have been made yet. Dodds said the district is gauging interest from potential buyers before moving forward. Ken Krasnow with Cushman and Wakefield, a real estate company working with the school district to sell the properties, said the buildings vary in condition and potential. "Some of these buildings are in better shape than others," Krasnow said. "Some of these buildings and some of the facilities have a different you know sort of value from a repurposing perspective." Krasnow said some buildings, like Rosewood Magnet School, could be transformed. "It's everything from repurposing medical office to quasi-flex space," Krasnow said. Krasnow said larger schools and properties could be redeveloped. "[It] will look more like commercial, maybe some retail out along the front, and then some residential in the back," Krasnow said. Dodds said the district will reexamine interest in the properties and whether they need to be sold around December or January. The school board will have final approval. A person died after being shot Wednesday night at a residence in the Seminole Mobile Home Park community, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. Deputies with the Sheriff's Office Patrol Operations Bureau and personnel from the St. Lucie County Fire District responded to the 3300 block of Orange Avenue at approximately 9:11 p.m. 12 following reports of a shooting. According to investigators, the initial caller reported that an individual had been shot while allegedly attempting to enter a residence. When deputies arrived, they found the victim suffering from a gunshot wound. The individual was transported to a local hospital, where they were later pronounced dead. Detectives with the Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Division and Crime Scene Investigators responded to both the scene and the hospital as the investigation unfolded. Authorities later obtained and executed a search warrant at the residence, where they recovered a firearm believed to have been used in the shooting. Investigators remained at the scene overnight, processing evidence and conducting interviews. Detectives and crime scene personnel completed their work and cleared the residence at approximately 6:11 a.m. The circumstances leading up to the shooting remain under investigation. At this time, authorities believe the incident was isolated and say there is no known immediate threat to the surrounding community. Anyone with information about the shooting, including possible witnesses or those with relevant video footage, is asked to contact the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office at 772-462-3230. Anonymous tips can be submitted through Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 800-273-TIPS (8477). A 45-year-old dump truck driver was killed after being hit by another construction vehicle inside a work zone on I-95 just south of Tradition on Monday night, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The driver stepped out of their dump truck on the northbound lanes and was struck by a tractor with a sweeper traveling south, repaving the area as part of an improvement project. The construction worker was transported to Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital, where they later died. The driver of the other truck was arrested on an unrelated warrant, FHP said. FHP s Traffic Homicide Investigation is ongoing.

A person died after being shot Wednesday night at a residence in the Seminole Mobile Home Park community, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. Deputies with the Sheriff's Office Patrol Operations Bureau and personnel from the St. Lucie County Fire District responded to the 3300 block of Orange Avenue at approximately 9:11 p.m. 12 following reports of a shooting. According to investigators, the initial caller reported that an individual had been shot while allegedly attempting to enter a residence. When deputies arrived, they found the victim suffering from a gunshot wound. The individual was transported to a local hospital, where they were later pronounced dead. Detectives with the Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Division and Crime Scene Investigators responded to both the scene and the hospital as the investigation unfolded. Authorities later obtained and executed a search warrant at the residence, where they recovered a firearm believed to have been used in the shooting. Investigators remained at the scene overnight, processing evidence and conducting interviews. Detectives and crime scene personnel completed their work and cleared the residence at approximately 6:11 a.m. The circumstances leading up to the shooting remain under investigation. At this time, authorities believe the incident was isolated and say there is no known immediate threat to the surrounding community. Anyone with information about the shooting, including possible witnesses or those with relevant video footage, is asked to contact the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office at 772-462-3230. Anonymous tips can be submitted through Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 800-273-TIPS (8477). An 8-year-old girl in Fort Pierce fractured her femur in a hit-and-run crash, and her mother is demanding justice after police arrested the suspect 11 days later. Police said the crash happened at the intersection of 25th Street and Avenue M when the girl and her brother were crossing the street. A Mercedes-Benz making a left turn struck the girl, and surveillance footage captured the incident. Lawrunda Robinson, the girl’s mother, described the moment she learned about the crash. "My son came home and said my baby got hit. I go, 'Boy, stop playing,' and the lady told me, 'No, she’s hit,'" Robinson said. The surveillance video appears to show 34-year-old Demetris Johnson exiting a gold Mercedes-Benz to check on the girl before getting back into the car and driving away. "How are you gonna hit a child and get out, make sure she’s not dead, and then keep going?" Robinson said. Michael Santiago of the Fort Pierce Police Department said Johnson was arrested on Wednesday and refused to speak with investigators. Officers confirmed that Johnson was driving with a suspended license. Robinson expressed her frustration over the situation. "So he was driving with a suspended license, and he hit my baby too. I ask my baby, 'What you want to happen to him?' She said she wants him to get jail time," Robinson said. Johnson now faces charges of leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injuries. The girl suffered a fractured femur and is currently using a wheelchair to get around. Her leg is in a cast, and her mother said the recovery process will be lengthy. "The doctor told me it would take a month before he take the cast off her leg. Then she got to go to physical therapy and learn how to walk again," Robinson said. Police are asking anyone with additional information about the crash to contact them. A Martin County senior citizen nearly lost $600,000 to a gold bar scam, but with the help of deputies, the crisis was averted. MCSO says that the victim was contacted by a fraudster claiming to be from his financial institution and was told that his bank account had been compromised. The scammer then convinced the senior citizen that he needed to protect his money by backing it up with gold. According to MCSO , the victim was then instructed to send $600,000 to a legitimate gold vendor. The scammer told the victim that the gold would then be picked up by a third-party driver and delivered to the bank. After going through with the transaction, the victim quickly realized something wasn’t right, and immediately went to his bank. The bank then recognized the situation as potential fraud and advised him to the sheriff's office. See also: Elderly woman accused of stealing nearly $2,000 worth of merchandise from Wellington Mall The responding deputy then spoke directly with the gold vendor and helped the victim stop the transaction from going through. MCSO says the victim confirmed he received a full refund of his $600,000.

For the fourth straight year, the Indian River County School District has been graded an A school district. All but one school in the district received an A rating. The only school to receive a B was Dodgertown Elementary School. District Superintendent Dr. David Moore says no matter which school parents choose for their children in Indian River County, they can expect a quality education. Moore says the district is maintaining its A grade by investing in teachers and staff who have helped improve the district over the past six years. He also says that by identifying pain points, school leaders can allocate resources and funding to address those issues and prevent the district from falling in the ratings. Moore says those efforts are also reflected in the number of parents choosing to keep their children in the public school system. "Because of our willingness for the last 6 years to transform the experience, for the second straight year, we are going to exceed the state’s projected enrollment for our community," Moore told CBS12 News. The School District of Indian River County is also ranked in nine out of 12 accountability components. The district says that demonstrates exceptional performance in educating students from the time they begin their education through graduation day.

A different approach to public education is taking shape in Indian River County this school year as district leaders expand school choice and reorganize several campuses. Families in the district have more flexibility in where their children attend school. Parents can choose to enroll their children at schools across the district, rather than being limited to the school assigned to their neighborhood. The district has also converted several campuses into K-8 schools and operates five charter schools. One of the biggest changes this school year involves the district’s former all-freshman high school. See also: Indian River County launches new feature to track school buses in real time The Freshman Learning Center has been converted into Vero Beach Middle School. Moore says the freshman center was expensive to operate and did not provide students with high-quality educational programs. He says moving ninth-graders back to traditional high schools will also give them earlier access to more academic opportunities. From a student’s perspective, it allows them access to programming that was only being offered at the high school. You shouldn’t have to wait until you’re in 10th grade to take some of those courses, Moore told CBS12 News. District leaders say the two high schools, Sebastian River High School and Vero Beach High School, have enough capacity to accommodate incoming freshmen. That means all incoming ninth-graders this school year will attend either Sebastian River High School or Vero Beach High School. The changes are part of the district’s broader effort to give families more educational options while restructuring how its schools serve students.

"I'm excited that it's a brand-new class," said Annabel Hamilton, a third grader at Liberty Magnet School. Excitement filled Liberty Magnet School as students returned to new classes, teachers, and friends. Cheers greeted them as they walked in for the first day of school. After a quiet summer, Principal Chris Taylor said he is happy to see the halls full again. "When we get students back, the energy is back to our school," Taylor said. Palm Beach County is locked in fierce competition with Texas, Tennessee, Virginia and the Carolinas for high-paying corporate jobs and headquarters, according to the county's top economic development executive who warns that the region's economic future depends on how quickly local governments adapt to changing business demands."There's very stiff competition for economic development projects throughout the United States. So, when these companies come in, we have one shot to pitch the Palm Beaches to make it to the shortlist," said Kelly Smallridge, president and CEO of the Business Development Board of Palm Beach County. "This is a competition, and as soon as they walk out our door, internal in the state of Florida, Miami, Jacksonville, Tampa are our biggest."WPTV's Joel Lopez spoke with Smallridge to examine what drives corporate relocation decisions in today's competitive market. The answer, she said, isn't what many residents expect."People think that companies come here for the beaches and the lifestyle. But the first question they ask is draw a 5-mile radius around the building that I would ideally would like to locate to and tell me the skill sets of the residents in that area," Smallridge said. It is the number one factor in whether or not they're going to be competitive."The Business Development Board serves as Palm Beach County's public-private economic development agency, helping recruit companies, retain existing employers and coordinate with municipalities across all 39 cities in the county.Smallridge, a Palm Beach County native who grew up in Palm Springs, said the organization was created more than 40 years ago, because residents wanted to diversify an economy once dominated by tourism, agriculture and construction."The residents came forward and said, 'It's too cyclical, very seasonal in nature. It's very low-paying,'" she said. "We want an entity that goes after high-quality, higher-paying jobs."Today, the county's economy is driven increasingly by sectors like life sciences, aviation and aerospace, technology, manufacturing and financial services. The transformation has been dramatic: the average age in Palm Beach County has dropped from 75 to 48-49, with an average resident wage of $78,000.Currently, 19,077 financial services companies in Palm Beach County create 119,483 jobs with an average salary of $126,340, according to Business Development Board data."We are the creators of the Wall Street South Initiative and tangential to that, we've created this tech and innovation-based initiative," Smallridge said. "AI, cybersecurity, quantum computing is coming to the Palm Beaches."The county's aerospace industry includes roughly 1,700 companies, serving as another major driver of growth. Local universities including Florida Atlantic University, Kaiser University, Palm Beach Atlantic University and Palm Beach State College are working to create workforce pipelines for these emerging sectors.One factor repeatedly determines whether Palm Beach County lands corporate deals: available commercial real estate."Buildings, office buildings, industrial buildings are usually at the top of the list," Smallridge said.That reality has helped cities like Boca Raton and West Palm Beach secure some of the county's biggest corporate relocations. Boca Raton currently has roughly 13 million square feet of office space, while downtown West Palm Beach has another 1.7 million square feet of Class A office space under development.Current office space rankings show Boca Raton leading with 13.1 million square feet, followed by West Palm Beach with 9.5 million square feet and Palm Beach Gardens with 4.1 million square feet.For industrial space, West Palm Beach leads with 2.8 million square feet, followed by Boca Raton with 850,000 square feet and Palm Beach Gardens with 556,000 square feet.Companies routinely ask for school ratings within a five-mile radius of proposed office sites, because employees want strong public school options for their children, according to Smallridge.She acknowledged that school quality varies widely across Palm Beach County and influences where families choose to live.Housing affordability is also becoming increasingly important, especially as companies recruit workers from outside South Florida. While executives may afford luxury communities, employers still need workforce housing options for their staff."What are the affordable housing options for our employees?" has become a routine question during corporate recruitment meetings, Smallridge said.Smallridge stressed that speed matters more than ever in economic development competition."I would suggest not to wait for the company to come to you," she said. "You need the process in order."That includes having shovel-ready sites, clear zoning rules and expedited permitting systems already in place before companies begin evaluating locations."Expedited is very, very critical to winning the deal," she said.The top questions executives ask when considering Palm Beach County relocation include site availability, permit speed, local talent for recruitment, school ratings and housing availability and affordability.Despite competition between cities, Smallridge emphasized that economic development benefits spill across municipal boundaries regardless of where companies physically locate."I never see a company locate to an area, hire everybody from that particular city, do all their business with small businesses in that city, send their kids to all the schools in that city," she said. There's a lot of movement."She cited Oxygen Development, a large cosmetics manufacturer in central Palm Beach County, as an example of a company drawing 800 employees from multiple nearby communities, with the majority coming from Lake Worth Beach.At the center of Smallridge's message was a broader warning: Palm Beach County can no longer rely solely on its beaches, weather and lifestyle to stay competitive."Just because we've had a great 5 to 10 years and we are living in somewhat of a bubble right now does not mean that we will be there in 10 years if we become complacent and sit where we are," Smallridge said. "We have to continue to maintain the very quality of life, the character and the charm that attracted everyone here, along with the balance of growth, good schools, good infrastructure. That all makes a difference to landing the deal and beating the other states."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A 37-year-old man was shot and killed after deputies say he entered a St. Lucie County home and attacked a 22-year-old man during a dispute. The shooting happened around 9 p.m. Wednesday at the Seminole Mobile Home Park. Lucie County Sheriff Richard R. Del Toro , the two men knew each other and had been involved in a dispute that included verbal arguments and threatening text messages. Investigators say the suspect, who has yet to be identified, made several threats before showing up at the home. Deputies say he knocked on the front door and was let inside before a brawl broke out. Investigators say he pushed the 22-year-old homeowner and punched him several times in the stomach. See also: Man arrested in Fort Pierce hit-and-run that seriously injured 7-year-old boy: Police "The victim disengaged from the deceased, pulled out a handgun, shot one time, and the threat was over," Sheriff Del Toro said. The suspect was taken to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead. "It's not fair, 'cause my son has no father now. He's five years old, and what am I gonna tell him? We didn't even get to say goodbye," said Naomi Pallarez, the girlfriend of the man who died. The sheriff said the homeowner remained at the home and cooperated with investigators. His girlfriend and sister were also inside the home and provided statements that investigators say corroborate his account. Deputies recovered the handgun after executing a search warrant at the residence. No charges have been filed against the homeowner at this time. Investigators are working with the State Attorney's Office to determine whether the shooting falls under Florida's stand-your-ground self-defense law. "Obviously, you have to be in defense of yourself, but at the same time, you have to be in fear for your life anytime you're gonna use deadly force," Sheriff Del Toro explained. Del Toro said investigators are still reviewing evidence, including text messages between the two men. The sheriff said the suspect had a criminal history, including drug-related and resisting-officer charges, domestic violence-related charges, and three felony convictions. He stressed that the man's criminal history was not a reason for him to be killed. The suspect's name has not been released because investigators have not yet notified his next of kin and they have not released the name of the man who was killed. "I am very much heartbroken. And now I'm a single mom," Pallarez said. The sheriff said there is no known threat to the surrounding community and described the shooting as an isolated incident. Del Toro urged anyone who receives threats and believes a situation could escalate to contact law enforcement before violence occurs. "I just wish that we'd gotten involved sooner rather than being reactive and called after the fact," Del Toro said. "Could've had a different outcome."

Deputies in Indian River County safely took a man into custody after a two-hour standoff on the 17th Street Bridge early Tuesday morning. The incident began around 1 a.m. when deputies responded to a call from Port St. Lucie police about a man wanted for burglary. The man had reportedly called his mother and told her he wanted to kill himself. Body camera footage showed the man sitting on a platform over the bridge railing, his feet dangling in the air. Traffic Deputy Edouard Gast, a member of the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office Crisis Negotiation Team, worked to establish a connection with the man. “He was on that platform with his feet hanging, just kind of kicking in the breeze,” Gast said. “At first, he didn’t want to talk, so it took a little time for me to eventually get a rapport with him, get him to open up and start to talk.” In the footage, Gast can be heard saying, “Come on, buddy, talk to me for a minute. You got a lot on your mind?” The man responded, “Yeah, I do, and I’m trying to think about it.” At one point, the man appeared ready to jump. Gast continued to plead with him, saying, “Come on, man, listen. Come on, man, don’t do this to your mom.” Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates “He flipped a switch, and that’s when he climbed on top, climbed over, and positioned himself to jump,” Gast said. “It just took me talking to him over and over again for him to come back over and stand on that platform and just continue to talk to him and let him know everything was going to be OK.” The sheriff’s office marine unit and fire rescue crews were stationed in the water below as a safety precaution. After two hours of negotiation, the man climbed back to the top of the bridge and shook the negotiator's hand. “This guy is wanted out of Port St. Lucie, but we still have a job to do,” Sgt. “Just because they may be wanted, we’re still going to treat them with due care and try to make sure they’re safe, and we can get them to answer for their crimes without doing this.” Officials confirmed the man was taken into custody without incident. For the fourth straight year, the Indian River County School District has been graded an A school district. All but one school in the district received an A rating. The only school to receive a B was Dodgertown Elementary School. District Superintendent Dr. David Moore says no matter which school parents choose for their children in Indian River County, they can expect a quality education. Moore says the district is maintaining its A grade by investing in teachers and staff who have helped improve the district over the past six years. He also says that by identifying pain points, school leaders can allocate resources and funding to address those issues and prevent the district from falling in the ratings. Moore says those efforts are also reflected in the number of parents choosing to keep their children in the public school system. "Because of our willingness for the last 6 years to transform the experience, for the second straight year, we are going to exceed the state’s projected enrollment for our community," Moore told CBS12 News. The School District of Indian River County is also ranked in nine out of 12 accountability components. The district says that demonstrates exceptional performance in educating students from the time they begin their education through graduation day.

Just days after 36 Border Collies were rescued from what authorities described as a severe animal hoarding situation in Palm City , shelter workers say the dogs are beginning to show signs of hope. The dogs were removed from a home on Southwest Alligator Street where Martin County deputies reported finding deplorable living conditions, including feces, urine-soaked materials, and debris throughout the residence. Homeowner Paige O'Donnell was arrested and faces animal cruelty and improper confinement charges . Now, all 36 dogs are in the care of the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, where staff members have spent the past several days working around the clock to help them recover physically and emotionally. "It's been completely insane. We've been working our tails off, no pun intended," said Humane Society spokesperson Sarah Fisher. According to Fisher, many of the dogs arrived severely matted, under-socialized, and frightened of human interaction. Since arriving at the shelter, the dogs have received vaccines, deworming treatments, medications and extensive grooming. Some of the grooming challenges have been staggering. "Yesterday we shaved one of the puppy's mats off, and it was three pounds just on the puppy," Fisher said. "So, you can imagine the big dogs are probably at least double that." The dogs range in age from puppies younger than four months old to adults believed to be as old as six years. Shelter workers say the younger dogs appear to be adjusting more quickly, while many of the older dogs remain fearful and withdrawn after what may have been years of neglect. "Overall, they're all very under-socialized and scared," Fisher said. Staff has only been able to work on 10 dogs so far due to their extreme conditions. See also: Animal Services responded to Palm City home roughly 20 times since 2020 Some dogs have required sedation for grooming and medical treatment. Others are beginning to slowly warm up to staff members. Fisher says every dog is progressing differently, but many still have a long road ahead. "They're going to take a lot of time to really come out of their shell," she said. The recovery effort comes just weeks after another large animal hoarding case in Martin County, leaving shelter staff emotionally exhausted but determined to continue helping animals in need. Still, Fisher says the community response has been overwhelming. After photos of the dogs were shared online, donations from across the Treasure Coast began pouring in. Community members have provided monetary support, supplies, and encouragement for staff caring for the rescued animals. "The amount of support is so heartwarming. I can't even believe it," Fisher said. "And our staff is so grateful." For now, the dogs cannot be adopted while legal proceedings continue. Once the case is resolved, the animals will be spayed and neutered, continue rehabilitation, and eventually be placed in foster homes or adopted by families prepared to meet their needs. That process could take weeks or even months. But despite the challenges ahead, shelter workers say they've already noticed a change in the dogs since they first arrived. "From yesterday to today, I think they realize that they're safe now," Fisher said. "And you can see just a small transformation, and it just brings everybody's spirits up. So, they haven't fully given up." If you'd like to help, the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast says its most urgent needs are wet dog food and monetary donations to support the ongoing care and rehabilitation of the rescued Border Collies. The shelter is also currently over capacity and is seeking foster families willing to temporarily care for other dogs and cats in its system, helping free up much-needed space as these animals recover. Fisher says the shelter also has a 'Name your price' adoption special until further notice. "We have a 'name your price' adoption special until further notice too. (12:31) So, it's a good time to adopt.

A person is dead after a shooting Wednesday night at a mobile home park in St. Lucie County that deputies said stemmed from an ongoing dispute. The sheriff's office and fire district responded to the shooting at 9:11 p.m. in the 3300 block of Orange Avenue at the Seminole Mobile Home Park community. WATCH BELOW: Stand your ground case under review after fatal shooting Deputies and St. Lucie County Fire District personnel found one person suffering from a gunshot wound. The person who was shot was taken to a local hospital, where they later died from their injuries. "During the investigation, we learned that there was a dispute between the shooter, who we believe is our victim here, and the suspect who arrived at the residence. What the dispute was over is kind of muddy right now," St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro said. The sheriff said the two people involved in the shooting had a dispute via text message and verbally, described as "ongoing." "(The person who was killed) shows up at the house, knocks on the door, bangs on the door. comes inside the residence once the door is open, immediately pushes our victim, who's the homeowner there, punches him two times in the midsection area, at which time the victim backed away from the suspect, pulled out a handgun, and shot the suspect one time point blank in the chest," Del Toro said. Investigators obtained and executed a search warrant at the residence, recovering a 9 mm semi-automatic pistol they believe was used in the shooting. "The handgun that was used was recovered during a search warrant at the residence. We worked all night, working about nine hours out at the residence," Del Toro said. The sheriff said they are working with the state attorney's office to determine whether a crime was committed or this is a stand-your-ground case. No charges have been filed in the case. Del Toro said the homeowner's sister and girlfriend were inside the home at the time of the shooting, corroborating the circumstances of the incident. The scene was cleared shortly after 6 a.m. Investigators believe this was an isolated incident and said there is no immediate threat to the surrounding community. The name of the person who was killed has not been released. The sheriff's office is asking anyone with information about the shooting to come forward. This includes witnesses who may have seen events leading up to the shooting or anyone with relevant video or other information. WPTV spoke with neighbors at the mobile home park, who said this shooting is out of character for their neighborhood. Tips can be submitted by calling the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office at 772-462-3230. Anonymous tips can also be made through Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 800-273-TIPS (8477).

A 16-year-old girl died after she fell through a hole in the roof of an abandoned four-story building last Saturday in Sebastian, deputies said.According to a new release from the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, deputies and fire rescue personnel responded to 9846 Riverside Preserve Drive in Sebastian at about 10:35 p.m. after receiving a 911 call reporting that the girl had fallen from a concrete structure and was critically injured. Deputies arrived and found a group of minors along with the critically injured teen on the second floor of the abandoned building. "The investigation determined the group had been trespassing on the property and was on the roof when the teen fell through a hole in the roof, dropping approximately 29 feet to the floor below," the sheriff's office said. The sheriff's office said one of the minors in the group knew CPR and immediately began life-saving measures. The 16-year-old was flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where she died from her injuries a short time later. Detectives are actively investigating the teen's death, but said, "At this time, all evidence indicates this was an accident." The victim's name has not been released. "The Indian River County Sheriff's Office extends its deepest sympathies to the family during this difficult time. We also want to remind the public, especially parents and teens, of the serious dangers posed by climbing on abandoned structures, and the legal consequences of trespassing on privately owned property," the sheriff's office said.

Boca Helping Hands reported on Thursday that there is an increased demand for food among the working poor at its distribution center in Lake Worth Beach. The organization said it typically serves 400 hot meals each week but an increasing number of local residents have been showing up for help, with 543 this past week, an increase of almost 36%."The growth in numbers over the last month may reflect the effect of more people falling off of the SNAP eligibility," Andrew Hagen, CEO of Boca Helping Hands, said. "Hundreds of thousands of Floridians have lost these benefits over the past year."The organization said it launched its Lake Worth Beach distribution site at Proclaim Church in 2021, working with a small group of volunteers, preparing hot meals for those in need. What began as a small experiment has grown into one the organization's most successful community programs.The program relies heavily on recovered and donated food and is supported by donors who help the organization continue meeting growing demand. For Hagen, though, the Friday evening distributions represent something beyond a meal count.“We are thrilled to offer a good meal to someone who needs it,” he said. “But I think the bigger thing we offer here is hope. People can’t live without it.”

Lucie Police Department officers have been placed on paid administrative leave as investigations continue into two separate incidents involving political campaign signs that occurred last week on Southwest Airoso Boulevard.WATCH BELOW: WPTV's Tyler Hatfield speaks with Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin after husband placed on administrative leaveThe officers placed on leave effective Tuesday, are Lieutenant Aaron Martin, Lieutenant Jason Vega and Detective Sergeant Joseph Alves. Chief Leo Niemczyk made the decision following a review of the initial facts and timeline surrounding the incidents. Lucie Police Department released more information regarding the incidents over the weekend.The first incident occurred on Aug. 5 near the intersection of SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thanksgiving Avenue.A Port St. Lucie Police sergeant observed Steven Giordano and an unidentified adult female near political campaign signs at a residence and initiated an investigation after one campaign sign was found on the ground while another had been placed in the yard.Detectives reviewed surveillance video from the area, which appears to show Giordano and the unidentified adult female arrive at the residence, approach campaign signs displayed in the yard, and interact with the signage. The video further appears to show the unidentified female remove a campaign sign supporting Mayor Shannon Martin before a different campaign sign was placed in the yard.Detectives collected the video evidence and are evaluating it alongside statements, physical evidence, and all other information gathered during the investigation.Officers and detectives are working to determine the circumstances surrounding the placement, movement, and authorization of the campaign signs, including whether the movement or replacement of the signs was authorized by the property owner at the time the incident occurred.The second incident occurred on Aug. 7 near SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thornhill Drive, where officers responded to a disturbance involving political campaign signs.During the investigation, officers learned that Lt. Aaron Martin and Steven Giordano were involved in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of campaign signs at a nearby residence.Officers reviewed video recordings provided by the involved parties, which depict Aaron Martin and Giordano engaged in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of political campaign signs at the residence.Investigators interviewed the homeowners and learned that both residents believed they had separately granted permission for campaign signs to be placed on the property. Officers determined that one homeowner communicated permission for one campaign's sign, while another resident of the home, who has limited English proficiency, separately conveyed permission to individuals associated with the opposing campaign.Investigators believe the language barrier contributed to a misunderstanding regarding which campaign signs were authorized to be displayed and whether previously placed signs could be moved or replaced.WATCH PREVIOUS COVERAGE BELOW: Port St. Lucie police release details on 2 separate political campaign sign investigationsThe Port St. Lucie Police Department says it remains committed to ensuring all investigations are conducted fairly and impartially, maintaining its longstanding commitment to integrity, professionalism and accountability.Lt. Aaron Martin's wife is Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin, who is currently running for re-election.WPTV's Tyler Hatfield spoke with the mayor on Thursday, following the news that her husband is on paid administrative leave with the Port St. Lucie Police Department following the investigation."Whenever there's a criminal investigation of any kind, it's standard operating procedure for the police department to place people on administrative leave pending the outcome of an investigation," she said.She said she hopes the incident will not impact her campaign and Tuesday's primary election."This issue about signage and campaign signs has nothing to do with my campaign in terms of how I have been leading the city and how I will continue to lead the city and the important issues that we're facing here in Port St. Lucie," Mayor Shannon Martin said.When asked what she wanted to tell voters learning about her husband's leave in real time, the mayor pushed back on the framing of the situation."It was blown way out of proportion, but the process has to work the way that the process has to work in order to ensure fairness and transparency," she said. "So that process will go forward, but that has nothing to do with the elections. It has nothing to do with my campaign, whatsoever."The mayor said she intends to press forward despite the circumstances."It's a disappointing situation. However, I'm going to continue to move forward and making sure that I am continuing my campaign. And continuing to work to earn residents' votes," Shannon Martin said.When asked to comment on the investigation itself, the mayor declined."I cannot comment on that. It has nothing to do with me. I'm not part of that process whatsoever. I've never been part of that process as a mayor. That is not my role, and it will never be part of part of my process," she said.

With five days remaining before Florida's primary, the candidates for governor are making their final sales — and the two parties are ending in very different places.Republicans are still fighting over their nominee. Byron Donalds is working to protect a commanding lead, while Lt. Jay Collins is escalating his attacks and trying to consolidate voters looking for an alternative. Democrats, meanwhile, appear close to settling their primary, allowing David Jolly and running mate Gwen Graham to begin making their case for November.Donalds, endorsed by President Donald Trump, sounded confident in an interview Thursday but stopped short of declaring the race over."You stay confident, you stay focused on what you're doing," Donalds said. "I think the fact that the other campaigns attack me every day kind of demonstrates that they, too, know where things are in this race."Recent polling supports that confidence. A James Madison Institute survey released in August placed Donalds at 49 percent among likely Republican primary voters, followed by Collins at 18 percent, former House Speaker Paul Renner at 8 percent and investor James Fishback at 4 percent. Twenty-one percent remained undecided.Donalds kept his closing message centered on affordability, blaming Democratic economic policies for inflation and promising to lower Florida property-insurance costs through changes to the state's Catastrophe Fund, reinsurance system and home-hardening programs. He also called the property-tax amendment headed to voters only a "first step" and argued that faster permitting could reduce housing and construction costs."We feel very good about where we stand today, but it's in the hands of the voters," Donalds said. "We'll see what happens Tuesday night."Collins is closing much more aggressively.During a lengthy virtual news conference, the former Green Beret cast himself as a "day-one ready" Florida executive and Donalds as a Washington celebrity disconnected from working families."I mow my own yard, I gassed up my own truck, I live the same Florida life that working families live because I'm one of the people," Collins said.He then added a more personal jab: "Byron, I don't think he probably mows his yard. My guess is he has a landscape architect."Collins' policy pitch included tighter insurance oversight, faster claims and storm permitting, expanded home hardening and the eventual elimination of property taxes on homesteaded homes. He also proposed broader sales-tax holidays for families and tradespeople, a permanent Second Amendment sales-tax holiday and a requirement that large data centers cover the utility costs associated with their operations.His campaign's central promise: "Life will get easier. We will be safer."Collins called the Republican contest a two-person race and urged Renner, Fishback and the remaining candidates without a viable path to rally behind him. That characterization, however, is not reflected in recent public polling, which consistently shows Donalds leading the field by wide margins.Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed Collins lieutenant governor in August 2025, giving Collins the executive experience he now emphasizes. DeSantis, however, has not endorsed anyone in the race to succeed him.Despite his attacks, Collins pledged to support the eventual Republican nominee if he loses Tuesday."Yes, I will support whoever the nominee is," Collins said. "And yes, I absolutely think all Republicans should step in and support whoever the nominee is."The Democratic race has far less suspense.Jolly, a former Republican congressman who later became a Democrat, held 47 percent in the latest JMI survey. No other Democratic candidate topped 5 percent. Six candidates remain on the Democratic ballot.His running mate, Gwen Graham, is already speaking directly to November.Graham, a former Democratic congresswoman and the daughter of former Gov. Bob Graham, cast her ballot Thursday at Florida A&M University. She chose the historically Black university to highlight voting rights, civil rights and youth participation.FAMU students helped launch the Tallahassee bus boycott in 1956 after Wilhelmina Jakes and Carrie Patterson were arrested for refusing to follow segregated seating rules."FAMU has had a long history of fighting for civil rights, fighting for voting rights," Graham said. "The students of FAMU have had a historical impact."While saying the campaign is taking nothing for granted, Graham made clear the Jolly-Graham ticket is already looking beyond Tuesday."It's a short sprint between Aug. "This race is not about being a Democrat, Republican or Independent. What it's about is the future of Florida."Graham described the ticket as centrist and moderate, with an agenda focused on housing affordability, education and healthcare access. She also promised to move Florida away from culture-war fights and what she called political interference in higher education.That appeal to voters outside the Democratic base will be essential. Florida had nearly 3.33 million voters registered with no party affiliation as of July 31, while Republicans held a registration advantage of more than 1.5 million over Democrats, according to the Florida Division of Elections.Democrats have not won a Florida governor's race since Lawton Chiles was reelected in 1994. The latest JMI survey showed Donalds leading Jolly 45 to 38 percent in a potential general-election matchup, with roughly one in six voters undecided.Florida's primary is Aug. The general election is Nov.

This school year, Indian River County classrooms will be nearly fully staffed with teachers and administrators. District officials tell CBS12 News there are currently only five teacher vacancies. Unlike many counties across the state of Florida, the district did not make any workforce reductions this year. David Moore attributes that to the district’s yearly budget review, which he says has saved the district more than $11 million dollars since he became superintendent in 2019. He says the annual review and reorganization of the budget have helped the district avoid cuts that could impact staffing and, ultimately, the quality of education. We just finished negotiations with our teachers and support staff, unions, and were able to provide them additional compensation for the hard work that they do," Moore told CBS12 News. Moore says all teachers in the district are receiving a raise. Teachers who have worked for more than 10 years will receive a raise of roughly $2,200 dollars, while teachers with less classroom experience will receive approximately $1,300 dollars. Support staff will receive raises ranging from three to four percent. The superintendent also shared that the district has created more efficient school bus routes, which have reduced the number of buses on the road. Moore says he does not expect rising fuel prices to become an issue for the Indian River County School District.

A person died after being shot Wednesday night at a residence in the Seminole Mobile Home Park community, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. Deputies with the Sheriff's Office Patrol Operations Bureau and personnel from the St. Lucie County Fire District responded to the 3300 block of Orange Avenue at approximately 9:11 p.m. 12 following reports of a shooting. According to investigators, the initial caller reported that an individual had been shot while allegedly attempting to enter a residence. When deputies arrived, they found the victim suffering from a gunshot wound. The individual was transported to a local hospital, where they were later pronounced dead. Detectives with the Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Division and Crime Scene Investigators responded to both the scene and the hospital as the investigation unfolded. Authorities later obtained and executed a search warrant at the residence, where they recovered a firearm believed to have been used in the shooting. Investigators remained at the scene overnight, processing evidence and conducting interviews. Detectives and crime scene personnel completed their work and cleared the residence at approximately 6:11 a.m. The circumstances leading up to the shooting remain under investigation. At this time, authorities believe the incident was isolated and say there is no known immediate threat to the surrounding community. Anyone with information about the shooting, including possible witnesses or those with relevant video footage, is asked to contact the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office at 772-462-3230. Anonymous tips can be submitted through Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 800-273-TIPS (8477).

This school year, Indian River County classrooms will be nearly fully staffed with teachers and administrators. District officials tell CBS12 News there are currently only five teacher vacancies. Unlike many counties across the state of Florida, the district did not make any workforce reductions this year. David Moore attributes that to the district’s yearly budget review, which he says has saved the district more than $11 million dollars since he became superintendent in 2019. He says the annual review and reorganization of the budget have helped the district avoid cuts that could impact staffing and, ultimately, the quality of education. We just finished negotiations with our teachers and support staff, unions, and were able to provide them additional compensation for the hard work that they do," Moore told CBS12 News. Moore says all teachers in the district are receiving a raise. Teachers who have worked for more than 10 years will receive a raise of roughly $2,200 dollars, while teachers with less classroom experience will receive approximately $1,300 dollars. Support staff will receive raises ranging from three to four percent. The superintendent also shared that the district has created more efficient school bus routes, which have reduced the number of buses on the road. Moore says he does not expect rising fuel prices to become an issue for the Indian River County School District.

A Martin County senior citizen nearly lost $600,000 to a gold bar scam, but with the help of deputies, the crisis was averted. MCSO says that the victim was contacted by a fraudster claiming to be from his financial institution and was told that his bank account had been compromised. The scammer then convinced the senior citizen that he needed to protect his money by backing it up with gold. According to MCSO , the victim was then instructed to send $600,000 to a legitimate gold vendor. The scammer told the victim that the gold would then be picked up by a third-party driver and delivered to the bank. After going through with the transaction, the victim quickly realized something wasn’t right, and immediately went to his bank. The bank then recognized the situation as potential fraud and advised him to the sheriff's office. See also: Elderly woman accused of stealing nearly $2,000 worth of merchandise from Wellington Mall The responding deputy then spoke directly with the gold vendor and helped the victim stop the transaction from going through. MCSO says the victim confirmed he received a full refund of his $600,000.

The Border Collies rescued from a Palm City home Monday where authorities found deplorable conditions are now receiving medical care, nourishment and grooming as they begin their recovery. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast said it has taken in the dogs rescued by the Martin County Sheriff's Office Animal Services Unit and is assessing their needs while determining the best path forward. Paige O'Donnell, 62, was booked in connection with the case and faces 72 charges: 36 third-degree felony counts involving alleged animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts alleging animals were kept without sufficient exercise and air. O'Donnell appeared before a judge on Tuesday. Her bond was set at $270,000 and she was told she could have no pets if she is released on bond. These innocent dogs were inhumanely kept in deplorable conditions, and while they are finally safe, their journey to recovery is just beginning, the shelter said. Authorities said 36 Border Collies had been removed from the home as of Monday, while crews continued working to safely remove the remaining dogs. Investigators said it was initially unclear exactly how many animals remained inside because some were skittish and hiding. See also: Homeowner in custody after 36 Border Collies found in Palm City hoarding case The shelter said its immediate focus is on the well-being of the dogs and asked for the public's patience as it works through the complex situation. It is also asking for donations to help cover the cost of caring for the neglected animals, saying the financial burden comes at a time when the shelter was already facing significant challenges. Every dollar makes a difference, the shelter said. Together, we can give these dogs the second chance they deserve. According to the arrest report, Monday’s search was the culmination of an investigation that stretched back weeks and drew on years of previous Animal Services contacts involving O'Donnell’s home. The latest investigation developed after authorities received renewed concerns about the number of dogs at the SW Alligator Street residence and their living conditions. In June, investigators observed the property from the roadway but did not make contact with anyone at the home. The following month, the Sheriff’s Office received a letter and photographs from neighbors documenting concerns about conditions at the property dating back several years. On July 22, Animal Services responded to another complaint alleging more than 20 dogs were inside the home, that several deceased animals may have been in the garage, that the home did not have functioning air conditioning and that the dogs had not been allowed outside since 2022, according to the report. An investigator reported smelling a strong odor from the roadway and hearing what sounded like a large number of dogs, including puppies, barking from inside. O'Donnell later met with Animal Services at a Palm City park with one dog but, according to the report, would not allow investigators inside her home. The dog she brought to the meeting was described as having heavily stained, matted fur. Investigators said O'Donnell told them she had buried one of her dogs and named several others she still owned. Investigators also checked veterinary records. According to the affidavit, an employee at a local animal hospital said O'Donnell had brought in numerous puppies over the years and that records showed roughly 38 adult dogs had been treated there, including some that were brought in deceased. The employee also told investigators the dogs were frequently dirty. The arrest report says Animal Services had a long history of responding to complaints involving the residence, with roughly 20 related incidents documented from 2020 through this year. One 2020 investigation documented about 25 dogs and described the home as severely unsanitary, with feces and urine covering the floor. Investigators said one elderly dog was in such poor condition that humane euthanasia was recommended. Another complaint in 2022 led investigators to report 10 to 20 dogs being kept in a backyard covered in feces and flies. The arrest report says the home's air conditioning was not functioning and investigators observed feces inside the residence. At a follow-up inspection a week later, authorities said the home had been cleaned, the air conditioning repaired and three dogs surrendered to a rescue. In December 2023, investigators again responded to complaints about more than 20 dogs. According to the report, they detected an overwhelming odor of urine and feces and heard more than 10 dogs barking inside, including what sounded like puppies. Neighbors say they'd been raising concerns for years. "Very frustrating, very angry. They say if you hear something, say something, and we said something, probably over a hundred times," said Kelsey Weidenheimer, a neighbor on SW Alligator Street. "When you called the Sheriff's Office, what did you tell them?" we asked her. "The dogs are in the house. They haven't been let out in years at this point. There's no A-C, 'cause the windows are open. When the wind blows, you can smell it," Weidenheimer explained. "What did they tell you?" we asked her. "As long as the dogs have food and shelter, it's fine," she said. Investigators said the number and identities of dogs O'Donnell reported owning changed during different contacts, and records did not always establish what happened to dogs she had previously said were in her possession. "Our interaction with her started back in 2020 when she was an AKC breeder and back then we had several calls for service that involved her maybe mistreating animals. Our Animal Control Officers came out at that point. She was not actually--didn't appear to be mistreating animals," said John Budensiek, Martin Co. According to the Sheriff, they learned from a previous animal hoarding case, that it's not always a smart decision to rush in and take all the dogs. "Unfortunately, 20 plus years ago, we experienced that here at the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. We hit a house that had over 100 dogs in it. Seized them all, fostered them all out and then we were sued and lost the lawsuit. And worse than losing the lawsuit, we had to return those animals to the deplorable conditions which we took them from. So learning from our mistakes years and years ago, we weren’t going to do that again," Sheriff Budensiek said. In the days before the search warrant was obtained, investigators returned to the Palm City property and again reported smelling feces and urine. A neighboring resident also provided video that, according to the arrest report, showed garbage and debris piled high inside the garage while numerous dogs could be heard barking inside the home. Investigators also reviewed a photograph from a 2020 case showing at least 12 Border Collies in a room where the dogs and floor appeared to be covered in fecal matter. Based on those observations, prior complaints and O'Donnell’s documented history with Animal Services, investigators obtained a search warrant. When authorities entered the home Monday, the arrest report says the residence was unlivable and unsanitary, with floors covered in feces, urine and garbage and an air-conditioning system that was not working. Investigators said the dogs were severely matted with feces and urine and that portions of the walls appeared to have been repeatedly chewed. Thirty-six dogs were removed from the residence. Sheriff Budensiek separately described the conditions as extremely concerning, saying some of the normally black-and-white Border Collies were so covered in feces that they appeared nearly solid black. Deputies and Animal Services employees wore protective clothing while working inside the house. The Martin County Sheriff's Office says viewers and residents can help the 36 Border Collies by donating to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast to help with medical and recovery care for the animals. The investigation remains ongoing as authorities assess the dogs’ conditions and determine the full scope of the case.

A Palm City woman is in custody on a $270,000 bond after authorities discovered 36 Border Collies living in severe neglect inside her home on Alligator Street, leading to 72 charges of animal cruelty. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the animals were in "deplorable conditions." The case dates back to 2020, when animal services first investigated Paige O'Donnell’s home and dogs. Court records show complaints continued through 2022 and 2023, with renewed concerns in 2026 leading to surveillance and multiple attempted inspections. After officers observed one dog this month, they obtained a search warrant, which led to the discovery of the 36 dogs and O'Donnell’s arrest. During her first court appearance, O'Donnell was ordered, "You may not possess either temporarily or permanently any animals as a condition of your bond." All 36 dogs are now being cared for at the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. (To donate to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, click here.) Sarah Fisher, a spokesperson for the organization, described the severity of the animals’ condition. "We had not only the matted and the underweight and the skin issues, we had glass and metal. We had their tongues were bleeding from them biting their tongues. There was feces in their mouths. Their tails might be falling off. I mean, it's the worst that I've seen," Fisher said. Fisher added that the focus is currently on assessing each dog’s physical and mental health. "Some of the dogs are just laying there, and they don't know what to do. They don't know to lift their head. They don't know how to interact with people. So you can tell they were institutionalized," Fisher said. Reflecting on the situation, Fisher said, "I don't know whether to be sad for her or angry. Because, you know, at one time in her life, she loved these dogs and she put everything towards these dogs. And somewhere along the way, something happened. And unfortunately, the dogs had to pay for it." The Humane Society said it could take time before the dogs are ready for foster homes or adoption. In the meantime, they are asking for community support to help with the recovery efforts. CBS12 News is continuing our coverage for back-to-school week. The Martin County School District is starting the new year on an academic high. The district earned an "A" rating for the second year in a row, while students also achieved the district's highest state assessment scores on record. Martin County is now celebrating back-to-back A’ ratings after spending seven years as a "B"-rated district. Superintendent Michael Maine credits the students, teachers, families and staff -- but says the work isn’t over. Every district-operated school earned at least a "C rating Stuart Middle, Indiantown Middle, and South Fork High all moved from a "B" to an "A" rating Hobe Sound Elementary improved from a "C" to a "B" Students also posted strong gains on state assessments: English language arts proficiency rose from 55% to 59% Math improved from 60% to 63% Geometry jumped nine points to 69%, ranking fourth in the state The district also finished eighth statewide in civics I'm extremely happy and proud of our teachers and all of the hard work that they do in the classroom every day. Our school administrators just continue to push themselves. We are not going to just settle. Our students deserve the very best, and in order to make sure they're getting the very best, we have to keep pushing at an exceptional level, said Superintendent Maine. To keep that momentum going, Maine says the district is focusing extra support on its five "C"-rated schools this year.

We are less than a week away from the August election and we have another story about campaign signs and bad blood and mud-slinging between candidates. Chris "Doc Collins, running for Martin County Commission Seat Two, posted a video to Facebook on a rant about his signs being stolen. In the video he claims the sign thief is in cahoots with a political enemy. Candidates try to increase their name recognition by putting out campaign signs along roads. One candidate for Martin County Commission says some of his campaign signs were missing recently, and he found out who the culprit is who took them. "Many people have been asking me, do you know who this guy is? What time of day?" Collins said in a video posted on Facebook, as he stands in front of a still photo of a man in a darkened area at night holding one of Collins' campaign signs. Chris Collins, formerly the Mayor of Stuart is now running for Martin County Commission Seat Two. He wanted to figure out why some of his campaign signs were disappearing, so he came up with a plan. See also: Third victim dies after South Bay crash that killed woman, two 13-year-old girls "I set up a hunting trail cam to get some receipts and we found out who's been doing it. This is Jim Gallegos at 3:58 in the morning on August 5, while biking down Palm City Road, you'll notice the bike shorts, taking my sign out of the ground," Collins said in the Facebook video. Collins goes on to say, he put Apple Airtags on some of the signs, and was able to pinpoint their location. He says they were at man named Jim Gallegos' house. He says Gallegos is a campaign advisor to Merritt Matheson. Matheson is another political candidate, though not in the same race as Collins. "Listen, I don't want to get the cops involved. Guys, bring me the signs back. Let's have a clean election," Collins said in the Facebook video. We met with Jim Gallegos and asked him about the accusations. "What we were doing was taking the signs down that the owner of the property had requested us to remove and that's what we were doing. That's what I was doing at that particular time," Gallegos explained. Merritt Matheson sent CBS12 News a text. He says Gallegos is not his campaign advisor. Nevertheless, the story of signs being stolen prompted a man named Derreck Ogden to confront Gallegos. Ogden is also running for election to be a Stuart City Commissioner. Their argument about the campaign signs was caught on camera. Gallegos, if you want to return the signs I don't think the other slow-growth candidates are gonna press charges. So if you want to ask your campaign, your campaign team to return the signs," Ogden says in a video posted on Facebook. "I never touched one of your signs! And that's an attack on me personally!" Gallegos says in the video posted on Facebook. "While our campaign is following the rules, other campaigns are not and I think it's important that people know that and we're the only ones that hold anybody responsible as the residents. So we have to hold these people to, you know, their feet to the fire," Ogden told CBS12 News. Gallegos says he no longer has the campaign signs. He says he removed about 30 campaign signs for various candidates, not just Chris Collins' campaign, because the property owner did not want the signs on his property.

New details are being released following the arrest of a 62-year-old Martin County woman who had 36 dogs living in severely unsanitary conditions inside her home, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office (MCSO) said. Paige O’Donnell was taken into custody on Monday, following a lengthy investigation into animal welfare concerns at her residence. When deputies executed a search warrant, they discovered dogs covered in feces and urine living in a home with no functioning air conditioning and floors covered in waste and garbage, a probable cause affidavit said. The investigation began after a neighbor contacted WFLX with concerns about the conditions at O’Donnell’s residence and reports that she was housing a large number of animals. Martin County Sheriff’s Office Animal Services said they reviewed call history at the address and identified approximately 20 related incidents spanning from 2020 through 2026, the affidavit said. Animal Control Officer Tabitha Queen documented a pattern of deteriorating conditions at the residence over several years, according to a probable cause affidavit released by MCSO. On July 22, the officer responded to a complaint that more than 20 dogs were inside the home without air conditioning and had not been allowed outside since 2022. “Upon arriving, the officer detected a strong odor consistent with decomposition from the roadway,” according to the arrest report. “She could hear a large number of dogs, including what sounded like puppies, barking from inside the residence.” When deputies arrived on Monday to execute the search warrant, O’Donnell was taking a bath, deputies said. When asked about the conditions of the home and dogs, she said only that she was in the process of cleaning. Deputies said they observed the residence to be in an unlivable and unsanitary condition, with floors throughout the home covered in feces, urine and garbage. The air-conditioning system was inoperable, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office report. Multiple dogs were found inside the residence covered in feces and urine with severely matted fur, investigators said. Deputies noted the condition of the dogs and surrounding environment was such that the animals were difficult to distinguish from the heavily soiled areas of the residence. Portions of the walls appeared to have been chewed or damaged by the dogs. The only water source observed was an automatic water container inside the master bathroom. No clean food dishes were found anywhere in the residence, investigators said. Animal hoarding cases like this highlight ongoing challenges in animal welfare enforcement and the need for community vigilance in reporting suspected neglect. The case also demonstrates how repeated interventions over several years can escalate when underlying issues aren’t addressed. During an August 3 meeting at Jock Leighton Park in Palm City, O’Donnell told the Animal Control Officer she owned only four dogs: Jeep, Jagger, Naughty and True. She presented one dog, “Jeep,” a black-and-white Border Collie whose white fur was heavily stained with what appeared to be urine and feces. However, records from Boulevard Animal Hospital painted a different picture, the affidavit said. A hospital employee who had worked there since 2015 knew O’Donnell as a dog breeder who would bring in numerous puppies over the years in filthy conditions. The clinic’s computer system identified approximately 38 adult dogs associated with O’Donnell, some documented as deceased. The employee said there were so many puppies brought in with O’Donnell that it was impossible to get an accurate count, according to the affidavit. The last recorded visit was June 25, 2022, when two dogs, Jeep and Naughty, were vaccinated for rabies. Neighbors provided investigators with video recordings capturing evidence of the conditions. One neighbor recorded video of O’Donnell’s garage area on August 6, days before the arrest, showing garbage and debris piled nearly to the ceiling of her garage and a large number of dogs barking from within the residence, the affidavit said. Another neighbor told investigators he had not observed any dogs outside the residence or seen garbage placed out for collection since at least 2022, according to the affidavit. He said he continued to notice a strong odor from the residence and had not heard the air-conditioning system operating since approximately 2022. One of the most significant prior incidents occurred April 4, 2020, when Animal Services responded after O’Donnell was placed under the Marchman Act. Deputies said they documented severely unsanitary conditions with approximately 25 dogs on the property that did not have adequate food or water. One dog required humane euthanization due to its deteriorated health, the affidavit said. Following that incident, Animal Services documented that O’Donnell made improvements, rehomed multiple dogs and stated she intended to keep only five dogs going forward, the affidavit said. A similar pattern emerged in June 2022, when Animal Control responded to complaints of 10 to 20 dogs being kept in the backyard covered in feces and flies, the affidavit said. A follow-up inspection found the residence had been cleaned, and O’Donnell voluntarily surrendered three dogs to Farm Dog Rescue. Investigators said they identified several inconsistencies in the number and identities of dogs O’Donnell reported owning across multiple Animal Control contacts between 2022 and 2023, with numbers ranging from five to 10 dogs. Deputies said they concluded that the conditions observed during the search warrant execution indicated the dogs had been maintained in conditions that failed to provide a sanitary and appropriate living environment and subjected them to unnecessary suffering. A judge set O’Donnell’s total bond at $275,000 and ordered that she may not own or possess either temporary or permanent any animals as conditions of her bond, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office said Tuesday. O’Donnell is facing 72 total charges — 36 counts of felony animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts for failing to provide the dogs with proper exercise or air, the sheriff’s office said. A two-hour standoff on the 17th Street Bridge ended safely after Indian River County deputies talked a man wanted for burglary back from the edge. According to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office , deputies were called to the bridge around 1 a.m. Sunday, August 2, after receiving information that a man wanted on a Port St. Lucie Police Department warrant for burglary with battery had contacted his mother and said he wanted to kill himself. Viewer discretion is advised. The following video contains footage involving a person threatening to jump from a bridge. Some viewers may find the content disturbing. Deputies located the man on top of the 17th Street Bridge after he climbed over the railing, down onto a platform and threatened to jump. Deputy Edouard Gast is a member of the Sheriff's Office Crisis Negotiation Team. He and the Assistant Team Commander Sgt. Matt Redstone said they found the man on a small platform about 55 feet above the intracoastal. Tell me what's going on," Deputy Edouard Gast can be heard saying in the body camera video. The man replied, "There's nothing you can help me with." "That's not true," said Gast. The Sheriff's Office Crisis Negotiation Team spent about two hours talking with him while the Marine Unit launched a boat below the bridge on standby. Fire Rescue also staged nearby as a safety precaution. "At the end of the day, jumping off this thing does not help anything," Deputy Gast said in the footage. The man said, "Yeah, I don't have to go to jail. I don't have to think of what happened today."
