"At the end of the day, you're still around to be with your family," Gast said during the negotiation. The man said he was worried about going to jail and the financial burden his family could face. Negotiators continued talking with him, eventually learning that he enjoyed playing video games. As the assistant team commander, Sgt. Matt Redstone said he was helping Gast as he was negotiating. "During Ed's negotiation with him, I was facilitating getting information from our partner agency at the Port St. Lucie Police Department, as well as providing Deputy Gast information," Sgt. "It's just little tips on how to talk to them, and then the information that we're getting from our partner agencies about the active case that they were working." As the conversation continued, deputies told him his mother was heading to the base of the bridge. The man eventually agreed to climb back over the railing. "When I let him know that his mom was here at the bridge and wanted to talk to him, I think in his mind he's like, 'Okay, I'm ready to go,'" said Deputy Gast. "It was just a matter of letting him know that he was loved, his mom and his sister, that he needed to be there for them." "There's light. There's a big, bright future for you," Gast said during the negotiation. Grab that ladder, brother. You got this." Body camera footage shows deputies encouraging him as he grabbed a ladder and climbed back onto the bridge. The man was then taken into custody without incident. The sheriff's office has not released the man's name but said he was not hurt. The Crisis Negotiation Team trains for these types of situations once a month. Deputy Gast has been a negotiator for six years and said that night on Aug. He said he's thankful everyone made it out safely. "For other people that are attempting suicide or want to attempt it, know that there is help out there," Gast said. "It might feel like it's dark and dreary, but there's light at the end of the tunnel." If you or someone you know is struggling with thoughts of suicide, help is available. Call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. You can also visit 988 Lifeline for support and resources.

New details are being released following the arrest of a 62-year-old Martin County woman who had 36 dogs living in severely unsanitary conditions inside her home, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office (MCSO) said. Paige O’Donnell was taken into custody on Monday, following a lengthy investigation into animal welfare concerns at her residence. When deputies executed a search warrant, they discovered dogs covered in feces and urine living in a home with no functioning air conditioning and floors covered in waste and garbage, a probable cause affidavit said. The investigation began after a neighbor contacted WFLX with concerns about the conditions at O’Donnell’s residence and reports that she was housing a large number of animals. Martin County Sheriff’s Office Animal Services said they reviewed call history at the address and identified approximately 20 related incidents spanning from 2020 through 2026, the affidavit said. Animal Control Officer Tabitha Queen documented a pattern of deteriorating conditions at the residence over several years, according to a probable cause affidavit released by MCSO. On July 22, the officer responded to a complaint that more than 20 dogs were inside the home without air conditioning and had not been allowed outside since 2022. “Upon arriving, the officer detected a strong odor consistent with decomposition from the roadway,” according to the arrest report. “She could hear a large number of dogs, including what sounded like puppies, barking from inside the residence.” When deputies arrived on Monday to execute the search warrant, O’Donnell was taking a bath, deputies said. When asked about the conditions of the home and dogs, she said only that she was in the process of cleaning. Deputies said they observed the residence to be in an unlivable and unsanitary condition, with floors throughout the home covered in feces, urine and garbage. The air-conditioning system was inoperable, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office report. Multiple dogs were found inside the residence covered in feces and urine with severely matted fur, investigators said. Deputies noted the condition of the dogs and surrounding environment was such that the animals were difficult to distinguish from the heavily soiled areas of the residence. Portions of the walls appeared to have been chewed or damaged by the dogs. The only water source observed was an automatic water container inside the master bathroom. No clean food dishes were found anywhere in the residence, investigators said. Animal hoarding cases like this highlight ongoing challenges in animal welfare enforcement and the need for community vigilance in reporting suspected neglect. The case also demonstrates how repeated interventions over several years can escalate when underlying issues aren’t addressed. During an August 3 meeting at Jock Leighton Park in Palm City, O’Donnell told the Animal Control Officer she owned only four dogs: Jeep, Jagger, Naughty and True. She presented one dog, “Jeep,” a black-and-white Border Collie whose white fur was heavily stained with what appeared to be urine and feces. However, records from Boulevard Animal Hospital painted a different picture, the affidavit said. A hospital employee who had worked there since 2015 knew O’Donnell as a dog breeder who would bring in numerous puppies over the years in filthy conditions. The clinic’s computer system identified approximately 38 adult dogs associated with O’Donnell, some documented as deceased. The employee said there were so many puppies brought in with O’Donnell that it was impossible to get an accurate count, according to the affidavit. The last recorded visit was June 25, 2022, when two dogs, Jeep and Naughty, were vaccinated for rabies. Neighbors provided investigators with video recordings capturing evidence of the conditions. One neighbor recorded video of O’Donnell’s garage area on August 6, days before the arrest, showing garbage and debris piled nearly to the ceiling of her garage and a large number of dogs barking from within the residence, the affidavit said. Another neighbor told investigators he had not observed any dogs outside the residence or seen garbage placed out for collection since at least 2022, according to the affidavit. He said he continued to notice a strong odor from the residence and had not heard the air-conditioning system operating since approximately 2022. One of the most significant prior incidents occurred April 4, 2020, when Animal Services responded after O’Donnell was placed under the Marchman Act. Deputies said they documented severely unsanitary conditions with approximately 25 dogs on the property that did not have adequate food or water. One dog required humane euthanization due to its deteriorated health, the affidavit said. Following that incident, Animal Services documented that O’Donnell made improvements, rehomed multiple dogs and stated she intended to keep only five dogs going forward, the affidavit said. A similar pattern emerged in June 2022, when Animal Control responded to complaints of 10 to 20 dogs being kept in the backyard covered in feces and flies, the affidavit said. A follow-up inspection found the residence had been cleaned, and O’Donnell voluntarily surrendered three dogs to Farm Dog Rescue. Investigators said they identified several inconsistencies in the number and identities of dogs O’Donnell reported owning across multiple Animal Control contacts between 2022 and 2023, with numbers ranging from five to 10 dogs. Deputies said they concluded that the conditions observed during the search warrant execution indicated the dogs had been maintained in conditions that failed to provide a sanitary and appropriate living environment and subjected them to unnecessary suffering. A judge set O’Donnell’s total bond at $275,000 and ordered that she may not own or possess either temporary or permanent any animals as conditions of her bond, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office said Tuesday. O’Donnell is facing 72 total charges — 36 counts of felony animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts for failing to provide the dogs with proper exercise or air, the sheriff’s office said. Florida homeowners insurance premiums largely depend on two critical roof factors: age and materials, according to local insurance experts who say the roof serves as a home's primary defense against weather damage."We call the roof the first line of defense," said Robert Norberg of Arden Insurance in Lantana.WATCH BELOW: Roof driving up your insurance? Local agent offers these optionsInsurance companies increasingly raise premiums on asphalt shingle roofs older than 15 years, while metal roofs receive favorable treatment for their 30-year-plus lifespan, according to industry professionals."If you have a 20-year-old roof it will wear and tear just like the tires on your car," said Lee Wiglesworth of Wiglesworth-Rindom Insurance in Stuart.Asphalt shingles remain Florida's most popular and economical roofing choice, but their vulnerability to heat and wind makes them less attractive to insurers as they age.Homeowners with shingle roofs over 15 years face shrinking insurance options, Wiglesworth explained."You have those companies that have the most competitive rates where they only want that under 15-year-old shingled roof, so if you're 16, we can still have options but you're starting to eliminate options for yourself," he said.Florida's insurance market has seen new companies enter the state, with more insurers willing to cover older homes. However, finding affordable coverage for aging roofs still requires strategic shopping and understanding available options.For homeowners reluctant to replace aging roofs, scheduled endorsements offer partial protection. Under this arrangement, insurers cover only 25% of an older roof's value while homeowners self-insure the remaining 75%."You still have some coverage there, but they won't give you a brand-new roof; it can be an option for some people absolutely adamant they do not need to replace their roof," Wiglesworth said.Metal roofs cost nearly twice as much as asphalt shingles but offer superior long-term protection and insurance advantages, according to Wiglesworth.His advice for homeowners considering roof replacement: "Call an agent who can shop multiple carriers and say, 'What would it save me if I got a new roof?' even before they get a new roof."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Residents in The Isles community are mounting opposition against a homeowners association plan that could eliminate more than 300 oak trees in Palm Beach Gardens over the next several years, with some neighbors now demanding citywide changes to tree removal approval processes.The HOA-approved infrastructure improvement plan, which received city approval, targets nearly half of the mature oak canopy that residents say defines their neighborhood's character and provides critical environmental benefits.WATCH BELOW: Palm Beach Gardens residents fight oak tree removal planBrian Rickert, a resident of The Isles community, expressed alarm at the potential environmental impact of removing nearly half of the area's oak trees."Just the thought of 47% of these trees being gone, and the sunlight coming in, the loss of shade, the extra heat on the homes," Rickert told WPTV.While residents support necessary infrastructure improvements, Rickert emphasized the community's unified stance on preserving the tree canopy."The community is 100% in favor of fixing the infrastructure. We are not in favor of taking the trees down," Rickert said. Records obtained by WPTV show Palm Beach Gardens city staff asked the HOA to explore tree preservation alternatives before approving the removal plan. The city requested the HOA consider root pruning, root barriers and relocating mature trees where feasible.However, the HOA's consulting team determined that mature oak trees could not be relocated due to site constraints. The replacement plan calls for smaller species including green buttonwood trees.Rickert criticized the proposed replacement species as inadequate compared to the existing mature oaks."The green buttonwood trees are much smaller than the oak trees," Rickert explained. "They give 50 percent less shade than these beautiful, magnificent oaks do."Ron Lamneck, an arborist working with The Isles residents, is now advocating for changes to Palm Beach Gardens municipal codes regarding tree removal approvals."Nothing in the municipal codes requires anyone to show that all mitigation options were considered first," Lamneck said.In nearby Jupiter, residents of The Bluffs community are dealing with the inverse problem of aging, potentially dangerous trees that haven't received proper maintenance.Tom Wickenhauser, a Bluffs resident, warned about hurricane risks from unmaintained trees in his community."If we don't address it, consequences are going to be even more serious," Wickenhauser said.Despite facing different tree-related challenges, residents in both Palm Beach County communities are calling for increased community participation in decision-making processes."All we're asking for is to be heard with our concerns and for the community to be able to vote on it," Rickert said.The controversy highlights broader questions about balancing infrastructure needs with environmental preservation in South Florida's established residential communities, where mature tree canopies provide crucial benefits including storm protection, energy savings and property values.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Two moms whose children struggled to read launched a movement nearly 15 years ago. Now, four schools in Indian River County have reached a 90% reading proficiency goal. WATCH BELOW: 'From third grade on, you're reading to learn,' Rosewood principal Adam Faust tell WPTV's Jon Shiainman Indian River County's schools are drawing national attention for a community-driven literacy program that started with a simple but ambitious goal: get 90% of third graders reading at grade level. The effort is called the Moonshot Moment, born in 2012 through The Learning Alliance, a nonprofit co-founded by parent Liz Remington, whose son struggled with reading. "You are afraid and looking for answers and we really struggled with what is going on and how do we problem solve," Remington said. The nonprofit brings together schools, philanthropists, and business owners to fund added resources, including reading coaches, in elementary classrooms. "It means the community has to come together and be an unstoppable team," Remington said. When I first met Remington in 2017, just 56% of third graders in the district were reading at grade level. Today, four schools have reached the 90% milestone, including Rosewood Magnet School. "From birth to third grade, you're learning to read. From third grade on, you're reading to learn," said Rosewood principal Adam Faust. Faust said the achievement came down to the final day. "We had six kids to test to make the 90%. We needed three to be at proficiency or above, and it turned out five of those kids made it," Faust said. At Osceola Magnet School, principal Jennifer Norris said students will return to a new campus building and a new reading challenge after the school also cleared the 90% threshold. "We're shooting for 95% this year," Norris said. The stakes behind that goal are significant. "If students are reading at grade level by third grade, the data show they are going to be proficient readers for the rest of their life," Norris said. Other school districts across Florida are now looking at adopting the Moonshot Moment model — a continuation of a mission that started with one parent's child and has since helped thousands of students. "Put the systems in place and you build your team and implementing collectively and collaboratively and it's so powerful," Remington said. A driver is in custody after a hit-and-run crash seriously injured a 7-year-old in Fort Pierce earlier this month, police said. A 48-year-old Vero Beach man riding an electric bicycle was killed after being struck by a pickup truck that fled the scene Sunday night in unincorporated Indian River County. According to the Florida Highway Patrol , the crash happened around 8:57 p.m. Sunday at the intersection of 8th Street and 14th Avenue. FHP said the bicyclist was traveling west in the westbound lane of 8th Street and approaching 14th Avenue. A light-colored Ford F-150, believed to be a 2015 to 2020 model, was traveling behind him in the same lane, investigators said. See also: 19-year-old identified as victim in deadly Boynton Beach shooting s the pickup approached the bicyclist, the driver took evasive action, traveling southwest and partially entering the eastbound lane. However, troopers said the truck was unable to avoid the bicyclist and the right side of the pickup struck him. The bicyclist tumbled onto the roadway and came to rest in the eastbound lane of 8th Street. FHP said the driver fled the scene without rendering aid or contacting law enforcement. Investigators said the Ford F-150 is believed to be missing its right-side rearview mirror as a result of the crash. The bicyclist was taken to Lawnwood Hospital, where he was pronounced dead. His identity has not been released pending notification of next of kin. Both eastbound and westbound lanes of 8th Street were blocked while troopers investigated the crash. Anyone with information about the vehicle or driver is asked to contact the Florida Highway Patrol.

"At the end of the day, you're still around to be with your family," one negotiator told him. The man said he was worried about going to jail and the financial burden his family could face. Negotiators continued talking with him, eventually learning that he enjoyed playing video games. As the conversation continued, deputies told him his mother was heading to the base of the bridge. The man eventually agreed to climb back over the railing. There's a big, bright future for you," the negotiator told him. Body camera footage shows deputies encouraging him as he grabbed a ladder and climbed back onto the bridge. The man was then taken into custody without incident. The Border Collie Society of America confirmed Wednesday that Paige O'Donnell, 62, was formerly a member and board member of the organization but had not held membership for many years. Deputies rescued the dogs Monday from conditions so severe that videos show feces piled inches high and dogs so filthy they blended into the garbage surrounding them.WATCH BELOW: 'Worst case we've ever seen': Humane Society caring for 36 rescued dogsThe Palm City hoarding case highlights ongoing challenges in animal welfare oversight and the importance of community reporting in preventing animal suffering. The case developed after WPTV shared neighbor complaints with the Martin County Sheriff's Office, leading to the largest animal rescue in the county's recent history."The circumstances reported in this case do not reflect the values, principles, or standards of care that BCSA promotes for the Border Collie breed," the Border Collie Society of America stated in a Facebook post Wednesday.The organization unequivocally condemned the neglect and mistreatment, calling the reported conditions "wholly inconsistent with the standard of care every border collie deserves."The 36 Border Collies remain in the care of the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, where staff members are working to assess their medical needs and begin rehabilitation."Right now they're very, very shut down. Some of them aren't even walking. They're just laying on their sides," Sarah Fisher, a spokeswoman for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, told WPTV Investigative Reporter Jamie Ostroff on Tuesday.Veterinary teams are shaving matted fur and examining each dog individually to determine the extent of medical treatment needed, according to Fisher.WATCH BELOW: Dogs rescued after WPTV investigation into suspected animal hoardingAn 11-page arrest affidavit details how O'Donnell repeatedly avoided law enforcement contact after neighbors reported concerns about a large number of dogs at her Palm City home since at least 2020. A WPTV investigation that aired before O'Donnell's arrest documented previous attempts by the sheriff's office to investigate as O'Donnell continued to wall herself off from authorities.When deputies began questioning O'Donnell in July, she exhibited deceptive behavior according to the affidavit. She refused to allow deputies into her home and blamed the stench that lingered across the road on "missed trash collection" and "old seafood."After multiple canceled meetings with investigators, O'Donnell eventually agreed to meet in a park with one dog, claiming she owned only four animals total. That single dog's condition provided enough evidence for deputies to secure a search warrant.The Border Collie Society of America said it has donated $1,000 to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast and is directing donations to its rescue fund through Sept. 11 to the same organization."The financial and volunteer resources required to provide veterinary care, rehabilitation, food, housing, and ongoing support for dogs rescued from circumstances such as these are substantial, and every contribution can make a meaningful difference," the organization stated.The breed organization acknowledged the work of Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies, animal control personnel, veterinarians, and volunteers involved in the rescue operation.The organization used the Palm City case to address the broader dog community about responsible breeding and ownership extending beyond producing puppies to ensuring appropriate care throughout each animal's lifetime."We recognize that challenging situations can arise for any dog owner or breeder, and we encourage anyone who finds themselves unable to adequately care for their dogs to seek help from trusted resources, rescue organizations, veterinarians, the BCSA, or members of the border collie community," the organization stated.The Border Collie Society of America emphasized that no one should feel ashamed to ask for help, noting that reaching out for support can prevent both people and animals from suffering.WATCH BELOW: 'She really has legally walled us off from investigating,' Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek tells Chief Investigative Reporter Jamie OstroffO'Donnell was arrested Monday as deputies executed the search warrant at her Palm City home. According to the arrest affidavit, she was taking a bath when law enforcement arrived to serve the warrant.A judge set O’Donnell’s total bond at $275,000 and ordered that she may not own or possess either temporary or permanent any animals as conditions of her bond, the Martin County Sheriff's Office said Tuesday.She is facing 72 total charges — 36 counts of felony animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts for failing to provide the dogs with proper exercise or air, the sheriff's office said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Proposed change would require no warnings be issued when officers consider the noise ‘so loud, excessive or disruptive that it constitutes a clear and substantial disturbance or breach of the peace.’ FORT PIERCE – For people complaining about neighborhood noise that impedes their sleep, or drivers who feel vibration caused by loud music from other vehicles, Fort Pierce city officials are considering tougher enforcement. According to city statistics, law enforcement responded to nearly 2,000 noise complaint calls in the city between April 1, 2025 and April 30, 2026. And officials say about one in three of those complaints came from the same 14 city locations. Half of all calls currently come in Sundays, between 10 p.m. Now city leaders have proposed ordinance amendments that would expand police enforcement authority, beef up penalties that could include fines of up to $250-$500 per day of violation and allow the city to place unpaid fines as liens against the properties where violations take place. In addition, officials are recommending that parents/guardians be made responsible for the penalties levied against juvenile offenders. District 1 Commissioner Arnold Gaines suggested chronic noise offenders are now using loopholes in the current ordinances that should be closed, giving “more teeth to enforcement.” For example, Gaines said those violators will continue to offend until they get the three warnings from police, then turn down their music. Gaines said violators also may make loud noise in one location where police respond, then move down the street or to another parking lot to continue the obnoxious noise. Police currently issue written “warnings” if violations occur within the same 24 hours at the same location. Proposed change would require no warnings be issued when officers consider the noise “so loud, excessive or disruptive that it constitutes a clear and substantial disturbance or breach of the peace.” In instances not considered severe, the city is proposing penalties when the same individuals are cited during a 48- or 72-hour period at any location in the city. They would get five minutes to comply after the first warning and a citation to appear would be issued if the violation continued another five minutes or if it was a third violation. An arrest would be made for a fourth offense or if another five minutes passed without correcting the current violation. Chronic violations would be defined as three or more verified noise complaints at the same location within 30 days, or six or more within 90 days. If an offender fails to follow a compliance plan or new complaints continue, the incidents could be treated as a public nuisance that’s referred to the city’s Nuisance Abatement Road where daily fines of up to $250-$500 can be ordered. If the fines are not paid, a lien may be placed on the property where the incident occurs and the city can foreclose to collect the lien after three months, affecting the violator and the property owner. Quieter hours would be observed from 10 or 11 p.m. on specified days or seven days a week, depending upon the commission’s final action. Rather than spending an estimated $80,000 to have a sound study conducted to scientifically define “loud” noise, city staff is recommending officers use what a “reasonable person” would consider excessive or audible from a vehicle to an officer at least 25 feet away. “That’s all some of the residents want – more teeth in enforcement,” Gaines said, supporting the recommendations. “If you put citations in their hands, the noise will stop.” An implementation date has not been determined yet. City Clerk Linda Cox said recommended ordinance changes require two public hearings once final ordinance language is drafted. Your comment has been submitted. A driver is in custody after a hit-and-run crash seriously injured a 7-year-old in Fort Pierce earlier this month, police said. The Fort Pierce Police Department said Wednesday that they arrested Demetris Johnson, 34, in a hit-and-run that occurred on Aug. 1 at the intersection of North 25th Street and Avenue M.Investigators said Johnson was located and arrested at 2905 U.S. He faces charges of leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury and driving while license suspended.The crash occurred at approximately 8:55 p.m. at the intersection of North 25th Street and Avenue M. Police said two children were crossing the roadway in a marked crosswalk when Johnson struck one of the children. "Surveillance video obtained from a nearby business captured the crash and shows Johnson exiting his vehicle to check on the children before returning to his vehicle and fleeing the scene," police said in a statement. "Through the diligent work of responding officers and investigators, the suspect vehicle was quickly identified using available investigative technology and law enforcement databases. These resources also assisted officers in identifying Johnson as the driver."The 7-year-old has been released from the hospital and is currently recovering, police said.This investigation remains active and ongoing. Anyone with information on this incident is encouraged to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 800-273-8477.

Residents in The Isles community are mounting opposition against a homeowners association plan that could eliminate more than 300 oak trees in Palm Beach Gardens over the next several years, with some neighbors now demanding citywide changes to tree removal approval processes.The HOA-approved infrastructure improvement plan, which received city approval, targets nearly half of the mature oak canopy that residents say defines their neighborhood's character and provides critical environmental benefits.Brian Rickert, a resident of The Isles community, expressed alarm at the potential environmental impact of removing nearly half of the area's oak trees."Just the thought of 47% of these trees being gone, and the sunlight coming in, the loss of shade, the extra heat on the homes," Rickert told WPTV.While residents support necessary infrastructure improvements, Rickert emphasized the community's unified stance on preserving the tree canopy."The community is 100% in favor of fixing the infrastructure. We are not in favor of taking the trees down," Rickert said. Records obtained by WPTV show Palm Beach Gardens city staff asked the HOA to explore tree preservation alternatives before approving the removal plan. The city requested the HOA consider root pruning, root barriers and relocating mature trees where feasible.However, the HOA's consulting team determined that mature oak trees could not be relocated due to site constraints. The replacement plan calls for smaller species including green buttonwood trees.Rickert criticized the proposed replacement species as inadequate compared to the existing mature oaks."The green buttonwood trees are much smaller than the oak trees," Rickert explained. "They give 50 percent less shade than these beautiful, magnificent oaks do."Ron Lamneck, an arborist working with The Isles residents, is now advocating for changes to Palm Beach Gardens municipal codes regarding tree removal approvals."Nothing in the municipal codes requires anyone to show that all mitigation options were considered first," Lamneck said.In nearby Jupiter, residents of The Bluffs community are dealing with the inverse problem of aging, potentially dangerous trees that haven't received proper maintenance.Tom Wickenhauser, a Bluffs resident, warned about hurricane risks from unmaintained trees in his community."If we don't address it, consequences are going to be even more serious," Wickenhauser said.Despite facing different tree-related challenges, residents in both Palm Beach County communities are calling for increased community participation in decision-making processes."All we're asking for is to be heard with our concerns and for the community to be able to vote on it," Rickert said.The controversy highlights broader questions about balancing infrastructure needs with environmental preservation in South Florida's established residential communities, where mature tree canopies provide crucial benefits including storm protection, energy savings and property values.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. hero.headline: Indian River County schools earn 'A' rating for fourth straight year
hero.body:
The School District of Indian River County received an A rating for the fourth consecutive year, state education officials announced. All but one school in the district earned an A rating. Dodgertown Elementary School received the only B rating in the district.

District Superintendent Dr. David Moore said the district maintains its A grade by investing in teachers and staff who have helped improve the district over the past six years. Moore said school leaders identify pain points and allocate resources and funding to address those issues and prevent the district from falling in the ratings.

The district is ranked in nine out of 12 accountability components, demonstrating exceptional performance in educating students from the time they begin their education through graduation day. Moore said those efforts are reflected in the number of parents choosing to keep their children in the public school system.

For the second straight year, the district will exceed the state's projected enrollment for Indian River County. Moore said the district's willingness to transform the experience over the past six years has led parents to choose public schools in the county.
hero.article_text: For the fourth straight year, the Indian River County School District has been graded an A school district. All but one school in the district received an A rating. The only school to receive a B was Dodgertown Elementary School. District Superintendent Dr. David Moore says no matter which school parents choose for their children in Indian River County, they can expect a quality education. Moore says the district is maintaining its A grade by investing in teachers and staff who have helped improve the district over the past six years. He also says that by identifying pain points, school leaders can allocate resources and funding to address those issues and prevent the district from falling in the ratings. Moore says those efforts are also reflected in the number of parents choosing to keep their children in the public school system. "Because of our willingness for the last 6 years to transform the experience, for the second straight year, we are going to exceed the state’s projected enrollment for our community," Moore told CBS12 News. The School District of Indian River County is also ranked in nine out of 12 accountability components. The district says that demonstrates exceptional performance in educating students from the time they begin their education through graduation day.

hero.headline: Man shot and killed at Fort Pierce mobile home park, ex-girlfriend says 5-year-old son left without father
hero.body:
A 37-year-old man was shot and killed Wednesday night inside a mobile home at the Seminole Mobile Home Park on Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. The shooting happened inside trailer 51 at approximately 9:11 p.m.

The victim reportedly entered the home, where a 22-year-old man, his sister, and his girlfriend were present. The sheriff said the two men, who knew each other, had been arguing over text messages before the incident. The shooter allowed the person to come inside, at which time he was attacked by being pushed and then punched in the stomach multiple times, said Sheriff Richard R. The 22-year-old man then pulled out a gun and shot the victim once.

Naomi Pallarez, the victim's ex-girlfriend who shares a 5-year-old son with him, expressed her heartbreak. "It's not fair because my son has no father now. What am I going to tell him?" Pallarez said. "I am very much heartbroken, and now I am a single mom. We didn't even get to say goodbye, do anything. The father of my child's birthday is Saturday, and he's gone. As of the latest update, no charges have been filed in the case. Detectives with the Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Division and Crime Scene Investigators responded to both the scene and the hospital. Authorities later obtained and executed a search warrant at the residence, where they recovered a firearm believed to have been used in the shooting. Anyone with information about the shooting is asked to contact the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office at 772-462-3230. Anonymous tips can be submitted through Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 800-273-TIPS.

hero.headline: 17 arrested in Martin County cocaine bust; 4 kilos seized in Indiantown trafficking operation
hero.body:
Seventeen people are in custody and three others remain wanted following a months-long narcotics investigation that authorities say dismantled a cocaine trafficking operation centered in Indiantown. Operation Beneath the Surface resulted in the seizure of four kilograms of cocaine, three ounces of methamphetamine, two pounds of marijuana and eight guns, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The defendants collectively face more than 200 felony charges.

The investigation began in late 2025 when narcotics detectives conducting undercover drug buys began dealing with Khalil Thompson and Christopher Wilson. The two appeared to have a steady supply of cocaine, eventually leading detectives to Cecil Trimble of Indiantown, who authorities identified as the alleged leader of the operation. Investigators allege Trimble operated a car detailing business in Indiantown that served as a front for a larger cocaine operation. Trimble was on federal probation at the time of his arrest.

Investigators obtained court-authorized wiretaps involving several of the suspected key players. The investigation showed cocaine was being supplied to dealers in Indiantown, Stuart and Port St. Lucie, while other people were allegedly used as drug mules to transport cocaine to the Daytona Beach area. Antonio Honor was stopped by the Florida Highway Patrol while traveling north on Interstate 95 and was found with a kilogram of cocaine. Chiquita Adamson was also accused of transporting cocaine for the organization.

Investigators executed three residential search warrants during the operation, two in Indiantown and one in Stuart. The four kilograms of cocaine seized represent one of the most significant drug seizures investigators have made in the Booker Park area of Indiantown. Authorities estimated the cocaine was being purchased at the kilogram level for about $20,000 each. Trimble, Thompson, Wilson and Janarie Jones are among the defendants facing racketeering charges. Sheriff John Budensiek said most of the cases are expected to remain at the state level, although some charges could be pursued federally.
hero.article_text: Seventeen people are in custody and three others remain wanted following a months-long narcotics investigation that authorities say dismantled a significant cocaine trafficking operation centered in Indiantown. "We're not going to tolerate that here in Martin County. If we can catch you, we're gonna prosecute you and we're gonna prosecute you legally and we're gonna put you away for as long as we can put you away," said John Budensiek, Martin County Sheriff. The investigation, dubbed Operation Beneath the Surface, resulted in the seizure of four kilograms of cocaine, three ounces of methamphetamine, two pounds of marijuana and eight guns, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. Authorities said the defendants collectively face more than 200 felony charges. Sheriff’s officials said the investigation began in late 2025, when narcotics detectives conducting undercover drug buys began dealing with Khalil Thompson and Christopher Wilson. Investigators said the two appeared to have a steady supply of cocaine, eventually leading detectives to Cecil Trimble of Indiantown, who authorities identified as the alleged leader of the operation. Investigators allege Trimble operated a car detailing business in Indiantown that served as a front for a much larger cocaine operation. The business inspired the name Operation Beneath the Surface, authorities said. According to the sheriff’s office, investigators obtained court-authorized wiretaps involving several of the suspected key players. Authorities said the investigation showed cocaine was being supplied to dealers in Indiantown, Stuart and Port St. Lucie, while other people were allegedly used as drug mules to transport cocaine to the Daytona Beach area. In one case, authorities said Antonio Honor was stopped by the Florida Highway Patrol while traveling north on Interstate 95 and was found with a kilogram of cocaine. Another woman, Chiquita Adamson, was also accused of transporting cocaine for the organization, though authorities said she was not caught with the drugs in her possession. Officials said Trimble also used women he was involved with to help facilitate parts of the operation. His live-in girlfriend allegedly assisted with some drug transactions, while Adamson was described as one of the people used to transport drugs. Authorities said other women connected to Trimble had not been arrested as of Friday. The sheriff’s office said the four kilograms of cocaine seized represent one of the most significant drug seizures investigators have made in the Booker Park area of Indiantown. Authorities estimated the cocaine was being purchased at the kilogram level for about $20,000 each, while its potential street value could be substantially higher once divided for individual sales. "It's a huge deal for us and it will send reverberating effects in the Booker Park area. We've got a lot of good citizens that live out there in Booker Park. They don't want this going on in their community. Especially at this level," Sheriff Budensiek said. Aubrey Gilchrist, a retired park maintenance worker originally from Jamaica, says he has lived in Booker Park for about 50 years. He says the drug trade hurts the area. Because they walk the street, they don't like to work," Gilchrist said. Investigators executed three residential search warrants two in Indiantown and one in Stuart as part of the operation. Drugs were also seized during traffic stops and undercover purchases. See also: Family remembers teen, pushes for safety changes after fatal fall at abandoned condo Authorities said Trimble, Thompson, Wilson and Janarie Jones are among the defendants facing racketeering charges. Trimble was also on federal probation at the time of his arrest, according to the sheriff’s office. Sheriff’s officials said most of the cases are expected to remain at the state level, although some charges could be pursued federally. As of Friday, 17 defendants had been arrested and three remained at large. Authorities said the remaining suspects know they are being sought and urged them to turn themselves in. The sheriff’s office said investigators are still working to determine the original source of the cocaine. At least one shipment allegedly came through the mail from another state, while investigators believe some of the drugs may have originated in South Florida. Sheriff Budensiek says illegal drugs can cause significant harm to users. "We see, and I hate to say it like this, you almost see walking dead people that are out there on the streets. They sell their bodies, their souls, literally their bodies, their minds or souls, sometimes their families, just to get high. You went through the 80's and '90s, and the crack cocaine nightmares that we had and this is starting to come back, and we're trying to get ahead of that happening again," he explained.

hero.teaser: Paige Anne ODonnell faces 36 felony counts after deputies and animal services officers found 36 Border Collies living in deplorable conditions at her Southwest Alligator Street home in Palm City.
hero.body:
Paige Anne ODonnell, 62, of the 1200 block of Southwest Alligator Street in Palm City, remains in the Martin County Jail on a $275,000 bond after being arrested August 10 following the rescue of 36 Border Collies from her home. Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies and Animal Services Unit employees confiscated the dogs from what Sheriff John Budensiek said were deplorable conditions. ODonnell faces 36 third-degree felony counts of torture involving pain, serious physical injury or death, and 36 first-degree misdemeanor counts of keeping animals in an enclosure without exercise and air.

The conditions inside the home were so deplorable that deputies and Animal Services officers had to wear Tyvek protective clothing while working. Feces, urine-soaked materials, boxes and debris throughout the residence made the process of locating and safely removing the animals extremely challenging. The home is near Southwest Mapp Road and south of Southwest Martin Highway. An inoperable air-conditioning system demonstrated that the animals had been maintained in conditions that subjected them to unnecessary suffering, according to an arrest affidavit.

During her first appearance in court on August 11, a judge set the bail and ordered that ODonnell may not own or possess, either temporarily or permanently, any animals as a condition of the bond. Throughout the investigation, which actually began in 2020, ODonnell claimed she had no more than five dogs inside the home. All the animals were turned over to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast in Palm City where they are being evaluated, cleaned, treated and cared for.

During her first appearance in court on Aug. 11, a judge set the bail and ordered that O’Donnell may not own or possess, either temporarily or permanently, any animals as a condition of the bond, the sheriff’s office wrote in a Facebook posting. Inside was a much different story,” the sheriff’s office wrote in the Facebook posting. “The conditions were so deplorable that deputies and Animal Services officers had to wear Tyvek protective clothing while working inside the home. However, once the sheriff’s office was able to obtain a search warrant, officers discovered the 36 Border Collies inside the house “under conditions that failed to provide a sanitary and appropriate living environment and restricted their ability to obtain appropriate exercise and adequate environmental conditions,” according to an arrest affidavit. In addition, an “inoperable air-conditioning system demonstrated that the animals had been maintained in conditions that subjected them to unnecessary suffering,” according to the arrest affidavit. cards.headline: 17 arrested in Martin County cocaine trafficking bust, 4 kilos seized in Indiantown operation
cards.body:
A months-long investigation dubbed Operation Beneath the Surface resulted in the arrest of 17 people and the seizure of four kilograms of cocaine, marking one of the most significant drug busts in the Booker Park area of Indiantown in Martin County's history. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek announced the results of the multi-agency operation at a press conference Friday, flanked by federal partners from the FBI, DEA, and Homeland Security Investigations.

The investigation targeted a cocaine trafficking organization led by Cecil Trimble, a career criminal who was operating under the guise of a car detailing business in Indiantown. Trimble, who was on federal probation for a previous cocaine trafficking conviction, was supplying cocaine throughout Martin County and beyond, including dealers in Stuart, Port St. Lucie, and using mules to transport drugs to Daytona Beach. The investigation began when Martin County Sheriff's Office narcotics detectives started working with informants and conducting undercover purchases, initially focusing on two younger suspects, Khalil Thompson and Christopher Wilson, who appeared to have an unlimited supply of cocaine.

Authorities seized four kilograms of cocaine, three ounces of methamphetamine, two pounds of marijuana, and eight firearms. The street value of the seized drugs ranges from $100,000 to $200,000, according to investigators. During the investigation, authorities intercepted Antonio Honor on I-95 with assistance from the Florida Highway Patrol, seizing one kilogram of cocaine. Another suspect, Chiquita Adamson, was identified as a mule transporting cocaine to the Daytona Beach area. The investigation included the execution of three search warrants, two in Indiantown and one in Stuart.

The 20 defendants face more than 200 felony charges combined, with 16 of the suspects having previous criminal histories involving cocaine sales, possession, or trafficking. The top four defendants, Trimble, Thompson, Wilson, and Janarie Jones, are facing racketeering charges. Seventeen suspects are currently in custody, while authorities are still searching for three additional suspects. Budensiek emphasized the impact on the Booker Park community, stating that residents don't want this going on in their community, especially at this level.

hero.headline: Sheriff's deputies recover firearm in fatal Fort Pierce mobile home park shooting
hero.teaser: St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies recovered a firearm believed to have been used in a fatal shooting at the Seminole Mobile Home Park in Fort Pierce.
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is investigating a fatal shooting that happened at about 9:11 p.m. on Aug. 12 at the Seminole Mobile Home Park in the 3300 block of Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce. A caller reported that an individual was shot while allegedly attempting to enter a home. Upon arrival, deputies found a person suffering from a gunshot wound. The victim was transported to a local hospital and was later pronounced deceased.

Detectives with the Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Division and Crime Scene Investigators responded to the scene and the hospital as part of the investigation. Detectives subsequently obtained and executed a search warrant at the residence, resulting in the recovery of the firearm believed to have been used in the shooting. Detectives and crime scene investigators completed their work at the scene and cleared the home at about 6:11 a.m. on Aug. 13.

Investigators believe this to be an isolated incident and there is no known immediate threat to the surrounding community. Anyone with information regarding this incident is asked to call the Sheriff's Office at 772-462-3230. Anonymous tips can also be submitted through Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 800-273-TIPS.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce shooting leaves 5-year-old without father as investigation continues
cards.teaser: A 37-year-old man was shot and killed Wednesday night inside a mobile home at the Seminole Mobile Home Park on Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce.
cards.body:
A 37-year-old man was shot and killed Wednesday night inside a mobile home at the Seminole Mobile Home Park on Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. The shooting happened inside trailer 51, where the victim reportedly entered the home where a 22-year-old man, his sister, and his girlfriend were present. The sheriff said the two men, who knew each other, had been arguing over text messages before the incident.

Sheriff Richard R. said the shooter allowed the person to come inside, at which time he was attacked by being pushed and then punched in the stomach multiple times. The sheriff said the 22-year-old man then pulled out a gun and shot the victim once. Naomi Pallarez, the victim's ex-girlfriend, said the two share a 5-year-old son. She said the victim's birthday is Saturday. As of Friday, no charges have been filed in the case.

cards.headline: Uber passenger accused of beating driver, stealing Tesla in Fort Pierce carjacking
cards.body:
A 25-year-old man is accused of beating an Uber driver and stealing the car in Fort Pierce, police said. On Wednesday, officers responded to the area of South 25th Street and Virginia Avenue regarding a reported carjacking involving an Uber driver. The investigation revealed that the passenger allegedly struck the driver multiple times, causing him to exit the vehicle. The suspect then took the Tesla Model Y.

An officer quickly located the stolen vehicle traveling on Virginia Avenue and attempted a traffic stop. The driver initially failed to stop but was taken into custody a short time later after the vehicle came to a stop on Oleander Boulevard.

The suspect, identified as Daniel Presume, was arrested and faces charges of carjacking, battery, fleeing and eluding, and grand theft. Presume was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail and was being held on $55,000 bond.

Fort Pierce police continue to investigate the incident.

hero.headline: 17 arrested in Indiantown cocaine trafficking bust, 3 still wanted after Operation Beneath the Surface
hero.body:
Seventeen people are in custody and three others remain wanted following a months-long narcotics investigation that authorities say dismantled a significant cocaine trafficking operation centered in Indiantown. The investigation, dubbed Operation Beneath the Surface, resulted in the seizure of four kilograms of cocaine, three ounces of methamphetamine, two pounds of marijuana and eight guns. The defendants collectively face more than 200 felony charges.

The investigation began in late 2025, when narcotics detectives conducting undercover drug buys began dealing with Khalil Thompson and Christopher Wilson. The two appeared to have a steady supply of cocaine, eventually leading detectives to Cecil Trimble of Indiantown, who authorities identified as the alleged leader of the operation. Investigators allege Trimble operated a car detailing business in Indiantown that served as a front for a much larger cocaine operation. Trimble was on federal probation at the time of his arrest.

Authorities obtained court-authorized wiretaps involving several of the suspected key players. The investigation showed cocaine was being supplied to dealers in Indiantown, Stuart and Port St. Lucie, while other people were allegedly used as drug mules to transport cocaine to the Daytona Beach area. Antonio Honor was stopped by the Florida Highway Patrol while traveling north on Interstate 95 and was found with a kilogram of cocaine. Another woman, Chiquita Adamson, was also accused of transporting cocaine for the organization.

Investigators executed three residential search warrants, two in Indiantown and one in Stuart. The four kilograms of cocaine seized represent one of the most significant drug seizures investigators have made in the Booker Park area of Indiantown. Authorities estimated the cocaine was being purchased at the kilogram level for about $20,000 each. Trimble, Thompson, Wilson and Janarie Jones are among the defendants facing racketeering charges. Sheriff John Budensiek said most of the cases are expected to remain at the state level, although some charges could be pursued federally.

"We're not going to tolerate that here in Martin County. If we can catch you, we're gonna prosecute you and we're gonna prosecute you legally and we're gonna put you away for as long as we can put you away," said John Budensiek, Martin County Sheriff. The investigation, dubbed Operation Beneath the Surface, resulted in the seizure of four kilograms of cocaine, three ounces of methamphetamine, two pounds of marijuana and eight guns, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. Authorities said the defendants collectively face more than 200 felony charges. Sheriff’s officials said the investigation began in late 2025, when narcotics detectives conducting undercover drug buys began dealing with Khalil Thompson and Christopher Wilson. Investigators said the two appeared to have a steady supply of cocaine, eventually leading detectives to Cecil Trimble of Indiantown, who authorities identified as the alleged leader of the operation. Investigators allege Trimble operated a car detailing business in Indiantown that served as a front for a much larger cocaine operation. The business inspired the name Operation Beneath the Surface, authorities said. According to the sheriff’s office, investigators obtained court-authorized wiretaps involving several of the suspected key players. Authorities said the investigation showed cocaine was being supplied to dealers in Indiantown, Stuart and Port St. Lucie, while other people were allegedly used as drug mules to transport cocaine to the Daytona Beach area. In one case, authorities said Antonio Honor was stopped by the Florida Highway Patrol while traveling north on Interstate 95 and was found with a kilogram of cocaine. Another woman, Chiquita Adamson, was also accused of transporting cocaine for the organization, though authorities said she was not caught with the drugs in her possession. Officials said Trimble also used women he was involved with to help facilitate parts of the operation. His live-in girlfriend allegedly assisted with some drug transactions, while Adamson was described as one of the people used to transport drugs. Authorities said other women connected to Trimble had not been arrested as of Friday. The sheriff’s office said the four kilograms of cocaine seized represent one of the most significant drug seizures investigators have made in the Booker Park area of Indiantown. Authorities estimated the cocaine was being purchased at the kilogram level for about $20,000 each, while its potential street value could be substantially higher once divided for individual sales. "It's a huge deal for us and it will send reverberating effects in the Booker Park area. We've got a lot of good citizens that live out there in Booker Park. They don't want this going on in their community. Especially at this level," Sheriff Budensiek said. Aubrey Gilchrist, a retired park maintenance worker originally from Jamaica, says he has lived in Booker Park for about 50 years. He says the drug trade hurts the area. Because they walk the street, they don't like to work," Gilchrist said. Investigators executed three residential search warrants two in Indiantown and one in Stuart as part of the operation. Drugs were also seized during traffic stops and undercover purchases. Trimble was also on federal probation at the time of his arrest, according to the sheriff’s office. Sheriff’s officials said most of the cases are expected to remain at the state level, although some charges could be pursued federally. As of Friday, 17 defendants had been arrested and three remained at large. Authorities said the remaining suspects know they are being sought and urged them to turn themselves in. The sheriff’s office said investigators are still working to determine the original source of the cocaine. At least one shipment allegedly came through the mail from another state, while investigators believe some of the drugs may have originated in South Florida. Sheriff Budensiek says illegal drugs can cause significant harm to users. "We see, and I hate to say it like this, you almost see walking dead people that are out there on the streets. They sell their bodies, their souls, literally their bodies, their minds or souls, sometimes their families, just to get high. You went through the 80's and '90s, and the crack cocaine nightmares that we had and this is starting to come back, and we're trying to get ahead of that happening again," he explained.

cards.headline: 36 Border Collies rescued from Palm City hoarding case overwhelm Humane Society
cards.teaser: The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is caring for 36 Border Collies rescued from a Palm City hoarding case that staff describe as the worst animal neglect they have ever seen.
cards.body:
The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is feeling the pressure after 36 Border Collies were rescued from a hoarding case in Palm City this week. Sarah Fisher with the Humane Society said the latest case is the worst animal neglect she has ever seen. Teams at the Humane Society are overwhelmed by the amount of care and rehabilitation these Border Collies will need.

Fisher said it will be some time before the dogs are ready for adoption. Once they are ready to find their forever homes, the Humane Society plans to identify families with experience caring for Border Collies. They will also look for families who have plenty of patience, because the dogs will need extensive socialization, training and time to adjust to their new surroundings.

hero.body:

The operation, dubbed Operation Beneath the Surface, focused on the Booker Park area and resulted in more than 200 felony charges against the defendants.

Authorities identified Cecil Trimble as the leader of the trafficking organization, which operated under the guise of a car detailing business in Indiantown. Trimble, who was on federal probation for a previous cocaine trafficking conviction, supplied cocaine to dealers in Stuart, Port St. Lucie, and used couriers to transport drugs to Daytona Beach. The investigation began when narcotics detectives conducted undercover purchases from Khalil Thompson and Christopher Wilson, who led investigators to Trimble.

In addition to the four kilograms of cocaine, authorities seized three ounces of methamphetamine, two pounds of marijuana, and eight firearms. Authorities executed three search warrants, two in Indiantown and one in Stuart. Three additional suspects remain at large. Budensiek said the four kilograms of cocaine represents one of the most significant drug seizures in the Booker Park area. Most cases will be prosecuted at the state level, though Trimble faces additional federal charges for violating his probation.

cards.headline: Palm City woman jailed on $275,000 bond after 36 Border Collies rescued from home
cards.teaser: Paige Anne ODonnell, 62, faces 36 felony counts after Martin County Sheriff's Office and Animal Services Unit removed 36 Border Collies from her home on Southwest Alligator Street in deplorable conditions.
cards.body:
Paige Anne ODonnell, 62, remains in Martin County Jail on $275,000 bond after authorities rescued 36 Border Collies from her Palm City home on August 10. ODonnell faces 36 third-degree felony counts of torture involving pain, serious physical injury or death, and 36 first-degree misdemeanor counts of keeping animals in an enclosure without exercise and air. During her first appearance in court on August 11, a judge set the bail and ordered that ODonnell may not own or possess any animals as a condition of the bond.

Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies and Animal Services Unit employees found the dogs living in deplorable conditions at the home in the 1200 block of Southwest Alligator Street, near Southwest Mapp Road and south of Southwest Martin Highway. Deputies and Animal Services officers had to wear Tyvek protective clothing while working inside the home. Feces, urine-soaked materials, boxes and debris throughout the residence made the process of locating and safely removing the animals extremely challenging. An inoperable air conditioning system subjected the animals to unnecessary suffering.

Sheriff John Budensiek said that from the outside, the home appeared well-maintained, neatly groomed and fenced off. The investigation began in 2020. Throughout the investigation, ODonnell claimed she had no more than five dogs inside the home. All the animals were turned over to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast in Palm City, where they are being evaluated, cleaned, treated and cared for. The Humane Society is asking for public donations toward the care of the 36 dogs.

MARTIN COUNTY – The owner of 36 Border Collies rescued on Aug. 10 from her Palm City home remains in the Martin County Jail on a $275,000 bond, as of Aug. 12, according to the jail web site. Paige Anne O’Donnell, 62, of the 1200 block of Southwest Alligator Street in Palm City, was arrested on Aug. 10 after Martin County Sheriff’s Office deputies and Animal Services Unit employees confiscated the 36 dogs from what Sheriff John Budensiek said were living in “deplorable conditions.” O’Donnell faces 36 third-degree felony counts of torture involving pain, serious physical injury or death; and 36 first-degree misdemeanor counts of keeping animals in an enclosure without exercise and air. During her first appearance in court on Aug. 11, a judge set the bail and ordered that O’Donnell may not own or possess, either temporarily or permanently, any animals as a condition of the bond, the sheriff’s office wrote in a Facebook posting. All the animals were turned over to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast in Palm City where they are being evaluated, cleaned, treated and care for, the sheriff’s office noted in its Facebook posting. Feces, urine-soaked materials, boxes and debris throughout the residence made the process of locating and safely removing the animals extremely challenging.” Throughout the investigation, which actually began in 2020, O’Donnell claimed she had no more than five dogs inside the home, the Sheriff’s Office noted. However, once the sheriff’s office was able to obtain a search warrant, officers discovered the 36 Border Collies inside the house “under conditions that failed to provide a sanitary and appropriate living environment and restricted their ability to obtain appropriate exercise and adequate environmental conditions,” according to an arrest affidavit. In addition, an “inoperable air-conditioning system demonstrated that the animals had been maintained in conditions that subjected them to unnecessary suffering,” according to the arrest affidavit. cards.teaser: Daniel Presume, 25, faces charges of carjacking, battery, fleeing and eluding, and grand theft after police say he beat an Uber driver and stole his Tesla Model Y.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police arrested Daniel Presume, 25, after he allegedly beat an Uber driver and stole the car on Wednesday. Officers responded to the area of South 25th Street and Virginia Avenue regarding a reported carjacking involving an Uber driver. The investigation revealed that the passenger struck the driver multiple times, causing him to exit the vehicle. The suspect then took the Tesla Model Y.

An officer quickly located the stolen vehicle traveling on Virginia Avenue and attempted a traffic stop. The driver initially failed to stop but was taken into custody a short time later after the vehicle came to a stop on Oleander Boulevard. Presume faces charges of carjacking, battery, fleeing and eluding, and grand theft. He was being held in St. Lucie County Jail on $55,000 bond.

hero.headline: Man shot and killed at Seminole Mobile Home Park in Fort Pierce, no charges filed
hero.body:
A 37-year-old man was shot and killed Wednesday night inside a mobile home at the Seminole Mobile Home Park on Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. The shooting happened inside trailer 51 at approximately 9:11 p.m. Deputies with the Sheriff's Office Patrol Operations Bureau and personnel from the St. Lucie County Fire District responded to the 3300 block of Orange Avenue following reports of a shooting.

The victim reportedly entered the home, where a 22-year-old man, his sister, and his girlfriend were present. The Sheriff's Office said the two men, who knew each other, had been arguing over text messages before the incident. Sheriff Richard R. said the shooter allowed the person to come inside, at which time he was attacked by being pushed and then punched in the stomach multiple times. The 22-year-old man then pulled out a gun and shot the victim once.

Naomi Pallarez, the victim's ex-girlfriend who shares a 5-year-old son with him, expressed her heartbreak. "I am very much heartbroken, and now I am a single mom," she said. "We didn't even get to say goodbye, do anything. The father of my child's birthday is Saturday, and he's gone." When deputies arrived, they found the victim suffering from a gunshot wound. The individual was transported to a local hospital, where they were later pronounced dead.

Detectives with the Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Division and Crime Scene Investigators responded to both the scene and the hospital as the investigation unfolded. Authorities later obtained and executed a search warrant at the residence, where they recovered a firearm believed to have been used in the shooting. Detectives and crime scene personnel completed their work and cleared the residence at approximately 6:11 a.m. As of the latest update, no charges have been filed in the case. Authorities believe the incident was isolated and say there is no known immediate threat to the surrounding community.

hero.headline: 17 arrested in Indiantown cocaine trafficking ring after months-long investigation seizes 4 kilos of cocaine
hero.body:
Seventeen people are in custody and three others remain wanted following a months-long narcotics investigation that authorities say dismantled a significant cocaine trafficking operation centered in Indiantown. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek announced the results of Operation Beneath the Surface at a press conference Friday, describing the seizure of four kilograms of cocaine as one of the most significant drug busts in the Booker Park area of Indiantown in Martin County history. The investigation also seized three ounces of methamphetamine, two pounds of marijuana, and eight firearms. The defendants collectively face more than 200 felony charges.

The investigation began in late 2025 when narcotics detectives conducting undercover drug buys began dealing with Khalil Thompson and Christopher Wilson. Investigators said the two appeared to have a steady supply of cocaine, eventually leading detectives to Cecil Trimble of Indiantown, who authorities identified as the alleged leader of the operation. Trimble, who was on federal probation for a previous cocaine trafficking conviction, operated a car detailing business in Indiantown that authorities said served as a front for the cocaine operation. The business inspired the name Operation Beneath the Surface.

Investigators obtained court-authorized wiretaps involving Trimble, Thompson, Wilson, and Janarie Jones. The wiretaps revealed that Trimble was supplying cocaine to dealers in Indiantown, Stuart and Port St. Lucie, while other people were allegedly used as drug mules to transport cocaine to the Daytona Beach area. Antonio Honor was stopped by the Florida Highway Patrol while traveling north on Interstate 95 and was found with a kilogram of cocaine. Chiquita Adamson was also accused of transporting cocaine for the organization. Authorities estimated the cocaine was being purchased at the kilogram level for about $20,000 each, while its potential street value could range from $100,000 to $200,000.

Investigators executed three residential search warrants, two in Indiantown and one in Stuart, as part of the operation. Trimble, Thompson, Wilson and Jones are among the defendants facing racketeering charges. Most of the cases are expected to remain at the state level, although some charges could be pursued federally. The operation involved collaboration between the Martin County Sheriff's Office and federal agencies including the FBI, DEA, and Homeland Security Investigations. Authorities said the remaining three suspects know they are being sought and urged them to turn themselves in.

cards.headline: New nonprofit in Indiantown targets youth sports funding and facility upgrades
cards.teaser: The Youth Athletics Foundation of Indiantown will seek private local business investment to support youth athletics programs and upgrade aging facilities like Big Mound Park.
cards.body:
The Economic Council of Indiantown launched the Youth Athletics Foundation of Indiantown at a Thursday night meeting. The new nonprofit aims to raise money from local businesses to fund new and existing youth sports programs, as well as upgrades to aging facilities.

Deborah Resos, Director of Parks and Recreation for Indiantown, described challenges at Big Mound Park, including an 80-yard football field that falls short of the official 100-yard requirement. Resos also noted rusted fences and compacted turf. Scott Watson, who has worked with youth sports in Indiantown for decades, said sports like football require significant financial support for equipment, organization, insurance and standard operating procedures.

With the 800-acre Terra Lago community under construction and more families expected to move to Indiantown, Watson said the demand for space will only grow. Watson said the community needs more fields and better quality facilities as time goes on.

cards.headline: Humane Society of the Treasure Coast strained after rescuing 36 Border Collies from Palm City hoarding case
cards.teaser: Sarah Fisher with the Humane Society says the Palm City case is the worst animal neglect she has ever seen, with teams overwhelmed by the amount of care and rehabilitation the dogs will need.
cards.body:
The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is feeling the pressure after 36 Border Collies were rescued from a hoarding case in Palm City this week. Sarah Fisher with the Humane Society told CBS12 News the latest case is the worst animal neglect she has ever seen. Teams at the Humane Society are overwhelmed by the amount of care and rehabilitation the Border Collies will need, but are prepared to provide the dogs with the medical care, attention and support they desperately need.

Fisher says it will be some time before the dogs are ready for adoption. hero.headline: New nonprofit in Indiantown launches to fund youth sports programs and upgrade aging facilities
hero.body:
The Economic Council of Indiantown launched the Youth Athletics Foundation of Indiantown at a Thursday night meeting to raise money from local businesses for youth sports programs and facility improvements. The nonprofit aims to fund new and existing youth sports programs and upgrade aging facilities across the community.

Deborah Resos, Director of Parks and Recreation for Indiantown, said Big Mound Park faces several challenges. The football field measures only 80 yards instead of the official 100 yards required. The facilities also suffer from rusted fences and compacted turf. Resos said the fields are safe to play on but are old and compacted.

Scott Watson, who has worked with youth sports in Indiantown for decades, said current programming falls short of community needs. Watson said football requires significant financial support including new equipment, organization, insurance, and standard operating procedures. The 800-acre Terra Lago community is under construction and expected to bring more families to Indiantown.

Watson said the demand for fields will grow as the community expands. He said more fields and better quality facilities will be needed as time goes on. Watson said reaching young people early is central to the effort, stating that the hearts and minds of kids must be captured before they turn 15 years old.

hero.headline: 17 arrested in Indiantown cocaine trafficking operation, 4 kilos of cocaine seized in Martin County
hero.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office arrested 17 people and seized four kilograms of cocaine in a months-long investigation that targeted a cocaine trafficking organization operating in the Booker Park area of Indiantown. Sheriff John Budensiek announced the results of Operation Beneath the Surface at a press conference, describing the four kilograms as one of the most significant drug seizures investigators have made in the Booker Park area in Martin County history.

The investigation targeted Cecil Trimble, who ran a car detailing business in Indiantown that served as a front for the cocaine operation. Martin County Sheriff's Office narcotics detectives initially focused on Khalil Thompson and Christopher Wilson, who appeared to have an unlimited supply of cocaine. The investigation led detectives to Trimble, who was on federal probation for a previous cocaine trafficking conviction. Investigators obtained court-ordered wiretaps on Trimble, Thompson, Wilson, and Janarie Jones that revealed Trimble was supplying cocaine to dealers in Stuart, Port St. Lucie, and using mules to transport drugs to Daytona Beach.

Authorities intercepted Antonio Honor on I-95 with assistance from the Florida Highway Patrol and seized one kilogram of cocaine. Chiquita Adamson was identified as a mule transporting cocaine to the Daytona Beach area. In addition to the four kilograms of cocaine, authorities seized three ounces of methamphetamine, two pounds of marijuana, and eight firearms. The street value of the seized drugs ranges from $100,000 to $200,000. The 20 defendants face more than 200 felony charges combined, with 16 of the suspects having previous criminal histories involving cocaine sales, possession, or trafficking.

The top four defendants, Trimble, Thompson, Wilson, and Jones, are facing racketeering charges. Investigators executed three search warrants, two in Indiantown and one in Stuart. The operation involved collaboration between the Martin County Sheriff's Office and federal agencies including the FBI, DEA, and Homeland Security Investigations. Most cases will be prosecuted at the state level, though Trimble faces additional federal charges for violating his probation. Authorities are still searching for three additional suspects.

hero.headline: Man shot and killed at Fort Pierce mobile home park after argument over texts
hero.body:
A 37-year-old man was shot and killed Wednesday night inside a mobile home at the Seminole Mobile Home Park on Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. The shooting happened inside trailer 51 at approximately 9:11 p.m. The victim reportedly entered the home, where a 22-year-old man, his sister, and his girlfriend were present.

Sheriff Richard R said the two men, who knew each other, had been arguing over text messages before the incident. The shooter allowed the person to come inside, at which time he was attacked by being pushed and then punched in the stomach multiple times, according to the sheriff. The 22-year-old man then pulled out a gun and shot the victim once. When deputies arrived, they found the victim suffering from a gunshot wound. The individual was transported to a local hospital, where he was later pronounced dead.

Naomi Pallarez, the victim's ex-girlfriend, said she shares a 5-year-old son with him. Its not fair because my son has no father now. What am I going to tell him? said Pallarez. I am very much heartbroken, and now I am a single mom. We didnt even get to say goodbye, do anything. The father of my childs birthday is Saturday, and hes gone.

Detectives with the Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Division and Crime Scene Investigators responded to both the scene and the hospital. Authorities obtained and executed a search warrant at the residence, where they recovered a firearm believed to have been used in the shooting. Detectives and crime scene personnel completed their work and cleared the residence at approximately 6:11 a.m. As of the latest update, no charges have been filed in the case. Anyone with information about the shooting is asked to contact the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office at 772-462-3230. Anonymous tips can be submitted through Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 800-273-TIPS (8477).
