hero.headline: Fort Pierce proposes fines up to $500 per day for chronic noise violators
hero.body:
Fort Pierce city officials are considering tougher noise enforcement that would allow fines of $250 to $500 per day for chronic violators and let the city place liens on properties where violations occur. Law enforcement responded to nearly 2,000 noise complaint calls in Fort Pierce between April 1, 2025 and April 30, 2026, with about one in three complaints coming from the same 14 city locations. Half of all calls currently come in Sundays between 10 p.m. and morning hours.

The proposed ordinance amendments would expand police enforcement authority and allow officers to issue citations without warnings when noise is so loud, excessive or disruptive that it constitutes a clear and substantial disturbance or breach of the peace. District 1 Commissioner Arnold Gaines said chronic noise offenders are using loopholes in current ordinances by continuing to offend until they receive three warnings from police, then turning down their music. Proposed changes would define chronic violations as three or more verified noise complaints at the same location within 30 days, or six or more within 90 days.

Under the proposal, officers would give violators five minutes to comply after the first warning. A citation to appear would be issued if the violation continued another five minutes or if it was a third violation. An arrest would be made for a fourth offense or if another five minutes passed without correcting the current violation. Parents and guardians would be made responsible for penalties levied against juvenile offenders.

If an offender fails to follow a compliance plan or new complaints continue, incidents could be treated as a public nuisance referred to the city's Nuisance Abatement Board where daily fines of up to $250 to $500 can be ordered. If fines are not paid, a lien may be placed on the property where the incident occurs and the city can foreclose to collect the lien after three months. City Clerk Linda Cox said recommended ordinance changes require two public hearings once final ordinance language is drafted.
hero.article_text: Proposed change would require no warnings be issued when officers consider the noise ‘so loud, excessive or disruptive that it constitutes a clear and substantial disturbance or breach of the peace.’ FORT PIERCE – For people complaining about neighborhood noise that impedes their sleep, or drivers who feel vibration caused by loud music from other vehicles, Fort Pierce city officials are considering tougher enforcement. According to city statistics, law enforcement responded to nearly 2,000 noise complaint calls in the city between April 1, 2025 and April 30, 2026. And officials say about one in three of those complaints came from the same 14 city locations. Half of all calls currently come in Sundays, between 10 p.m. Now city leaders have proposed ordinance amendments that would expand police enforcement authority, beef up penalties that could include fines of up to $250-$500 per day of violation and allow the city to place unpaid fines as liens against the properties where violations take place. In addition, officials are recommending that parents/guardians be made responsible for the penalties levied against juvenile offenders. District 1 Commissioner Arnold Gaines suggested chronic noise offenders are now using loopholes in the current ordinances that should be closed, giving “more teeth to enforcement.” For example, Gaines said those violators will continue to offend until they get the three warnings from police, then turn down their music. Gaines said violators also may make loud noise in one location where police respond, then move down the street or to another parking lot to continue the obnoxious noise. Police currently issue written “warnings” if violations occur within the same 24 hours at the same location. Proposed change would require no warnings be issued when officers consider the noise “so loud, excessive or disruptive that it constitutes a clear and substantial disturbance or breach of the peace.” In instances not considered severe, the city is proposing penalties when the same individuals are cited during a 48- or 72-hour period at any location in the city. They would get five minutes to comply after the first warning and a citation to appear would be issued if the violation continued another five minutes or if it was a third violation. An arrest would be made for a fourth offense or if another five minutes passed without correcting the current violation. Chronic violations would be defined as three or more verified noise complaints at the same location within 30 days, or six or more within 90 days. If an offender fails to follow a compliance plan or new complaints continue, the incidents could be treated as a public nuisance that’s referred to the city’s Nuisance Abatement Road where daily fines of up to $250-$500 can be ordered. If the fines are not paid, a lien may be placed on the property where the incident occurs and the city can foreclose to collect the lien after three months, affecting the violator and the property owner. Quieter hours would be observed from 10 or 11 p.m. on specified days or seven days a week, depending upon the commission’s final action. Rather than spending an estimated $80,000 to have a sound study conducted to scientifically define “loud” noise, city staff is recommending officers use what a “reasonable person” would consider excessive or audible from a vehicle to an officer at least 25 feet away. “That’s all some of the residents want – more teeth in enforcement,” Gaines said, supporting the recommendations. “If you put citations in their hands, the noise will stop.” An implementation date has not been determined yet. City Clerk Linda Cox said recommended ordinance changes require two public hearings once final ordinance language is drafted. Your comment has been submitted. hero.headline: Indian River County School District earns 'A' rating for fourth consecutive year
hero.body:
The Indian River County School District received an A grade for the fourth straight year, with all but one school in the district earning an A rating. Dodgertown Elementary School was the only school to receive a B rating.

District Superintendent Dr. David Moore said parents can expect a quality education no matter which school they choose in Indian River County. The district maintains its A grade by investing in teachers and staff who have helped improve the district over the past six years. School leaders identify pain points and allocate resources and funding to address those issues and prevent the district from falling in the ratings.

Moore said those efforts are reflected in the number of parents choosing to keep their children in the public school system. The district exceeded the state's projected enrollment for the community for the second straight year due to its willingness to transform the student experience over the last six years.

The School District of Indian River County is ranked in nine out of 12 accountability components. The district says that demonstrates exceptional performance in educating students from the time they begin their education through graduation day.
hero.article_text: For the fourth straight year, the Indian River County School District has been graded an A school district. All but one school in the district received an A rating. The only school to receive a B was Dodgertown Elementary School. District Superintendent Dr. David Moore says no matter which school parents choose for their children in Indian River County, they can expect a quality education. Moore says the district is maintaining its A grade by investing in teachers and staff who have helped improve the district over the past six years. He also says that by identifying pain points, school leaders can allocate resources and funding to address those issues and prevent the district from falling in the ratings. Moore says those efforts are also reflected in the number of parents choosing to keep their children in the public school system. "Because of our willingness for the last 6 years to transform the experience, for the second straight year, we are going to exceed the state’s projected enrollment for our community," Moore told CBS12 News. The School District of Indian River County is also ranked in nine out of 12 accountability components. The district says that demonstrates exceptional performance in educating students from the time they begin their education through graduation day.

cards.headline: Indian River County deputies end standoff on 17th Street Bridge in Vero Beach
cards.teaser: A two-hour standoff on the 17th Street Bridge ended safely after Indian River County deputies talked a man wanted for burglary back from the edge.
cards.body:
Indian River County sheriff's deputies successfully ended a two-hour standoff on the 17th Street Bridge in Vero Beach on Sunday, August 2, after talking a man wanted for burglary back from the edge. Deputies were called to the bridge after receiving information that a man wanted on a Port St. Lucie Police Department warrant for burglary with battery had contacted his mother and made concerning statements.

Deputies located the man on top of the 17th Street Bridge after he climbed over the railing and threatened to jump. The Sheriff's Office Crisis Negotiation Team spent about two hours talking with him while the Marine Unit launched a boat below the bridge. Fire Rescue also staged nearby as a safety precaution.

Body camera footage shows negotiators working to keep the man talking and convince him to come back over the railing. The man said he was worried about going to jail and the financial burden his family could face. Negotiators continued talking with him, eventually learning that he enjoyed playing video games. The man eventually agreed to climb back over the railing and was taken into custody without incident.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce driver arrested in hit-and-run that seriously injured 7-year-old
hero.body:
The Fort Pierce Police Department arrested Demetris Johnson, 34, on Wednesday in connection with a hit-and-run crash that seriously injured a 7-year-old at the intersection of North 25th Street and Avenue M on Aug. 1. Johnson faces charges of leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury and driving while license suspended. Investigators said Johnson was located and arrested at 2905 U.S. Highway 1.

The crash occurred at approximately 8:55 p.m. when two children were crossing the roadway in a marked crosswalk. Police said Johnson struck one of the children. Surveillance video obtained from a nearby business captured the crash and shows Johnson exiting his vehicle to check on the children before returning to his vehicle and fleeing the scene.

The Fort Pierce Police Department said responding officers and investigators quickly identified the suspect vehicle using available investigative technology and law enforcement databases. These resources also assisted officers in identifying Johnson as the driver.

The 7-year-old has been released from the hospital and is currently recovering, police said. The investigation remains active and ongoing. Anyone with information on this incident can contact the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 800-273-8477.

hero.headline: Palm City home condemned after woman arrested on 72 animal cruelty charges in Border Collie hoarding case
hero.body:
The Martin County Building Department condemned a Palm City home on Wednesday after Paige O'Donnell was arrested on 72 charges in connection with the hoarding of 36 Border Collies. O'Donnell, 62, was arrested Monday following a search warrant execution at her residence on Alligator Street, where deputies discovered dogs covered in feces and urine living in a home with no functioning air conditioning and floors covered in waste and garbage, according to a probable cause affidavit.

The Building Department posted a notice of condemnation to the gate of the home Wednesday. The notice states occupancy is prohibited as the structure is unfit for human occupancy as defined by section 21.75.3, citing an unsanitary single family residence. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is caring for all 36 rescued Border Collies in what officials have called the worst animal hoarding case the organization has ever seen.

O'Donnell faces 36 counts of felony animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts for failing to provide the dogs with proper exercise or air. A judge set her total bond at $275,000 and ordered that she may not own or possess either temporary or permanent any animals as conditions of her bond. When deputies executed the search warrant Monday, O'Donnell was taking a bath, according to the arrest affidavit.

Videos from the rescue show feces piled inches high and dogs so filthy they blended into the garbage surrounding them. The case developed after a news investigation shared neighbor complaints with the Martin County Sheriff's Office, leading to what authorities describe as the largest animal rescue in the county's recent history. Sarah Fisher, a spokeswoman for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said some of the dogs are very shut down and some are not even walking, just laying on their sides.

cards.headline: Rescued Border Collies begin recovery at Humane Society of the Treasure Coast after Palm City hoarding case
cards.teaser: The Humane Society is assessing the medical needs of the 36 Border Collies and beginning rehabilitation after they were removed from deplorable conditions Monday.
cards.body:
The 36 Border Collies rescued from a Palm City home Monday are now receiving medical care, nourishment and grooming as they begin their recovery at the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. Sarah Fisher, a spokeswoman for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said the dogs are very shut down, with some not even walking and just laying on their sides. Veterinary teams are shaving matted fur and examining each dog individually to determine the extent of medical treatment needed.

Fisher described the severity of the animals' condition in detail. We had not only the matted and the underweight and the skin issues, we had glass and metal. We had their tongues were bleeding from them biting their tongues. There was feces in their mouths. Their tails might be falling off. I mean, it's the worst that I've seen, Fisher said. She added that some of the dogs are just laying there and do not know what to do, do not know to lift their head, and do not know how to interact with people, showing they were institutionalized.

The shelter said it could take time before the dogs are ready for foster homes or adoption. The shelter is asking for donations to help cover the cost of caring for the neglected animals, saying the financial burden comes at a time when the shelter was already facing significant challenges. These innocent dogs were inhumanely kept in deplorable conditions, and while they are finally safe, their journey to recovery is just beginning, the shelter said.
cards.article_text: The Border Collies rescued from a Palm City home Monday where authorities found deplorable conditions are now receiving medical care, nourishment and grooming as they begin their recovery. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast said it has taken in the dogs rescued by the Martin County Sheriff's Office Animal Services Unit and is assessing their needs while determining the best path forward. Paige O'Donnell, 62, was booked in connection with the case and faces 72 charges: 36 third-degree felony counts involving alleged animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts alleging animals were kept without sufficient exercise and air. O'Donnell appeared before a judge on Tuesday. Her bond was set at $270,000 and she was told she could have no pets if she is released on bond. These innocent dogs were inhumanely kept in deplorable conditions, and while they are finally safe, their journey to recovery is just beginning, the shelter said. Authorities said 36 Border Collies had been removed from the home as of Monday, while crews continued working to safely remove the remaining dogs. Investigators said it was initially unclear exactly how many animals remained inside because some were skittish and hiding. See also: Homeowner in custody after 36 Border Collies found in Palm City hoarding case The shelter said its immediate focus is on the well-being of the dogs and asked for the public's patience as it works through the complex situation. It is also asking for donations to help cover the cost of caring for the neglected animals, saying the financial burden comes at a time when the shelter was already facing significant challenges. Every dollar makes a difference, the shelter said. Together, we can give these dogs the second chance they deserve. According to the arrest report, Monday’s search was the culmination of an investigation that stretched back weeks and drew on years of previous Animal Services contacts involving O'Donnell’s home. The latest investigation developed after authorities received renewed concerns about the number of dogs at the SW Alligator Street residence and their living conditions. In June, investigators observed the property from the roadway but did not make contact with anyone at the home. The following month, the Sheriff’s Office received a letter and photographs from neighbors documenting concerns about conditions at the property dating back several years. On July 22, Animal Services responded to another complaint alleging more than 20 dogs were inside the home, that several deceased animals may have been in the garage, that the home did not have functioning air conditioning and that the dogs had not been allowed outside since 2022, according to the report. An investigator reported smelling a strong odor from the roadway and hearing what sounded like a large number of dogs, including puppies, barking from inside. O'Donnell later met with Animal Services at a Palm City park with one dog but, according to the report, would not allow investigators inside her home. The dog she brought to the meeting was described as having heavily stained, matted fur. Investigators said O'Donnell told them she had buried one of her dogs and named several others she still owned. Investigators also checked veterinary records. According to the affidavit, an employee at a local animal hospital said O'Donnell had brought in numerous puppies over the years and that records showed roughly 38 adult dogs had been treated there, including some that were brought in deceased. The employee also told investigators the dogs were frequently dirty. The arrest report says Animal Services had a long history of responding to complaints involving the residence, with roughly 20 related incidents documented from 2020 through this year. One 2020 investigation documented about 25 dogs and described the home as severely unsanitary, with feces and urine covering the floor. Investigators said one elderly dog was in such poor condition that humane euthanasia was recommended. Another complaint in 2022 led investigators to report 10 to 20 dogs being kept in a backyard covered in feces and flies. The arrest report says the home's air conditioning was not functioning and investigators observed feces inside the residence. At a follow-up inspection a week later, authorities said the home had been cleaned, the air conditioning repaired and three dogs surrendered to a rescue. In December 2023, investigators again responded to complaints about more than 20 dogs. According to the report, they detected an overwhelming odor of urine and feces and heard more than 10 dogs barking inside, including what sounded like puppies. Neighbors say they'd been raising concerns for years. "Very frustrating, very angry. They say if you hear something, say something, and we said something, probably over a hundred times," said Kelsey Weidenheimer, a neighbor on SW Alligator Street. "When you called the Sheriff's Office, what did you tell them?" we asked her. "The dogs are in the house. They haven't been let out in years at this point. There's no A-C, 'cause the windows are open. When the wind blows, you can smell it," Weidenheimer explained. "What did they tell you?" we asked her. "As long as the dogs have food and shelter, it's fine," she said. Investigators said the number and identities of dogs O'Donnell reported owning changed during different contacts, and records did not always establish what happened to dogs she had previously said were in her possession. "Our interaction with her started back in 2020 when she was an AKC breeder and back then we had several calls for service that involved her maybe mistreating animals. Our Animal Control Officers came out at that point. She was not actually--didn't appear to be mistreating animals," said John Budensiek, Martin Co. According to the Sheriff, they learned from a previous animal hoarding case, that it's not always a smart decision to rush in and take all the dogs. "Unfortunately, 20 plus years ago, we experienced that here at the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. We hit a house that had over 100 dogs in it. Seized them all, fostered them all out and then we were sued and lost the lawsuit. And worse than losing the lawsuit, we had to return those animals to the deplorable conditions which we took them from. So learning from our mistakes years and years ago, we weren’t going to do that again," Sheriff Budensiek said. In the days before the search warrant was obtained, investigators returned to the Palm City property and again reported smelling feces and urine. A neighboring resident also provided video that, according to the arrest report, showed garbage and debris piled high inside the garage while numerous dogs could be heard barking inside the home. Investigators also reviewed a photograph from a 2020 case showing at least 12 Border Collies in a room where the dogs and floor appeared to be covered in fecal matter. Based on those observations, prior complaints and O'Donnell’s documented history with Animal Services, investigators obtained a search warrant. When authorities entered the home Monday, the arrest report says the residence was unlivable and unsanitary, with floors covered in feces, urine and garbage and an air-conditioning system that was not working. Investigators said the dogs were severely matted with feces and urine and that portions of the walls appeared to have been repeatedly chewed. Thirty-six dogs were removed from the residence. Sheriff Budensiek separately described the conditions as extremely concerning, saying some of the normally black-and-white Border Collies were so covered in feces that they appeared nearly solid black. Deputies and Animal Services employees wore protective clothing while working inside the house. The Martin County Sheriff's Office says viewers and residents can help the 36 Border Collies by donating to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast to help with medical and recovery care for the animals. The investigation remains ongoing as authorities assess the dogs’ conditions and determine the full scope of the case.

cards.headline: Two Martin County animal hoarding cases in three weeks raise questions about Florida's animal cruelty laws
cards.teaser: Two severe animal hoarding cases in Martin County just three weeks apart are raising questions about whether Florida's laws do enough to protect animals.
cards.body:
The first case unfolded at the 11500 block of Southwest Meadowlark Circle, where the Martin County Sheriff's Office rescued more than 100 dogs and cats. Weeks later, 36 dogs were rescued from a Palm City home on Alligator Street. Former Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg said prosecuting these cases is difficult under current law because the laws are not tough enough and it is too easy to escape incarceration if you engage in these horrible acts of animal cruelty.

Aronberg said Florida law does not classify hoarding as a crime on its own, which creates a barrier for prosecutors. Hoarding by definition is not considered a crime under Florida law, so you need, I think, perhaps an anti-hoarding law to make it easier to prosecute these individuals, a specific anti-hoarding law that lowers the threshold for felony prosecution in severe multi-animal neglect cases, Aronberg said. He explained even when cases do rise to the level of criminal charges, the consequences are limited. As a misdemeanor, these cases typically result in no jail time. As a felony, some jail time is possible, but only if prosecutors can prove intent to harm.

Aronberg said the stakes extend beyond animal welfare because studies show animal cruelty can escalate to child abuse and domestic violence, making enforcement a public safety issue. It's a gateway crime and that's why you need to treat it very strictly at the beginning. If you give it a slap on the wrist, you're just inviting more outrageous conduct that can hurt people, Aronberg said.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce driver arrested in hit-and-run that seriously injured 7-year-old in crosswalk
hero.body:
Fort Pierce police arrested a 34-year-old driver Wednesday in connection with a hit-and-run crash that seriously injured a 7-year-old child at the intersection of North 25th Street and Avenue M on Aug. 1. Demetris Johnson was arrested at 2905 U.S. Highway 1 and faces charges of leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury and driving while license suspended.

The crash occurred at approximately 8:55 p.m. when two children were crossing the roadway in a marked crosswalk. Police said Johnson struck one of the children. Surveillance video obtained from a nearby business captured the crash and shows Johnson exiting his vehicle to check on the children before returning to his vehicle and fleeing the scene.

Investigators quickly identified the suspect vehicle using available investigative technology and law enforcement databases. These resources also assisted officers in identifying Johnson as the driver, according to the Fort Pierce Police Department.

The 7-year-old has been released from the hospital and is currently recovering, police said. The investigation remains active and ongoing. Anyone with information on this incident is encouraged to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 800-273-8477.

hero.headline: Indian River County deputies talk wanted man off 17th Street Bridge after two-hour standoff
hero.body:
Indian River County sheriff's deputies successfully ended a two-hour standoff on the 17th Street Bridge in Vero Beach after talking a man wanted for burglary back from the edge. Deputies were called to the bridge on Sunday, August 2, after receiving information that a man wanted on a Port St. Lucie Police Department warrant for burglary with battery had contacted his mother and made concerning statements.

Deputies located the man on top of the 17th Street Bridge after he climbed over the railing and threatened to jump. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office Crisis Negotiation Team spent about two hours talking with him while the Marine Unit launched a boat below the bridge. Fire Rescue also staged nearby as a safety precaution.

Body camera footage shows negotiators working to keep the man talking and convince him to come back over the railing. The man said he was worried about going to jail and the financial burden his family could face. Negotiators continued talking with him, eventually learning that he enjoyed playing video games. As the conversation continued, deputies told him his mother was heading to the base of the bridge.

The man eventually agreed to climb back over the railing. Body camera footage shows deputies encouraging him as he grabbed a ladder and climbed back onto the bridge. The man was then taken into custody without incident. hero.headline: Construction worker killed by vehicle in I-95 work zone south of Tradition
hero.body:
A 45-year-old dump truck driver was killed after being hit by another construction vehicle inside a work zone on I-95 just south of Tradition on Monday night, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The driver stepped out of their dump truck on the northbound lanes and was struck by a tractor with a sweeper traveling south, repaving the area as part of an improvement project.

The construction worker was transported to Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital, where they later died. The driver of the other truck was arrested on an unrelated warrant, FHP said.

The incident occurred during an improvement project on I-95 in Port St. Lucie. Workers were actively repaving the area when the fatal collision took place. The agency has not released the names of those involved in the crash.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County officials outline 2026 master plan for Port of Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: Port officials discussed a master plan Tuesday that includes a mega-yacht marine facility and support hub for launch and rocket recovery operations at the Port of Fort Pierce.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County officials discussed the 2026 master plan for the Port of Fort Pierce during an informal meeting in Fort Pierce Tuesday morning, aiming to clarify confusion about the plan's scope and details. The port, home to Derecktor Shipyards where mega-yacht maintenance and repairs take place, is set to see significant changes under the proposed plan. It includes a mega-yacht marine facility to expand the repair area and a support hub for launch and rocket recovery operations, which county officials believe aligns well with the port's existing capabilities.

The plan also proposes upgrades to the boat ramps at Harbour Pointe Park and the potential addition of an event center and fishing pier at Museum Pointe Park. Residents raised concerns about the history center located in Museum Pointe Park, which some fear could be removed to accommodate the project. County officials reassured attendees that the museum would remain in Fort Pierce.

Port officials plan to present the master plan to the City of Fort Pierce and the Town of St. Lucie Village to gather feedback and share it with the board. Joshua Revord, the county's director of port, inlet and beaches, said the plan could bring significant capital dollars and work volume to the area through maintenance, repair and overhaul of large vessels used in the industry.

hero.headline: Palm City woman faces 72 animal cruelty charges after 36 Border Collies found in deplorable conditions
hero.body:
Paige O'Donnell, 62, was arrested Monday after Martin County deputies executed a search warrant at her home on Alligator Street in Palm City and discovered 36 Border Collies living in severe neglect. O'Donnell faces 72 criminal charges: one felony animal torture charge and one misdemeanor confinement charge for each dog. Her bond was set at $270,000, and a judge ordered her not to possess any animals if released.

Deputies found the dogs covered in feces and urine inside a home where the air conditioning was not working and floors were covered in waste and garbage. Sheriff John Budensiek said some of the normally black-and-white Border Collies were so covered in feces they appeared nearly solid black. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast in Palm City took in all 36 dogs, including three puppies up to six months old. Sarah Fisher, a spokeswoman for the shelter, called it the worst case the organization has ever seen. Staff found rusted metal and glass shards stuck in the dogs' matted fur, and some dogs had bleeding tongues from biting themselves. One puppy had three pounds of mats removed during grooming.

The arrest followed an investigation that began in July after authorities received a letter and photographs from neighbors documenting concerns about the property. O'Donnell met with Animal Services at a Palm City park with one dog but would not allow investigators inside her home. An employee at a local animal hospital told investigators O'Donnell had brought in numerous puppies over the years and that records showed roughly 38 adult dogs had been treated there, including some brought in deceased. The arrest report says Animal Services had responded to roughly 20 incidents involving the residence from 2020 through this year.

The Humane Society said many of the dogs have skin and eye infections and appear withdrawn and catatonic. Some are being shaved under mild sedation due to emotional distress and physical pain. The shelter asked for monetary donations to its emergency medical fund to cover the cost of care. Fisher said the dogs will not be ready for adoption any time soon, but the shelter is running a name-your-own-price promotion to encourage adoptions of other animals and clear space.
hero.article_text: Staff at the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast (HSTC) in Palm City are in the midst of an arduous process: medically grooming, bathing and examining 36 Border Collies brought to them Monday by Martin County deputies. Their fur was caked with feces and mats the size of apples."This is the worst case we've ever seen," said Sarah Fisher, a spokeswoman for HSTC. "We've seen throughout the years a dog or a cat, here and there, coming in with severe medical needs, but not 36 of them in this shape all at the same time."WATCH BELOW: 'Worst case we've ever seen': Humane Society caring for 36 rescued dogsDeputies rescued the Border Collies from a Palm City home Monday. Videos released by the sheriff's office show feces piled inches high inside the home and dogs that were so filthy that they blended in with the garbage and feces around them."Right now they're very, very shut down. Some of them aren't even walking. They're just laying on their sides," Fisher said. "We're going one by one and we are shaving-- cutting down the mats, and trying to see the extent of their medical (needs)."Fisher said many of the dogs have eye and skin infections, requiring special care during a shaving process that can take an hour for each dog."As we're cutting and we're shaving, we're finding lots of pieces of metal — rusted metal, sharp metal — that have been stuck in their fur, along with shards of glass," Fisher said. "We did shave a puppy and three pounds of mats came off her."The dogs' former owner, Paige O'Donnell, was arrested Monday as deputies broke through her door. According to her arrest affidavit, she was taking a bath when law enforcement arrived to serve a warrant.O'Donnell now faces 72 criminal charges: one felony animal torture charge and one misdemeanor confinement charge for each dog. She remains in the Martin County Jail with bond set at $270,000.The 11-page affidavit details a renewed interest from investigators in O'Donnell's home after WPTV shared a neighbor's complaint with the sheriff's office. That neighbor, and others, had been reporting concerns about a large number of dogs at O'Donnell's home since at least 2020. A WPTV investigation that aired last week, before O'Donnell's arrest, detailed previous attempts by the sheriff's office to investigate, as O'Donnell continued to wall herself off from law enforcement.As deputies kept an eye on O'Donnell's home and began to ask her questions in July, the affidavit describes deceptive behavior from O'Donnell. She would not let deputies into her home, and blaming the stench that lingered across the road on "missed trash collection" and "old seafood."After multiple canceled meetings with investigators, O'Donnell eventually agreed to meet in a park with one dog, which she said was one of only four she owned, according to the affidavit."It was... evident that he had been freshly bathed, as his coat was still wet," animal control officer Tabitha Queen wrote of the meeting. "I observed that Paige had attempted to cut away some of the matted fur; however, his coat remained matted and unkempt."Asked why the dog's fur was stained, "she stated she did not see anything."When deputies arrived at O'Donnell's home Monday, she was asked about the conditions of the home and dogs. "She only said she was in the process of cleaning it," the affidavit said."My heart's completely broken," Fisher said. "It hurts so bad knowing that these animals trusted a human. They trust humans and that these humans do this to them."Donna Turner and Tina Smith visited the Humane Society Tuesday after seeing images of Monday's rescue."We were just heartbroken," Smith said."Neighbors have pitched in towels and blankets and everything else, so we're just trying to help out," Turner said, as she and Smith hauled bags of dog food and clean towels from their car to the lobby. "We're just trying to help out."The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is asking for the public's help, particularly after also taking in more than 100 animals from another alleged hoarder in July."Our biggest need is monetary donations to our emergency medical fund," Fisher said. "This is depleting our emergency medical fund."Fisher said the Border Collies will not be ready to leave the Humane Society any time soon, but there are adoptable animals available now. They're running a name-your-own-price promotion to encourage adoptions and clear space in the shelter.Click here to see adoptable animals or make a donation.

cards.headline: Two Martin County hoarding cases expose gaps in Florida animal cruelty laws
cards.teaser: Two severe animal hoarding cases in Martin County within three weeks have raised questions about whether Florida laws adequately protect animals from cruelty.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office rescued more than 100 dogs and cats from the 11500 block of Southwest Meadowlark Circle in one case, followed three weeks later by the rescue of 36 dogs from a Palm City home on Alligator Street. Former Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg said prosecuting these cases is difficult because Florida law does not classify hoarding as a crime on its own.

Aronberg said even when cases rise to the level of criminal charges, the consequences are limited. As a misdemeanor, these cases typically result in no jail time, and as a felony, some jail time is possible only if prosecutors can prove intent to harm. He called for a specific anti-hoarding law that would lower the threshold for felony prosecution in severe multi-animal neglect cases.

Martin County Sheriff John Buddensiek said limited visible evidence of abuse prevented deputies from acting sooner on neighbor concerns in the 36-dog case. Aronberg said the stakes extend beyond animal welfare, noting that studies show animal cruelty can escalate to child abuse and domestic violence.
cards.article_text: Two severe animal hoarding cases in Martin County, just three weeks apart, are raising questions about whether Florida's laws do enough to protect animals.The first case unfolded at the 11500 block of Southwest Meadowlark Circle, where the Martin County Sheriff's Office rescued more than 100 dogs and cats. Weeks later, 36 dogs were rescued from a Palm City home on Alligator Street.Former Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg said prosecuting these cases is difficult under current law."The laws are not tough enough. It's too easy to escape incarceration if you engage in these horrible acts of animal cruelty," Aronberg said.He said Florida law does not classify hoarding as a crime on its own, which creates a barrier for prosecutors."Hoarding by definition is not considered a crime under Florida law, so you need, I think, perhaps an anti-hoarding law to make it easier to prosecute these individuals [...] A specific anti-hoarding law that lowers the threshold for felony prosecution in severe multi-animal neglect cases," Aronberg said.Aronberg explained even when cases do rise to the level of criminal charges, the consequences are limited. As a misdemeanor, these cases typically result in no jail time. As a felony, some jail time is possible, but only if prosecutors can prove intent to harm.Martin County Sheriff John Buddensiek explained to Chief Investigator Jamie Ostroff in an interview last week that limited visible evidence of abuse prevented deputies from acting sooner on neighbor concerns in the 36-dog case."Federal law, state law only allows you to go so far when you have any type of investigation," Buddensiek said. "If there was something that we could see from the outside that, you know, dogs are being mistreated, malnourished, not taken care of, we would absolutely get a search warrant and go in there."Aronberg said the stakes extend beyond animal welfare. Studies show animal cruelty can escalate to child abuse and domestic violence, making enforcement a public safety issue."It's a gateway crime and that's why you need to treat it very strictly at the beginning. If you give it a slap on the wrist, you're just inviting more outrageous conduct that can hurt people," Aronberg said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. hero.headline: Martin County reviews first development proposal under new state agricultural enclave law
hero.body:
Martin County is reviewing its first agricultural enclave proposal under Senate Bill 686, a new state law that took effect July 1 and allows landowners to build homes and businesses on land designated as agricultural enclaves. To qualify, a property must be surrounded on at least 75 percent of its boundaries by existing development and must have been in continuous use for bona fide agriculture purposes for five years prior to the date of an application, said Martin County senior planner Jenna Knobbe.

On the same day the bill became law, the county received its first application for a 396-acre property known as Waterside. The site consists of three parcels located just west of Kanner Highway and south of Southwest 96th Street. Up to 1,200 homes were initially planned on the property.

County staff recommended the enclave designation be denied. Knobbe said the county reviewed the property tax records for the three parcels in the application and found that not all of the property was classified for agricultural purposes from the property appraiser's office. The Waterside proposal was expected to be discussed at a Martin County Commission meeting Tuesday, but the applicant asked for the item to be pulled from the agenda. The property owners declined to comment.

How much pushback local governments can mount against the law remains unclear. Johns County commissioners agreed last week to have the county attorney examine whether there are legal grounds to challenge the new law, which expires Jan. 1, 2028.

cards.headline: Two Martin County hoarding cases highlight gaps in Florida animal cruelty laws
cards.teaser: Two severe animal hoarding cases in Martin County, just three weeks apart, are raising questions about whether Florida's laws do enough to protect animals.
cards.body:
Two severe animal hoarding cases in Martin County, just three weeks apart, are raising questions about whether Florida's laws do enough to protect animals. The first case unfolded at the 11500 block of Southwest Meadowlark Circle, where the Martin County Sheriff's Office rescued more than 100 dogs and cats. Weeks later, 36 dogs were rescued from a Palm City home on Alligator Street.

Former Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg said prosecuting these cases is difficult under current law. The laws are not tough enough. It's too easy to escape incarceration if you engage in these horrible acts of animal cruelty, Aronberg said. He said Florida law does not classify hoarding as a crime on its own, which creates a barrier for prosecutors. Hoarding by definition is not considered a crime under Florida law, so you need, I think, perhaps an anti-hoarding law to make it easier to prosecute these individuals. A specific anti-hoarding law that lowers the threshold for felony prosecution in severe multi-animal neglect cases, Aronberg said.

Aronberg explained even when cases do rise to the level of criminal charges, the consequences are limited. As a misdemeanor, these cases typically result in no jail time. As a felony, some jail time is possible, but only if prosecutors can prove intent to harm. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek explained that limited visible evidence of abuse prevented deputies from acting sooner on neighbor concerns in the 36-dog case. Federal law, state law only allows you to go so far when you have any type of investigation, Budensiek said. If there was something that we could see from the outside that, you know, dogs are being mistreated, malnourished, not taken care of, we would absolutely get a search warrant and go in there.

hero.headline: Palm City woman faces 72 animal cruelty charges after 36 Border Collies rescued from Alligator Street home
hero.body:
A Palm City woman is in custody on a $270,000 bond after authorities discovered 36 Border Collies living in severe neglect inside her home on Alligator Street, leading to 72 charges of animal cruelty. Paige O'Donnell, 62, faces 36 counts of felony animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts for failing to provide the dogs with proper exercise or air. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the animals were in deplorable conditions.

Deputies executed a search warrant Monday and found dogs covered in feces and urine living in a home with no functioning air conditioning and floors covered in waste and garbage. The dogs' fur was caked with feces and mats the size of apples. Videos released by the sheriff's office show feces piled inches high inside the home and dogs that were so filthy that they blended in with the garbage and feces around them. During her first court appearance, O'Donnell was ordered not to possess any animals as a condition of her bond.

The case dates back to 2020, when animal services first investigated O'Donnell's home and dogs. Court records show complaints continued through 2022 and 2023, with renewed concerns in 2026 leading to surveillance and multiple attempted inspections. Martin County Sheriff's Office Animal Services reviewed call history at the address and identified approximately 20 related incidents spanning from 2020 through 2026. After officers observed one dog this month, they obtained a search warrant, which led to the discovery of the 36 dogs and O'Donnell's arrest.

All 36 dogs are now being cared for at the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast in Palm City. Sarah Fisher, a spokesperson for the organization, described the severity of the animals' condition as the worst case the shelter has ever seen. Fisher said many of the dogs have eye and skin infections, and staff found pieces of rusted metal and shards of glass stuck in their fur. Some of the dogs are not even walking and are just laying on their sides. The Humane Society said it could take time before the dogs are ready for foster homes or adoption and is asking for community support to help with the recovery efforts.

Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the animals were in "deplorable conditions." The case dates back to 2020, when animal services first investigated Paige O'Donnell’s home and dogs. Court records show complaints continued through 2022 and 2023, with renewed concerns in 2026 leading to surveillance and multiple attempted inspections. After officers observed one dog this month, they obtained a search warrant, which led to the discovery of the 36 dogs and O'Donnell’s arrest. During her first court appearance, O'Donnell was ordered, "You may not possess either temporarily or permanently any animals as a condition of your bond." All 36 dogs are now being cared for at the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. (To donate to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, click here.) Sarah Fisher, a spokesperson for the organization, described the severity of the animals’ condition. "We had not only the matted and the underweight and the skin issues, we had glass and metal. We had their tongues were bleeding from them biting their tongues. There was feces in their mouths. Their tails might be falling off. I mean, it's the worst that I've seen," Fisher said. Fisher added that the focus is currently on assessing each dog’s physical and mental health. "Some of the dogs are just laying there, and they don't know what to do. They don't know to lift their head. They don't know how to interact with people. So you can tell they were institutionalized," Fisher said. Reflecting on the situation, Fisher said, "I don't know whether to be sad for her or angry. Because, you know, at one time in her life, she loved these dogs and she put everything towards these dogs. And somewhere along the way, something happened. And unfortunately, the dogs had to pay for it." The Humane Society said it could take time before the dogs are ready for foster homes or adoption. In the meantime, they are asking for community support to help with the recovery efforts. hero.headline: Four Indian River County elementary schools hit 90% reading proficiency milestone in national model program
hero.body:
Four elementary schools in Indian River County reached a 90% reading proficiency goal set by the Moonshot Moment, a community-driven literacy program that has drawn national attention. The program, launched in 2012 through The Learning Alliance nonprofit, was co-founded by parent Liz Remington after her son struggled with reading. When Remington first met with reporters in 2017, just 56% of third graders in the district were reading at grade level.

The nonprofit brings together schools, philanthropists, and business owners to fund added resources, including reading coaches, in elementary classrooms. Rosewood Magnet School and Osceola Magnet School are among the four schools that cleared the 90% threshold. At Rosewood, principal Adam Faust said the achievement came down to the final day. The school had six students to test to reach 90%, needed three to be at proficiency or above, and five of those students made it.

At Osceola Magnet School, principal Jennifer Norris said students will return to a new campus building after also reaching the 90% milestone. The school is now targeting 95% proficiency this year. Norris said if students are reading at grade level by third grade, data show they will be proficient readers for the rest of their life.

Other school districts across Florida are now looking at adopting the Moonshot Moment model. Remington said the program's success comes from putting systems in place and building teams that implement collectively and collaboratively. The effort continues a mission that started with one parent's child and has since helped thousands of students.

The FWC's guidance emphasizes that while bobcats typically do not pose a threat to humans, residents should still exercise caution and maintain distance when they spot these wild animals. The commission's warning serves as a reminder that even animals that appear regularly in neighborhoods remain unpredictable wildlife that deserve respect and space.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County reviews Port of Fort Pierce master plan with mega-yacht marina, spaceport facility
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County commissioners Tuesday reviewed proposals for the Port of Fort Pierce's 2026 Master Plan that would add a mega-yacht marina, spaceport recovery facility and expanded boat ramps.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County commissioners Tuesday reviewed proposals for the Port of Fort Pierce's 2026 Master Plan that would transform the waterfront with a mega-yacht marina, spaceport recovery facility and expanded boat ramps, according to county officials. The comprehensive plan addresses critical boating infrastructure needs in St. Lucie County, where nearly 15,000 registered boats compete for just 147 boat trailer parking spaces within three miles of the Fort Pierce Inlet, county data shows.

The master plan's centerpiece involves redeveloping Harbour Pointe to create the Treasure Coast's largest boat ramp facility, Commissioner James Clasby told residents at Tuesday's meeting. The Harbour Pointe development would include a marine commercial district featuring restaurants, an amphitheater, education center and living shoreline designed to enhance both recreation and environmental protection, according to Joshua Revord, director of St. Lucie County Port Inlet and Beaches. Beyond marine improvements, the master plan proposes establishing a spaceport recovery facility at the Port of Fort Pierce to capitalize on Florida's expanding aerospace sector.

The plan's most controversial element involves redeveloping Museum Pointe waterfront park with a mega-yacht marina and clubhouse, according to master plan renderings shared with commissioners. Fort Pierce resident Sean DeRosa expressed opposition to the Museum Pointe proposal during Tuesday's meeting, saying there are many places to put marinas but blocking the water view and picnic area is not the right spot. The Port of Fort Pierce master plan remains under review by St. Lucie County commissioners, with final approval authority resting with Fort Pierce city officials.

hero.headline: Florida homeowners face insurance premium paradox after investing in expensive metal roofs
hero.body:
Florida homeowners who invested tens of thousands of dollars in premium metal roofs to protect against hurricanes are discovering that the upgrades do not guarantee lower insurance premiums, with some facing higher costs despite installing more durable materials. Anier Sosa of West Palm Beach installed a new metal roof to replace aging shingles two years ago, expecting the upgrade to reduce his homeowners insurance costs. Instead, his premium did not decrease. When he asked his insurer why, the company told him the roof was too expensive to cover, creating what Sosa described as a lose-lose situation.

Metal roofs cost more than $50,000 to install, roughly double the price of conventional asphalt shingles, but offer superior protection and can last up to 40 years compared to traditional materials. The significant price difference creates a complex insurance calculation that does not always favor homeowners who make the premium investment. Insurance companies typically require roofs to be 15 years old or newer to qualify for the best rates, according to Robert Norberg of Arden Insurance in Lantana. After the 15-year mark, premiums generally increase regardless of roofing material.

Recent Florida legislation prevents insurance companies from canceling policies solely based on roof age, though higher premiums often apply to older roofing systems. Mark Friedlander of the Insurance Information Institute said the previous issue in Florida was that homeowners policies were being canceled because of roof age. The new laws ensure older roofs remain insurable, but typically at higher premium costs. Insurance experts recommend homeowners have their roofs professionally inspected when they reach 10 years old to identify potential issues early and demonstrate proper maintenance to insurance companies.

Friedlander advised that homeowners should have their roofs inspected at least at the 10-year mark because the roof serves as the first line of defense against Florida's weather conditions, including heat and storms. While Florida's insurance commissioner previously suggested phasing out traditional asphalt shingles in favor of more durable materials, insurance experts say such a transition is not practical given that traditional shingle roofs cost approximately half the price of metal alternatives. Even as Florida's insurance market shows signs of improvement and stability, roof condition and age remain primary factors insurance companies evaluate when setting premiums.

hero.headline: Martin County reviews first agricultural enclave proposal under new state law
hero.teaser: Martin County received its first application under Senate Bill 686, which took effect July 1 and allows landowners to build homes and businesses on land designated as agricultural enclaves.
hero.body:
Martin County is reviewing its first agricultural enclave proposal under Senate Bill 686, which took effect July 1 and allows landowners to build homes and businesses on land designated as agricultural enclaves. To qualify, a property must be surrounded on at least 75% of its boundaries by existing development. The property must have been in continuous use for bona fide agriculture purposes for five years prior to the date of an application, Martin County senior planner Jenna Knobbe said.

On the same day the bill became law, the county received its first application for a 396-acre property known as Waterside. The site consists of three parcels located just west of Kanner Highway and south of Southwest 96th Street. Up to 1,200 homes were initially planned on the property. County staff recommended the enclave designation be denied because not all of the property was classified for agricultural purposes from the property appraiser's office, Knobbe said.

The Waterside proposal was expected to be discussed at a Martin County Commission meeting Tuesday, but the applicant asked for the item to be pulled from the agenda. The property owners declined to comment. How much pushback local governments can mount against the law remains unclear. Johns County commissioners agreed last week to have the county attorney examine whether there are legal grounds to challenge the new law, which expires Jan. 1, 2028.

cards.headline: Port of Fort Pierce master plan proposes mega-yacht marina, spaceport recovery facility
cards.body:
St. Lucie County commissioners Tuesday reviewed proposals for the Port of Fort Pierce's 2026 Master Plan that would transform the waterfront with a mega-yacht marina, spaceport recovery facility and expanded boat ramps. The comprehensive plan addresses critical boating infrastructure needs in St. Lucie County, where nearly 15,000 registered boats compete for just 147 boat trailer parking spaces within three miles of the Fort Pierce Inlet, county data shows.

The master plan's centerpiece involves redeveloping Harbour Pointe to create the Treasure Coast's largest boat ramp facility, Commissioner James Clasby told residents at Tuesday's meeting. The Harbour Pointe development would include a marine commercial district featuring restaurants, an amphitheater, education center and living shoreline designed to enhance both recreation and environmental protection, according to Joshua Revord, director of St. Lucie County Port Inlet and Beaches. Adding the facility will almost double the boat ramp capacity for parking, Clasby said during the public discussion.

The plan's most controversial element involves redeveloping Museum Pointe waterfront park with a mega-yacht marina and clubhouse, according to master plan renderings shared with commissioners. Fort Pierce resident Sean DeRosa expressed opposition to the Museum Pointe proposal during Tuesday's meeting, saying there are many places to put marinas but blocking that water view and picnic area is not the right spot. Neighbor Paul Sinnott raised concerns about relocating the existing history center. Revord clarified that displacing the museum was never intended and that the facility would either be incorporated into new development or relocated appropriately.

Beyond marine improvements, the master plan proposes establishing a spaceport recovery facility at the Port of Fort Pierce to capitalize on Florida's expanding aerospace sector. In Canaveral there's limited space for space, Revord explained, referencing capacity constraints at Kennedy Space Center. The Port of Fort Pierce master plan remains under review by St. Lucie County commissioners, with final approval authority resting with Fort Pierce city officials. The 2026 Master Plan represents a multi-year development timeline addressing both immediate boating infrastructure needs and long-term economic diversification goals for the Port of Fort Pierce.

hero.headline: Motorcycle crash survivor returns to Fort Pierce hospital to thank medical team
hero.teaser: Victor Lopez walked back into HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital eight months after a life-threatening motorcycle crash to thank the team that saved his life.
hero.body:
Victor Lopez walked back into HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce eight months after a life-threatening motorcycle crash, this time to thank the team that helped save his life. Lopez, who is now back home recovering and cherishing time with his family, returned to the hospital to express his gratitude to the medical professionals and first responders who cared for him during his critical moments.

Last December, Lopez was brought to the hospital in a coma-like state after a serious motorcycle crash. Doctors feared he might not survive. Dr. Jason Moore, a trauma and acute care surgeon at HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, said the team was very concerned about significant traumatic brain injury and signs of anoxic brain injury, which is lack of oxygen to the brain from a significant head injury.

Lopez spent nearly three months in the hospital before he was able to return home to his girlfriend Stefany Sorto, their son, and their newborn daughter Juliet, who was born in January while Lopez was still hospitalized. Donny Stefani, deputy chief of operations for the St. Lucie County Fire District, said crews immediately called a trauma alert and notified the local trauma center at Lawnwood so they would be prepared. Lopez credits his recovery to the medical teams who cared for him and the family who stood by his side.

cards.headline: Centennial High School student hit by car at Port St. Lucie intersection
cards.teaser: A 16-year-old Centennial High School student was hit by a vehicle Monday morning while crossing against the pedestrian signal at Crosstown Parkway and Southwest Cameo Boulevard.
cards.body:
A 16-year-old Centennial High School student was hit by a vehicle Monday morning while attempting to cross a Port St. Lucie intersection against the pedestrian signal. The incident occurred shortly after 7 a.m. at the intersection of Crosstown Parkway and Southwest Cameo Boulevard, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.

Police say the preliminary investigation indicates the teenager attempted to cross Crosstown Parkway against the pedestrian signal, entering the roadway in front of oncoming traffic that had the right of way. The teen told investigators they believed they could make it across the street before an approaching vehicle reached them. However, the driver was unable to avoid striking the student.

The 16-year-old sustained superficial injuries but declined medical transport at the scene. The teen's guardians were notified of the incident. The vehicle involved in the crash sustained minor cosmetic damage. In March 2024, a 15-year-old student was hit by a car making a right turn onto Crosstown Parkway at Southwest Cameo Boulevard and was taken to the hospital with minor injuries.

cards.headline: WPTV investigation leads to rescue of 36 dogs from Palm City home
cards.teaser: The Martin County Sheriff's Office conducted a search warrant Monday at a Palm City home following a WPTV investigation into an alleged Border Collie hoarding case on Southwest Alligator Street.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office conducted a search warrant Monday at a Palm City home in connection with an alleged animal hoarding case. Deputies rescued 36 dogs from a home in the 1245 block of Southwest Alligator Street following a WPTV investigation. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the owner of the home, Paige O'Donnell, will face 72 criminal charges, 36 felony torture charges and 36 misdemeanor charges. She's accused of keeping animals enclosed without exercise and air. This comes after investigators said she never let the dogs outside, something that neighbors previously told WPTV had been occurring.

Budensiek said the house is so deteriorated that about a foot and a half of drywall is gone. The furniture is destroyed, and the animals are in deplorable condition. The food bowls, the water bowls in there are covered in feces. The animals themselves, the dogs, which are supposed to be Border Collies, beautiful dogs, are covered in feces. Monday's search warrant comes after WPTV's investigation revealed that Martin County Animal Control officers and sheriff's deputies had visited homes in the area at least 11 times since 2020, all related to concerns about dogs and their owners. As law enforcement continued to respond, the homeowner built a fence and stopped letting deputies in, making it hard to find probable cause for a warrant.

After WPTV started asking the sheriff's office about the house, they decided to look into it once again. The sheriff said that after days of surveillance and trying to negotiate with O'Donnell, she agreed last week to surrender one of the dogs. Budensiek said that dog appeared to be malnourished, giving them the probable cause to execute a warrant Monday. O'Donnell, a former AKC Border Collie breeder, had been living in this house and was taking a bath when they arrived to serve the warrant. The 36 dogs rescued on Monday will be taken to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast for care.

hero.headline: Florida deploys drones inside high schools as first state to test active shooter defense program
hero.body:
Florida has become the first state in the nation to fund and deploy drones inside school buildings as part of a pilot program designed to stop active shooters before they become deadly. Specialized drones are now installed at high schools in Leon, Volusia and Broward counties as thousands of students return to campus this week.

The pilot program places 40 drones throughout selected buildings at each participating school, with 13 boxes containing three drones each positioned in high-volume locations including auditoriums, cafeterias, gyms and classrooms. At Deltona High School near Orlando, where about 1,800 students are returning, the drones are mounted and being finalized. When an alert is triggered, the encrypted drones deploy within seconds and are piloted remotely from Austin, Texas by championship drone racing pilots. The drones can track a potential shooter and deploy flashing lights, sirens, pellet bangs and pepper spray. Bill King, a co-founder of Campus Guardian Angel, the Austin-based company that developed the technology, said the goal is to distract shooters from targeting people.

Just over half a million dollars in state funding is paying for the initial deployment at Godby High School in Leon County, Deltona High in Volusia County, and Boyd Anderson High in Broward County. Additional state funding was recently added to bring three more school districts into the program, though those districts have not yet been announced by Florida's Department of Education. All participating schools are expected to have the drones fully installed by this fall. At Deltona High, Deputy Trevor Autrey said the drones will give him eyes and ears on a threat's location and help him respond faster.

The program has drawn cautious interest from Parkland families. Debbie Hixon, whose husband Chris was among 17 victims killed at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School on Feb. 14, 2018, said the technology is hard to fully embrace until it is seen in action. Justin Marston, founder of Campus Guardian Angel, said the concept originated from watching drone technology used in combat in Ukraine and applying it to school shootings like Parkland and Uvalde.

LaGrone visited the company's Austin, Texas command center back in November 2025."I had the idea originally just looking at how successful these little drones were against people with guns in Ukraine and then looking at Parkland and Uvalde and shootings like that,” said Justin Marston, Campus Guardian Angel founder.Here’s how the program will work: When an alert is triggered, the encrypted drones — designed for low delay — deploy within seconds and are piloted from their command center in Austin, more than 1,000 miles away from Florida, by championship drone racing pilots.The pilots will use the drones to track a potential shooter and can deploy what company leaders describe as "non-lethal distractors": flashing lights, sirens, pellet bangs and, if needed, pepper spray."If we can get a shooter to do anything besides shoot people, we're winning, right?" said Bill King, a co-founder of the company and is helping to lead drone operations.At Deltona High, which is already equipped with gates, guardians and a full-time school resource officer, Deputy Trevor Autrey said the drones add a critical layer to his response capability."They will be able to give me eyes and ears of where the active threat is, and help me get there quicker, and also be a distraction device if I had to engage them," said Autrey.Just over a half million dollars in state funding is paying for the pilot program, with additional funding recently added to bring three more school districts into the mix. Those districts have not yet been announced by Florida's Department of Education.In a state that knows the pain of school shootings, Parkland families are watching the program with cautious interest."It's not that it's implausible, but it's different. So it's hard to just jump on the bandwagon until you see it in action,” said Debbie Hixon, whose husband, Chris, was the athletic director at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School and among 17 victims killed during the shooting on Feb. 14, 2018.Godby High School in Leon County, Deltona High in Volusia County, and Boyd Anderson High in Broward County are all expected to have the drones fully installed by this fall.

cards.headline: Planet parade, Perseid meteor shower and European solar eclipse converge this week
cards.teaser: Stargazers can view multiple celestial events this week, including a predawn planet parade and the peak of the Perseid meteor shower.
cards.body:
In the predawn hours early Wednesday morning, a parade of planets including Saturn, Mars, Jupiter and Mercury will be visible. Binoculars will help to see Mercury and Jupiter, which will sit very low on the predawn horizon. The current sunrise time in West Palm Beach is 6:50 a.m.

The Perseid meteor shower peaks overnight from Wednesday, Aug. 12 into the early morning of Thursday, Aug. 13. Up to 30 to 50 meteors are anticipated per hour. The meteor shower coincides with two other active meteor showers, allowing for an even better opportunity to catch a shooting star. A new moon offers darker skies and better viewing.

A total solar eclipse will take place in portions of Europe on Wednesday, visible for portions of Spain, Greenland, Iceland and Russia. This is the first total solar eclipse in Europe since 1999.

hero.headline: Martin County reviews first agricultural enclave proposal under new state law
hero.body:
Martin County is reviewing its first agricultural enclave proposal under Senate Bill 686, which took effect July 1 and allows landowners to build homes and businesses on land designated as agricultural enclaves. The county received an application on the same day the law took effect for a 396-acre property known as Waterside, located west of Kanner Highway and south of Southwest 96th Street, with plans for up to 1,200 homes.

To qualify for agricultural enclave designation, a property must be surrounded on at least 75 percent of its boundaries by existing development and must have been in continuous use for bona fide agriculture purposes for five years prior to the date of an application, according to Martin County senior planner Jenna Knobbe. The Waterside site consists of three parcels.

County staff recommended the enclave designation be denied after reviewing property tax records. Knobbe said not all of the property was classified for agricultural purposes by the property appraiser's office. The Waterside proposal was expected to be discussed at a Martin County Commission meeting Tuesday, but the applicant asked for the item to be pulled from the agenda. The property owners declined to comment.

Johns County commissioners agreed last week to have the county attorney examine whether there are legal grounds to challenge the new law, which expires January 1, 2028. How much pushback local governments can mount against the law remains unclear.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce has no legal options to block Causeway Cove development on South Hutchinson Island
cards.teaser: A 43-acre mixed-use development on South Hutchinson Island meets all state law requirements, leaving Fort Pierce city government with no apparent leverage to stop the five-building high-rise project.
cards.body:
Plans for a massive mixed-used development on South Hutchinson Island meet all existing state law requirements, Fort Pierce city planners have concluded, leaving local government no apparent leverage over the 43-acre project. Fort Pierce planning director Kev Freeman told the Fort Pierce City Commission Monday that provisions of a state law known as Live Local allow the developer to sidestep some traditional density, height, zoning and land use standards because it promises to maintain at least 40 percent of the residential units as affordable housing for the next 30 days.

G. FLASH General Partners Inc., West Palm Beach, headed by Ashton DePeyster, a Palm Beach philanthropist and real estate developer, designed the plan for Causeway Cove to include housing, a hotel, commercial space and a marina. Commissioner Michael Broderick, who along with Mayor Linda Hudson lives on South Hutchinson Island, said DePeyster had done an excellent job of designing the plan to meet all the nuances of the state law. Broderick called the development an improper development at an improper location and said the Live Local law is one of the worst written laws of this state.

Live Local provisions require approval of Causeway Cove building heights that meet the highest levels found in commercial and residential buildings located within a mile radius of the proposed location. Freeman said that means state law allows the proposed structures to rise 200 feet. According to Freeman, the city has no choice but to administratively approve the plan without public hearings because it meets the state's criteria. Broderick suggested local citizens may take up the flag of opposition, saying the will of the people has not been felt yet and the citizens of Fort Pierce are pissed off.
cards.article_text: FORT PIERCE – Plans for a massive, new mixed-used development on South Hutchinson Island meet all existing state law requirements, Fort Pierce city planners have concluded, leaving local government no apparent leverage over the 43-acre project. Now it appears a grassroots challenge focused on state lawmakers could be the only remaining roadblock to a five-building, high-rise project designed to include housing, a hotel, commercial space and a marina. Kev Freeman, city planning director, told the Fort Pierce City Commission Monday that provisions of a state law known as Live Local allow the developer to sidestep some traditional density, height, zoning and land use standards because it promises to maintain at least 40 percent of the residential units as “affordable housing” for the next 30 days. While commissioners have expressed unanimous opposition to the plan for Causeway Cove, they suggested Monday that they have no options, save a questionable legal battle that could cost local taxpayers millions with no guarantee of a favorable outcome. Commissioner Michael Broderick, who along with Mayor Linda Hudson lives on South Hutchinson Island, observed that G. FLASH General Partners Inc., West Palm Beach, headed by Ashton DePeyster, a Palm Beach philanthropist and real estate developer, had done “an excellent job” of designing the plan to meet all the nuances of the state law designed to promote affordable housing. “I’m not going to listen to this being the salvation of the city (tax base),” Broderick said. “This is an improper development at an improper location. This is one of the worst written laws of this state. It’s going to be a nightmare out there (South Hutchinson Island) and this city has no control.” Freeman said the city already has consulted with regional and state transportation officials with concerns about the ability of Seaway Drive to accommodate the traffic counts and emergency evacuation plans the development will impact. He said the state has set requirements for driveways, turn lanes, a water taxi connection between Causeway Cove and downtown Fort Pierce, installation of a new public transit stop and providing shuttle service to the beaches. Those are not expected to present roadblocks to development. Live Local provisions require approval of Causeway Cove building heights that meet the highest levels found in commercial/residential buildings located within a mile radius of the proposed location. Freeman said that means state law allows the proposed structures to rise 200 feet. According to Freeman, the city has no choice but to “administratively approve” the plan–without public hearings–because it meets the state’s criteria. Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky said he does not believe “the city can’t do anything,” arguing Fort Pierce should challenge the state’s “interpretations” of the Live Local Act. Commissioner Arnold Gaines, himself an attorney, said state law is preeminent over contradictory local statutes and he warned other members to “be careful about throwing out hope.” Commissioner Curtis Johnson Jr. attached blame to state lawmakers, saying, “We need to help our citizens understand this was done by people they put in (state) office” and he lauded city planners for “doing their job and doing it correctly.” Hudson said she agrees with community sentiment opposed to the plan. “Do I want a dense development like this? “The property should be developed but not this way. If you’re looking for your local government to stand up for you and stop this plan, you’re looking in the wrong place.” Broderick suggested local citizens may take up the flag of opposition. “They haven’t taken into account the will of the people,” he said. “Citizens are going to rally together and take action on their own. The will of the people has not been felt yet. The citizens of Fort Pierce are pissed off.” Broderick did not elaborate on what specific citizen actions could be contemplated. hero.headline: Indian River County schools add metal detectors, crisis alert badges as students return
hero.body:

The district implemented a crisis alert badge system last fall that allows teachers to notify staff of emergencies or disruptions with the push of a button worn around their necks.
