hero.headline: Border Collies rescued from Palm City hoarding case begin recovery as owner faces 72 charges
hero.body:
Martin County authorities removed 36 Border Collies from a Palm City home on SW Alligator Street after discovering the dogs living in deplorable conditions covered in feces, and owner Paige O'Donnell, 62, now faces 72 animal cruelty charges including 36 third-degree felony counts of torture involving pain, serious physical injury or death and 36 first-degree misdemeanor counts of keeping animals in an enclosure without exercise and air. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast has taken in the rescued dogs and begun providing medical care, nourishment and grooming as the animals start their recovery.

Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek described the conditions inside the home as extremely concerning, saying the dogs were covered in feces and the residence was filled with feces, urine-soaked materials, boxes and other debris. Deputies and animal services workers wore Tyvek protective clothing while working inside the home. Budensiek said the house was extremely hot and may not have had air conditioning, about a foot and a half of drywall was missing, furniture had been destroyed and food and water bowls were covered in feces.

Authorities served the search warrant Monday and continued working to safely remove remaining dogs from the home as some animals were skittish and hiding. O'Donnell was booked around noon Monday and all 72 counts are listed as no bond. Neighbor Kelsey Weidenheimer said it was really sad to see the dogs in such rough shape but she was very happy to see them finally getting out.

The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is asking for donations to help cover the cost of caring for the neglected animals, saying the financial burden comes at a time when the shelter was already facing significant challenges. The case comes weeks after a U.S. Postal Service carrier was arrested after more than 100 dogs and cats were found inside her Palm City home. O'Donnell is expected to make her first court appearance Tuesday.

cards.headline: Murray Middle School students return to Stuart campus as tornado rebuild continues
cards.teaser: Murray Middle School students are returning to class this week in Stuart to a campus undergoing major construction nearly two years after a tornado destroyed two buildings and damaged a third.
cards.body:
Murray Middle School students are heading back to class this week in Stuart to a campus that looks much different than when they left, as nearly two years after a tornado spawned by Hurricane Milton tore through the school, damaged buildings are now gone and a major rebuild is taking shape. The October 2024 tornado destroyed two buildings and left a third with major roof damage. Those spaces housed the school's band, chorus and agriculture programs.

Crews demolished two buildings over the summer to make way for a new administration building and media center, plus modern spaces for band, chorus and agriculture science. Crews will also renovate the gym. Superintendent Michael Maine says the programs never stopped and district leaders say the work zone is completely separated from the rest of campus so students can learn safely while crews rebuild.

The gym is expected to be finished by next August. The new administration building, media center and specialized classrooms are expected to follow in December 2027. The project is being paid for through state support, insurance reimbursements and district capital funds.

cards.headline: Animal welfare experts explain hoarding psychology after Palm City Border Collie rescue
cards.teaser: Paige O'Donnell, 62, was arrested Monday after deputies found more than three dozen Border Collies living in deplorable conditions inside her Palm City home, but animal welfare experts say cases like this are often more complex than simply owning too many pets.
cards.body:
Martin County deputies arrested Paige O'Donnell, 62, on Monday after executing a search warrant at her Palm City home where at least 36 Border Collies were removed from the property. Deputies described conditions as unsanitary and dangerous for both the animals and anyone entering the residence. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the animals themselves, the dogs, which are supposed to be Border Collies, beautiful dogs, are covered in feces. They're supposed to be white and black dogs, and they're solid black from the feces.

Dr. Maya Gupta, Vice President of Research at the ASPCA, said animal hoarding is often much more complicated than a love of animals. We do see a few different subtypes of hoarding. One is the person who is caring for animals, maybe caring for other people and just gets overwhelmed, Gupta said. Another common type involves what experts call a rescuer hoarder, someone who believes they are helping animals but gradually loses the ability to care for them or place them in new homes properly. Investigators said O'Donnell previously operated as a Border Collie breeder and all of the dogs recovered from the home appear to be Border Collies.

Gupta says one of the most powerful factors in animal hoarding is what she describes as a rescue mentality. When somebody starts to believe that they are the only one who can provide care for the animals, that's where it can get dangerous, Gupta said. The case comes weeks after another major animal hoarding investigation in Martin County where more than 100 dogs and cats were rescued from a different Palm City home. O'Donnell is expected to make her first court appearance Tuesday.
cards.article_text: A Palm City woman is facing dozens of animal cruelty charges after Martin County deputies say they found more than three dozen Border Collies living in deplorable conditions inside her home. But animal welfare experts say cases like this are often more complex than simply owning too many pets. According to investigators, 62-year-old Paige O'Donnell was arrested Monday after deputies executed a search warrant at her Palm City home. Authorities said at least 36 Border Collies were removed from the property, where deputies described conditions as unsanitary and dangerous for both the animals and anyone entering the residence. "The animals themselves, the dogs, which are supposed to be Border Collies, beautiful dogs, are covered in feces," Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said. "They're supposed to be white and black dogs, and they're solid black from the feces." See also: Homeowner in custody after 20+ Border Collies found in Palm City hoarding case For many people, cases like this prompt a difficult question: How do conditions become so severe? Experts at the ASPCA say animal hoarding is often much more complicated than a love of animals. While some people intentionally neglect animals, others begin with good intentions and eventually become overwhelmed by the number of pets in their care. "We do see a few different subtypes of hoarding," said Dr. Maya Gupta, Vice President of Research at the ASPCA. "One is the person who is caring for animals, maybe caring for other people and just gets overwhelmed." Another common type involves what experts call a "rescuer hoarder" someone who believes they are helping animals but gradually loses the ability to care for them or place them in new homes properly. The latest Palm City case may fit into that discussion. Investigators said O'Donnell previously operated as a Border Collie breeder, and all of the dogs recovered from the home appear to be Border Collies. Gupta says one of the most powerful factors in animal hoarding is what she describes as a rescue mentality. "When somebody starts to believe that they are the only one who can provide care for the animals, that's where it can get dangerous," Gupta said. Researchers say mental health can sometimes play a role in animal hoarding cases. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders identifies animal hoarding as a feature that can be associated with hoarding disorder. However, experts caution that not every person who hoards animals has a diagnosable mental health condition. Instead, hoarding often involves a combination of factors, including social isolation, emotional attachment to animals, and a diminished awareness of how serious conditions have become. "Something has gone wrong in the relationships that that person has with others around them," Gupta said. "That's not something we can definitely apply to every case, but it's something we see more often than not." Experts say another challenge is that many animal hoarding cases remain hidden for years. Individuals often avoid allowing visitors into their homes, and neighbors may only become aware of a problem after noticing strong odors, excessive numbers of animals, or concerns about the animals' welfare. The latest case comes just weeks after another major animal hoarding investigation in Martin County, where more than 100 dogs and cats were rescued from a different Palm City home. Authorities said that the owner claimed she was rescuing animals she encountered along her mail route. While the rescued Border Collies are now receiving care, Gupta says it's important to remember these situations impact more than animals. "This is not 'just' an animal problem," she said. "The welfare of the people living in these homes is often really compromised." Animal welfare experts say recognizing warning signs early and reporting concerns to local authorities can help prevent situations from escalating before animals and people are put at risk. O'Donnell is expected to make her first court appearance Tuesday. Deputies said the investigation remains ongoing.

hero.headline: Sheriff says Martin County woman kept Border Collies trapped in feces-covered home
hero.teaser: Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the Palm City home was so deteriorated that drywall was missing and animals were in deplorable condition.
hero.body:
Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said 62-year-old Paige O'Donnell kept 36 Border Collies trapped in her Palm City home at 1245 SW Alligator Street, where conditions were so severe that deputies and animal services officers had to wear hazmat suits to retrieve the animals. The house was so deteriorated that about a foot and a half of drywall was gone, and furniture was destroyed. The food and water bowls were covered in feces.

Budensiek said O'Donnell was previously an AKC breeder and the last time officials were allowed inside the home was in 2020, when the animals were in acceptable condition. Between 2020 and 2022, O'Donnell reportedly underwent treatment for alcohol abuse and began blocking officials from accessing her home. Some of the dogs were skittish and hiding, making it difficult for investigators to remove them.

All 36 dogs removed from the home will be taken to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. Neighbor Tessa Nabors said she hopes O'Donnell gets the help she needs but that she should not be subjecting animals to that type of situation. O'Donnell is expected to appear in court Tuesday.
hero.article_text: A Martin County woman is facing felony and misdemeanor animal cruelty charges after deputies discovered 36 dogs living in unsanitary conditions inside her Palm City home. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office executed a search warrant earlier today and spent much of the afternoon removing the animals, which ranged from puppies to adult border collies. Investigators wore hazmat suits as they worked to retrieve the dogs. “The animals are in deplorable conditions,” Sheriff John Budensiek said. Budensiek described the state of the home, saying, “The food bowls, the water bowls in there are covered in feces. The animals themselves, the dogs, which are supposed to be border collies, beautiful dogs, are covered in feces. They're supposed to be white and black dogs, and they're solid black from the feces.” He added that some of the dogs were skittish and hiding, making it difficult for investigators to remove them. “Currently right now, there's more dogs in there than what they've been able to get out because they're skittish, they're hiding,” Budensiek said. According to Budensiek, the homeowner, Paige O'Donnell, was previously an AKC breeder. He said the last time officials were allowed inside the home was in 2020, when the animals were in acceptable condition. However, between 2020 and 2022, O'Donnell reportedly underwent treatment for alcohol abuse and began “playing the legal game” to block officials from accessing her home. A neighbor, Tessa Nabors, expressed hope that the situation would lead to change. “Hopefully she gets the help that she also needs, but she shouldn't be subjecting animals to that type of situation because they're being forced to live in that, and that's disgusting on her part,” Nabors said. The sheriff confirmed that all 36 dogs removed from the home will be taken to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. To donate to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, click here. O'Donnell is expected to appear in court Tuesday. hero.body:

Motorists traveling through the area should expect delays and seek alternate routes while the closure remains in effect. Officials are urging drivers to use caution and avoid the area if possible.

The cause of the fire has not yet been released. The closure continues to affect northbound traffic on Florida's Turnpike in Martin County.

hero.headline: WPTV investigation leads to rescue of 36 dogs from Palm City home on SW Alligator Street
hero.teaser: A WPTV investigation into suspected animal hoarding prompted Martin County deputies to execute a search warrant that resulted in 36 Border Collies being rescued from a Palm City home.
hero.body:
Martin County deputies executed a search warrant Monday at a Palm City home in the 1245 block of Southwest Alligator Street following a WPTV investigation into alleged animal hoarding. Sheriff John Budensiek said the station keeping the story alive in its newsroom kept deputies engaged and prompted them to look into the case again after years of complaints.

Martin County Animal Control officers and sheriff's deputies had visited homes in the area at least 11 times since 2020 related to concerns about dogs and their owners. Homeowner Paige O'Donnell built a fence and stopped letting deputies in, making it hard to find probable cause for a warrant. After WPTV started asking the sheriff's office about the house, deputies conducted days of surveillance and negotiated with O'Donnell, who agreed last week to surrender one dog that appeared malnourished.

Budensiek said the malnourished dog gave them the probable cause to execute Monday's warrant. O'Donnell, a former AKC Border Collie breeder, was living in the house and taking a bath when deputies arrived. She did not come to the door, prompting deputies to bust it open. The 36 dogs rescued will be taken to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast for care. O'Donnell faces felony animal cruelty and misdemeanor improper confinement charges.

A crash on Interstate 95 southbound caused major delays Tuesday morning in Port St. Lucie near the Crosstown Parkway Exit. According to FL511, the crash was reported around 8:30 a.m. beyond Exit 120 for Crosstown Parkway, where two right lanes were blocked.

Fire trucks responded to the scene, narrowing traffic to one lane and causing a roughly two-mile backup. Drivers were urged to slow down or move over for emergency crews and Road Rangers working in the area.

The crash occurred as commuters navigated the morning rush hour on the major north-south corridor through St. Lucie County. The incident disrupted traffic flow on one of South Florida's busiest highways during peak travel times.

Officials reminded motorists to exercise caution when approaching the crash scene and to follow Florida's Move Over Law, which requires drivers to move over a lane or slow down when emergency vehicles are stopped on the roadside. The law applies to all emergency vehicles, including fire trucks and Road Ranger assistance vehicles responding to incidents on state highways.

hero.headline: Murray Middle School students return to class in Stuart as tornado rebuild continues
hero.teaser: Murray Middle School students are returning to class this week in Stuart to a campus undergoing major construction nearly two years after a tornado destroyed two buildings and damaged a third.
hero.body:
Students at Murray Middle School in Stuart are returning to class this week to a campus where crews demolished two buildings over the summer and are rebuilding spaces for band, chorus, and agriculture programs. The October 2024 tornado spawned by Hurricane Milton destroyed two buildings and left a third with major roof damage. Those spaces housed the school's band, chorus, and agriculture programs. District leaders say the work zone is completely separated from the rest of campus, so students can learn safely while crews rebuild.

Superintendent Michael Maine said the programs never stopped despite the damage. Crews will build a new administration building and media center, plus modern spaces for band, chorus, and agriculture science. Crews will also renovate the gym.

The gym is expected to be finished by next August. The new administration building, media center, and specialized classrooms are expected to follow in December 2027. The project is being paid for through state support, insurance reimbursements, and district capital funds.

hero.headline: Vindman's $14.5 million war chest leads Nixon ahead of Florida Democratic Senate primary
hero.body:
Retired Army Lt. Alex Vindman and state Rep. Angie Nixon are presenting sharply contrasting campaigns in the Florida Democratic Senate primary, with Vindman holding a substantial fundraising advantage of roughly $14.5 million raised through June. The Aug. 18 primary will determine which Democrat challenges Republican Sen. Ashley Moody in November's general election to complete the final two years of a former senator's term.

Vindman has outpaced even Moody in fundraising and is highlighting his military service while positioning himself as a candidate capable of reaching voters beyond the Democratic base. He has focused his campaign on the November election and the need for congressional checks on President Donald Trump, saying Republicans in office have abandoned their responsibilities to check executive power. Vindman has declined to debate Nixon during the primary.

Nixon is countering Vindman's national profile with her Florida roots, a more progressive platform, and a working-class message centered on wages and affordability. The Jacksonville Democrat's campaign social-media posts have highlighted everyday challenges including car trouble and a flat tire, portraying those moments as evidence she deals with problems confronting voters. At the Florida Capitol, Nixon has developed a reputation as an outspoken protester, using a bullhorn during the fight over Florida's congressional maps and facing charges following a sit-in demonstration at the governor's office.

Moody faces three lower-profile candidates in the Republican primary but is expected to advance easily to November, allowing her to concentrate on the general election. She is framing the race as a choice between Republicans and Democrats moving the country toward socialism and greater government control. The latest Decision Desk HQ polling average gives Moody a seven-point advantage over Vindman, 47% to 40%, placing the race within competitive territory though not yet a top-tier national toss-up. The winner in November will serve the remainder of the term and must run again in 2028 for a full six-year term.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie residents rescue autistic child from retention pond
cards.teaser: A group of Port St. Lucie residents pulled an autistic child from a retention pond on Saturday morning after spotting him wandering alone near the water.
cards.body:
A group of Port St. Lucie residents rescued an autistic child from a retention pond on Saturday morning after noticing him wandering alone near the water. The residents were on their way to grab coffee when they spotted the child and sensed something was wrong, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.

The group stopped to help and tried to guide the child to safety. When the child tried to enter the pond, the residents followed him into the water and pulled him to safety. The child was covered in fire ants when they reached him.

The residents immediately called 911 and stayed with the child until officers arrived. Body camera video from the Port St. Lucie Police Department shows deputies talking to the residents and wiping fire ants off the child. The Port St. Lucie Police Department advises residents to follow their instincts if they see someone who could be in danger.

Lucie Police Department says a group of Port St. Lucie residents were on their way to grab coffee when they noticed a child wandering alone near a retention pond. Feeling that something was off, the group of Good Samaritans stopped to help. hero.headline: Man lifts railroad gate to rescue woman trapped on tracks in Hobe Sound
hero.teaser: Josiah Baur ran across railroad tracks and lifted a crossing gate to free Debbie Spoelstra's car from the tracks at Bridge Road and Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound Friday evening as a freight train approached.
hero.body:
Josiah Baur, 23, lifted a railroad crossing gate Friday evening to free Debbie Spoelstra's car from the tracks at Bridge Road and Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound as a freight train approached. Spoelstra was turning onto Bridge Road from Dixie Highway when a railroad crossing arm came down on her car, leaving her trapped between the gates. The arm got stuck on her car antenna, preventing her from reversing.

Baur was on his way home to Port St. Lucie from work when he stopped at the crossing and saw Spoelstra trapped. He put his car in park and ran across the tracks to lift the gate. Spoelstra backed her car away from the tracks seconds before the train passed. Dash-cam video captured the rescue.

Spoelstra and Baur met again at the railroad crossing Sunday and hugged. Spoelstra said she was grateful to Baur and believes a total stranger helping another person is remarkable. Baur said he was fortunate that God put him where he was. Spoelstra said she was not texting or distracted while driving and was simply taken off guard by the crossing arms lowering. Witnesses say the crossing arm malfunctioned during the incident, and Spoelstra reported the problem to Florida East Coast Railway.
hero.article_text: An act of bravery and compassion is bringing two strangers together on the Treasure Coast. A young man rescued a woman whose car got stuck on a railroad crossing in Hobe Sound, saving her from near disaster. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Just a few days ago, Josiah Baur and Debbie Spoelstra didn’t know each other, but now, they share a special connection. “Friday, I was leaving work, and I was heading back home. I was trying to get home for a tire appointment, funny enough, and running late for it. Train crossing went down, and I looked down on my phone, and I glimpsed up, and I saw the car stuck behind the railroad crossing,” Baur said. Spoelstra was still inside that car, stuck on the train tracks at Bridge Road and Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound. What I did is, I put my car in reverse, and apparently the gate got stuck on top of my car on the antenna. So, when I tried to reverse, it would not let me reverse. I sat there, I saw the train,” Spoelstra said. Baur, realizing she was still in the car, didn’t hesitate and jumped out of his car to help. “I threw it in park and just took off running. Try to see what side the train was on to see if it would clear her or not. But it was on her side and didn't really want to take a chance. So, I ran across and tried to push up on the thingy to release her,” Baur said. That split-second decision helped to avoid what could have been a devastating crash from a freight train. “He came just like a hero. And lifted the gate up off of my car. And I was able to reverse and get off the tracks. And as soon as he did that, within seconds, the train passed by me. So it was very scary, you know, life-changing experience for me,” Spoelstra said. “We think of heroes, I think police officers and military, not what I did. It was just a good, good thing to do,” Baur said. The two said they’ve now bonded over this unique experience, attributing it to their shared faith. “He was put in one place, I was put in one place, and it was just fate. And it was a God thing, you know, and then once I told him my grandson was Josiah, and then he was just like, ‘Oh, wow. It's definitely a God thing.’ So, I don't know. I would just say, like I said, I'm so grateful for him,” Spoelstra said. He puts us exactly where we need to be. If you're running late for something, it's probably for a reason. Just trust his plan,” Baur said. Spoelstra said she wasn’t texting or distracted while driving and was simply just taken off guard by the railroad crossing arms lowering. She wants to pass this message on to other drivers: always be careful and look both ways before crossing train tracks. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

cards.headline: Palm City woman arrested after 36 Border Collies found living in feces-covered home
cards.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies arrested 62-year-old Paige O'Donnell Monday after executing a search warrant at her Palm City home at 1245 SW Alligator Street, where they found 36 Border Collies living in what Sheriff John Budensiek described as deplorable conditions. Deputies and animal services officers wore Tyvek protective clothing to remove the dogs from a home covered in feces, urine-soaked materials, boxes and debris. O'Donnell faces charges of felony animal cruelty and misdemeanor improper confinement.

Budensiek said the dogs, which should be white and black, were solid black from being covered in feces. The house deteriorated so badly that about a foot and a half of drywall was gone, furniture was destroyed, and food and water bowls were covered in feces. Some dogs were skittish and hiding inside the home, making removal difficult. Deputies said it was extremely hot and O'Donnell may not have had air conditioning.

O'Donnell previously operated as an AKC Border Collie breeder. Budensiek said the last time officials were allowed inside the home was in 2020, when animals were in acceptable condition. Between 2020 and 2022, O'Donnell reportedly underwent treatment for alcohol abuse and began blocking officials from accessing her home. The sheriff's office conducted days of surveillance and last week persuaded O'Donnell to surrender one dog, which appeared malnourished and provided probable cause for Monday's warrant.

All 36 dogs removed from the home will be taken to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. O'Donnell is expected to appear in court Tuesday and will face at least 40 charges, according to Budensiek. Neighbor Kelsey Weidenheimer said it was sad to see the dogs in rough shape but was happy they were finally getting out. The case comes weeks after another Palm City woman was arrested when more than 100 dogs and cats were found in her home.

cards.headline: Animal experts explain hoarding psychology after Palm City Border Collie case
cards.teaser: Animal welfare experts say hoarding cases like the Palm City home where 36 Border Collies were found Monday often involve people who begin with good intentions but become overwhelmed or believe they are the only ones who can provide care.
cards.body:
Martin County deputies arrested 62-year-old Paige O'Donnell Monday after at least 36 Border Collies were removed from her Palm City home, where deputies described conditions as unsanitary and dangerous. Sheriff John Budensiek said the dogs were covered in feces and investigators found food and water bowls covered in feces. O'Donnell previously operated as a Border Collie breeder.

Dr. Maya Gupta, Vice President of Research at the ASPCA, said animal hoarding is often more complicated than a love of animals. One type involves people caring for animals who become overwhelmed. Another common type is a rescuer hoarder, someone who believes they are helping animals but gradually loses the ability to care for them or place them in new homes properly. Gupta said one of the most powerful factors is when somebody starts to believe they are the only one who can provide care for the animals.

The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders identifies animal hoarding as a feature that can be associated with hoarding disorder, but experts caution that not every person who hoards animals has a diagnosable mental health condition. Gupta said hoarding often involves a combination of factors, including social isolation, emotional attachment to animals, and diminished awareness of how serious conditions have become. The case comes weeks after another major animal hoarding investigation in Martin County, where more than 100 dogs and cats were rescued from a different Palm City home.
cards.article_text: A Palm City woman is facing dozens of animal cruelty charges after Martin County deputies say they found more than three dozen Border Collies living in deplorable conditions inside her home. But animal welfare experts say cases like this are often more complex than simply owning too many pets. According to investigators, 62-year-old Paige O'Donnell was arrested Monday after deputies executed a search warrant at her Palm City home. Authorities said at least 36 Border Collies were removed from the property, where deputies described conditions as unsanitary and dangerous for both the animals and anyone entering the residence. "The animals themselves, the dogs, which are supposed to be Border Collies, beautiful dogs, are covered in feces," Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said. "They're supposed to be white and black dogs, and they're solid black from the feces." See also: Homeowner in custody after 20+ Border Collies found in Palm City hoarding case For many people, cases like this prompt a difficult question: How do conditions become so severe? Experts at the ASPCA say animal hoarding is often much more complicated than a love of animals. While some people intentionally neglect animals, others begin with good intentions and eventually become overwhelmed by the number of pets in their care. "We do see a few different subtypes of hoarding," said Dr. Maya Gupta, Vice President of Research at the ASPCA. "One is the person who is caring for animals, maybe caring for other people and just gets overwhelmed." Another common type involves what experts call a "rescuer hoarder" someone who believes they are helping animals but gradually loses the ability to care for them or place them in new homes properly. The latest Palm City case may fit into that discussion. Investigators said O'Donnell previously operated as a Border Collie breeder, and all of the dogs recovered from the home appear to be Border Collies. Gupta says one of the most powerful factors in animal hoarding is what she describes as a rescue mentality. "When somebody starts to believe that they are the only one who can provide care for the animals, that's where it can get dangerous," Gupta said. Researchers say mental health can sometimes play a role in animal hoarding cases. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders identifies animal hoarding as a feature that can be associated with hoarding disorder. However, experts caution that not every person who hoards animals has a diagnosable mental health condition. Instead, hoarding often involves a combination of factors, including social isolation, emotional attachment to animals, and a diminished awareness of how serious conditions have become. "Something has gone wrong in the relationships that that person has with others around them," Gupta said. "That's not something we can definitely apply to every case, but it's something we see more often than not." Experts say another challenge is that many animal hoarding cases remain hidden for years. Individuals often avoid allowing visitors into their homes, and neighbors may only become aware of a problem after noticing strong odors, excessive numbers of animals, or concerns about the animals' welfare. The latest case comes just weeks after another major animal hoarding investigation in Martin County, where more than 100 dogs and cats were rescued from a different Palm City home. Authorities said that the owner claimed she was rescuing animals she encountered along her mail route. While the rescued Border Collies are now receiving care, Gupta says it's important to remember these situations impact more than animals. "This is not 'just' an animal problem," she said. "The welfare of the people living in these homes is often really compromised." Animal welfare experts say recognizing warning signs early and reporting concerns to local authorities can help prevent situations from escalating before animals and people are put at risk. O'Donnell is expected to make her first court appearance Tuesday. Deputies said the investigation remains ongoing.

cards.headline: Martin County schools begin year with on-time buses and new academic goals
cards.teaser: Superintendent Michael Maine said Monday that all buses arrived on time on the first day of school and the district is focused on eliminating C-rated schools and ensuring 100% of students are on reading level.
cards.body:
Superintendent Michael Maine greeted bus drivers at the transportation department Monday morning as Martin County schools began the year. District officials said enrollment this school year is flat and bus routes were consolidated to increase efficiency and save costs. Maine said all reports showed everything was on time and all students arrived, though there were some delays due to traffic.

Traffic appeared manageable outside Hobe Sound Elementary Monday morning, and one crossing guard said it was the best day since they started working there. Maine visited the now B-rated Hobe Sound Elementary, where third grade teacher Crystal Brandt said her class would write expectations together. A fourth grader said they were excited to have friends again.

Maine outlined the district's goals for the year: eliminating C-rated schools, ensuring 100% of students are on reading level, and making sure every student arrives home safely. Maine said he hopes by the end of the first week students feel safe and excited to be back and are starting to get back into the academic routine.

hero.headline: Florida insurers now require roof replacements at 15 years for homeowners
hero.body:
Insurance companies across Florida have shortened the acceptable age for asphalt and composition shingle roofs from 20 years to 15 years, placing homeowners on a tighter timeline for costly replacements. Most companies now require roofs to be 15 years old or newer to qualify for the best rates, according to Robert Norberg of Arden Insurance in Lantana. The change affects thousands of Florida homeowners who carry asphalt shingle roofs, the most common roofing material in the state.

Insurers view asphalt shingles as vulnerable to Florida's intense sun and strong winds. Metal roofs receive more favorable treatment, with some companies accepting them up to 40 years old. Tile roofs also face less restrictive age limits than asphalt. The shift in standards means homeowners with roofs approaching 15 years face pressure to replace them or accept higher premiums and limited coverage options.

Melissa Burt DeVriese, president of Security First Insurance, said the age of a roof represents the biggest factor in determining homeowner insurance rates. She said replacing an old roof can save thousands of dollars annually in premiums. Vero Beach homeowner Kelly Hagen reported a premium of nearly $9,000 and said she cannot find better quotes because her roof turns 15 years old this month. Multiple insurance agents told her they cannot help her secure lower rates.

The tightened standards arrive as Florida officials point to improvements in the homeowners insurance market, including new companies entering the state and some rate declines. Homeowners in recent years have already paid thousands for roof replacements under pressure from insurance companies seeking to reduce risk exposure. The 15-year threshold now applies statewide, creating what industry observers describe as a countdown clock for property owners with asphalt shingle roofs who want to maintain affordable coverage and avoid being dropped or non-renewed by their carriers.

cards.headline: Vindman holds fundraising edge over Nixon in Florida Democratic Senate primary
cards.teaser: Retired Army Lt. Alex Vindman and state Rep. Angie Nixon present contrasting campaigns ahead of the Aug. 18 primary to challenge Republican Sen. Ashley Moody.
cards.body:
Retired Army Lt. Alex Vindman has raised roughly $14.5 million through June in the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate, outpacing both his primary opponent and Republican Sen. Ashley Moody. Vindman is highlighting his military service and presenting himself as a candidate who can reach voters beyond the Democratic base. He has focused his campaign on the November general election and the need to place a congressional check on President Donald Trump, saying a Democratic House and Senate are essential because Republicans in office have abandoned their responsibilities to check presidential power.

Vindman must first defeat state Rep. Angie Nixon, a Jacksonville Democrat whom he has declined to debate. Nixon is countering Vindman's national profile with her Florida roots, a more progressive platform, and a working-class message centered on wages and affordability. Her campaign's social media posts have highlighted car trouble and a flat tire as evidence she faces the same problems as the voters she hopes to represent. At the Florida Capitol, Nixon has built a reputation as an outspoken protester, using a bullhorn during the fight over Florida's congressional maps and later facing charges following a sit-in demonstration at the governor's office.

Moody faces three lower-profile candidates in the Republican primary, none expected to seriously threaten the appointed senator. The latest Decision Desk HQ polling average gives Moody a seven-point advantage over Vindman, 47% to 40%, placing the race within competitive territory. Florida's primary takes place Aug. 18. The November winner will complete the final two years of a term and must run again in 2028 for a full six-year term.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce police arrest three people on drug possession charges at 10th Street Park
hero.teaser: Three people face drug possession charges after Fort Pierce police conducted a narcotics investigation at 10th Street Park following complaints of illegal drug activity.
hero.body:
The Fort Pierce Police Department Crime Suppression Unit conducted a narcotics investigation at 10th Street Park on August 7 following complaints of illegal drug activity in the area. The investigation resulted in the arrest of three individuals on multiple charges, including possession of cocaine and drug paraphernalia.

Erica Josephs, 52, Michelle Sayles, 21, and April Reiss, 38, were taken into custody during the operation. According to the Fort Pierce Police Department, all three suspects face charges related to drug possession. The arrests were made as part of ongoing efforts to address illegal narcotics activity at the park location.

Following their arrests, all three individuals were transported to the St. Lucie County Jail. The Fort Pierce Police Department reported that the suspects were taken into custody without further incident during the booking process.

The Crime Suppression Unit's investigation was prompted by community complaints about illegal drug activity taking place at 10th Street Park. The Fort Pierce Police Department has not released additional details about the investigation or whether further arrests are anticipated in connection with the case.

cards.headline: Martin County deputies arrest Palm City woman after rescuing 36 Border Collies from hoarding case
cards.body:
Martin County sheriff's deputies arrested a 62-year-old Palm City woman Monday after rescuing 36 Border Collies from deplorable conditions at her home on Southwest Alligator Street. Paige O'Donnell faces felony animal cruelty charges and misdemeanor improper confinement charges after authorities executed a search warrant at 1245 SW Alligator Street. The warrant followed an ongoing investigation by Martin County Animal Services officers and sheriff's detectives.

Sheriff John Budensiek said the dogs were covered in feces and living in extreme filth. The house deteriorated so badly that about a foot and a half of drywall was gone, furniture was destroyed, and food and water bowls were covered in feces. Deputies and animal services officers wore Tyvek protective clothing because of extensive accumulations of feces, urine-soaked materials, boxes and debris throughout the residence. Budensiek said the dogs were supposed to be white and black but appeared solid black from the feces.

O'Donnell kept the dogs trapped inside the home and never let them outside, according to investigators. The conditions were extremely hot and she may not have had air conditioning. Some dogs remained skittish and hiding inside the home, making it difficult for deputies to determine the total number of animals. Neighbors said they were sad to see the dogs in such rough shape but happy they were finally rescued. Neighbor Kimberly Todd said O'Donnell was supposed to be an animal breeder.

Budensiek said O'Donnell will face at least 40 charges. She was scheduled to make her first appearance before a judge Tuesday. The 36 rescued dogs will be taken to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast for care. O'Donnell was a former AKC Border Collie breeder. This case comes weeks after a U.S. Postal Service carrier was arrested after more than 100 dogs and cats were found in her Palm City home.

hero.headline: Four Indian River County elementary schools reach 90% reading proficiency milestone
hero.body:
Four elementary schools in Indian River County have reached a 90% reading proficiency goal set by the Moonshot Moment, a community-driven literacy program that has drawn national attention. The program was born in 2012 through The Learning Alliance, a nonprofit co-founded by parent Liz Remington, whose son struggled with reading. The nonprofit brings together schools, philanthropists, and business owners to fund added resources, including reading coaches, in elementary classrooms.

When Remington first started the effort in 2017, just 56% of third graders in the district were reading at grade level. Today, Rosewood Magnet School and Osceola Magnet School are among the four schools that have cleared the 90% threshold. At Rosewood, principal Adam Faust said the achievement came down to the final day. The school had six kids to test to make the 90%, needed three to be at proficiency or above, and five of those kids made it.

At Osceola Magnet School, principal Jennifer Norris said students will return to a new campus building and a new reading challenge after the school also cleared the 90% threshold. The school is shooting for 95% this year. Norris said the stakes behind that goal are significant. If students are reading at grade level by third grade, the data show they are going to be proficient readers for the rest of their life.

Other school districts across Florida are now looking at adopting the Moonshot Moment model, a continuation of a mission that started with one parent's child and has since helped thousands of students. Remington said the key is to put the systems in place and build your team and implement collectively and collaboratively. From birth to third grade, you're learning to read, Faust said. From third grade on, you're reading to learn.

cards.headline: Indian River County school enrollment exceeds state projections with expanded programs
cards.teaser: Indian River County schools are starting the year with enrollment expected to exceed the state's projections, thanks to expanded programs and a focus on listening to families.
cards.body:
Indian River County school leaders say they are starting the year with enrollment expected to exceed the state's projections, thanks to expanded programs and a focus on listening to families. About 14,000 students are expected to begin the school year across the district. Liberty Magnet School is welcoming about 650 students this year, roughly the same as last year. Principal Chris Taylor said he is happy to see the halls full again after a quiet summer.

David Moore said the district has expanded its magnet and K-8 options to better meet families' needs. The district has also implemented other strategies to attract and retain families, including creating programming for homeschool students, removing attendance boundaries, and utilizing open choice. Moore said the district took time to sit back, relax, and understand what the community wants when it comes to educating children.

Moore said the district still sees a slight decline in enrollment year after year, but it is not significant enough to impact the budget. The Hamilton family said the support their children receive at Liberty Magnet keeps them coming back. All three of their children have gone to the school, and the school has been really invested in their success, parent Matt Hamilton said.

cards.headline: Hallandale Beach man faces charges of unlawful sexual conduct with minors in Indian River County
cards.teaser: A Broward County resident facing charges of unlawful sexual conduct with an underage girl in Brevard County is facing similar charges in Indian River County.
cards.body:
Emaad Mir, 27, from Hallandale Beach, was arrested on Saturday, Aug. 8 on charges of traveling to meet a minor for unlawful sexual activity, transmitting harmful information to minors and unlawful use of a two-way communication device. Two Indian River County Sheriff's Office deputies responded to a home on Thursday, Aug. 6, where they were told by a mother that her daughter was sexually battered by an adult man who went by the name of Adam. The victim said she believed the suspect was 21 years old and was contacted by the person on the messaging application TextNow.

The victim said she and the suspect arranged for Adam to pick her up near her residence during the early morning hours on July 31. Inside the suspect's vehicle, sexual contact occurred. The sheriff's office report notes that Adam allegedly had sexual contact with other underage girls who knew each other that occurred between June and July. Deputies created a TextNow account and used their phone to contact the suspect on the app. Pretending to be a victim, deputies persuaded the suspect to travel two hours to Vero Beach to meet. Deputies stopped a dark blue Kia sedan near the 1300 block of 29th Avenue and took the suspect into custody. Deputies determined the driver of the Kia was Mir.

During a court hearing on Sunday, Aug. 9, a court ordered Mir not to have contact with the vape pen victim, and he is being held in the Indian River County Jail on $1.75 million bail. This was not the first time Mir was accused of sexual activity with an underage girl. He was arrested on Feb. 11, 2026 by Rockledge Police on allegations that an officer observed a suspicious vehicle at Anderson Park at 12:48 a.m. Mir faces charges of lewd or lascivious battery of a victim between the ages of 12 and 16 years old and traveling to meet a minor after luring by computer in Brevard County. Mir has a scheduled court date in Brevard County on Aug. 11.

cards.headline: Indian River County converts Freshman Learning Center into Vero Beach Middle School
cards.teaser: The Freshman Learning Center has been converted into Vero Beach Middle School as Indian River County school leaders reorganize schools ahead of the new year.
cards.body:
A different approach to public education is taking shape in Indian River County this school year as district leaders expand school choice and reorganize several campuses. The Freshman Learning Center has been converted into Vero Beach Middle School. Moore says the freshman center was expensive to operate and did not provide students with high-quality educational programs. He says moving ninth-graders back to traditional high schools will also give them earlier access to more academic opportunities.

From a student's perspective, moving ninth-graders back allows them access to programming that was only being offered at the high school. Students should not have to wait until they are in 10th grade to take some of those courses, Moore said. District leaders say the two high schools, Sebastian River High School and Vero Beach High School, have enough capacity to accommodate incoming freshmen. That means all incoming ninth-graders this school year will attend either Sebastian River High School or Vero Beach High School.

Families in the district have more flexibility in where their children attend school. Parents can choose to enroll their children at schools across the district, rather than being limited to the school assigned to their neighborhood. The district has also converted several campuses into K-8 schools and operates five charter schools. The changes are part of the district's broader effort to give families more educational options while restructuring how its schools serve students.

cards.headline: Vero Beach High School marching band prepares for new school year at band camp
cards.teaser: The Vero Beach High School Fighting Indians Band, founded in 1934, is preparing for the new school year with band camp just days before classes begin.
cards.body:
The Vero Beach High School Fighting Indians Band held band camp at the school just a few days before school started. The band was founded in 1934 as part of the Federal Music Project during the Great Depression. Band director Sean Srigley is an alumnus of Vero Beach High School and was in the band himself. Srigley said the band has awesome academics and awesome athletics, and the band is right there with them. The band has marched in pretty much every big parade you could have in America.

The band performed in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in 1988, marching through the streets of New York City and playing Alexander's Ragtime Band for millions of television viewers. That single performance became one of the defining moments in the program's history and remains a source of pride for every new generation of members. The band has also performed in the Tournament of Roses Parade, the Fiesta Bowl Parade, the Orange Bowl and even Carnegie Hall. The program has earned decades of Superior ratings and national recognition while representing the Treasure Coast with pride.

Annabel Robbins plays flute piccolo and is a drum major. Brady, an incoming senior, is the woodwind captain and section leader. Brady said being in charge of a lot of kids is kind of scary, and you have to make sure they are all doing good. Joining the marching band for practice means discipline and the ability to stand for a long time in the Florida heat, something these kids do with incredible dedication.
cards.article_text: This week I'm at Vero Beach High School where students are getting ready to go back to school, and I decided to do something I've never done before – I joined the marching band! I crashed band camp at Vero Beach High School just a few days before school started, and let me tell you, it was an incredible experience. WATCH: The first time I stepped onto that practice field, I could feel the history before I even picked up my instrument. This wasn't just another high school band – this was a tradition stretching back to 1934, when the Fighting Indians Band was founded as part of the Federal Music Project during the Great Depression. Every student who had ever worn that uniform had helped build an incredible legacy. I got to meet some amazing students who are keeping that tradition alive, like Annabel Robbins who plays flute piccolo and is a drum major. Brady, an incoming senior, is the woodwind captain and section leader. "It's kind of scary, you know," Brady said. "You're in charge of a lot of kids, so you got to make sure they're all doing good. The band director, Sean Srigley, has a special connection to this program that goes way back. "I'm actually alumni of Vero Beach High School. I was in the band myself," Srigley explained. "The cool thing about Vero is we've got awesome academics, awesome athletics. Our band is right there with them. We've marched in pretty much every big parade you could have in America." And he's not exaggerating! This band has an absolutely incredible resume. They performed in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in 1988, marching through the streets of New York City and playing "Alexander's Ragtime Band" for millions of television viewers. That single performance became one of the defining moments in the program's history and remains a source of pride for every new generation of members. But that's not all – they've also performed in the Tournament of Roses Parade, the Fiesta Bowl Parade, the Orange Bowl and even Carnegie Hall! The program has earned decades of Superior ratings and national recognition while representing our Treasure Coast with pride. After learning about all this amazing history, it was time for me to get to work. But honestly, that wasn't really my thing, so I tried the drums next. But joining the marching band for practice meant more than just learning music and drill. It meant discipline and the ability to stand for a long time in that Florida heat – something these kids do with incredible dedication. As I marched onto the football field, I couldn't help but imagine all the students who had stood in that same place before me. Some had gone on to march through Manhattan in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. Others had performed in famous bowl games or international parades. As I left Vero Beach High School that day, I was thankful for the opportunity to be part of something so special, even for just one practice. These students aren't just making music – they're carrying on a legacy that's been building for nearly 90 years.

hero.headline: 16-year-old Centennial High School student hit by car crossing Port St. Lucie intersection
hero.body:
A 16-year-old Centennial High School student was hit by a vehicle Monday morning while attempting to cross Crosstown Parkway at Southwest Cameo Boulevard in Port St. Lucie against the pedestrian signal. The incident occurred shortly after 7 a.m., according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.

The preliminary investigation indicates the teenager attempted to cross Crosstown Parkway against the pedestrian signal, entering the roadway in front of oncoming traffic that had the right of way. The teen told investigators they believed they could make it across the street before an approaching vehicle reached them. The driver was unable to avoid striking the student.

The 16-year-old sustained superficial injuries but declined medical transport at the scene. The teen's guardians were notified of the incident. The vehicle involved in the crash sustained minor cosmetic damage.

In March 2024, a 15-year-old student was hit by a car making a right turn onto Crosstown Parkway at Southwest Cameo Boulevard and was taken to the hospital with minor injuries.

hero.headline: Palm City woman arrested after 24 Border Collies rescued from hoarding case on Southwest Alligator Street
hero.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies executed a search warrant Monday at a Palm City home on Southwest Alligator Street and rescued 24 Border Collies in an animal hoarding case that followed a WPTV investigation showing law enforcement had visited the area at least 11 times since 2020 over concerns about dogs and their owners. Paige O'Donnell, the homeowner in the 1245 block of Southwest Alligator Street, will face about 40 charges, one felony and one misdemeanor for each of the 24 dogs rescued, according to Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek.

Deputies and animal services officers wore Tyvek protective clothing because of extensive accumulations of feces, urine-soaked materials, boxes and debris throughout the residence. The conditions inside were described as extremely concerning, with Budensiek saying the house was stacked with garbage and had feces over every square inch. The heat was extreme and the home may not have had air conditioning.

The search warrant came after the homeowner built a fence and stopped letting deputies inside, making it hard to find probable cause for a warrant. O'Donnell agreed last week to surrender one dog to authorities, and that dog appeared to be malnourished, giving deputies the probable cause to execute Monday's warrant. Investigators swept the house to make sure no dogs were hiding inside or dead.

The 24 rescued dogs will be taken to the Humane Society in Martin County for care. O'Donnell is expected to make her first appearance before a judge on Tuesday. The case comes weeks after a U.S. Postal Service carrier was arrested after more than 100 dogs and cats were found in her Palm City home.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound man rescues woman trapped on railroad tracks at Bridge Road and Dixie Highway
cards.teaser: Josiah Baur lifted a railroad crossing gate to free Debbie Spoelstra's car from the tracks seconds before a freight train passed through Friday evening in Hobe Sound.
cards.body:
Josiah Baur, 23, rescued a woman whose car became trapped on train tracks at Bridge Road and Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound on Friday evening, lifting the crossing gate seconds before a freight train passed through. Debbie Spoelstra was turning onto Bridge Road from Dixie Highway when a railroad crossing arm suddenly came down on her car, leaving her stuck between the gates. Dash-cam video captured the tense moments as a train's horn sounded while it moved closer to Spoelstra's red car.

Baur was leaving work and heading home to Port Saint Lucie when he stopped at the crossing on the other side of the tracks. He saw the car stuck and Spoelstra still inside, threw his car in park and ran across the tracks. He looked to see which side the train was on, saw it was on her side, and lifted the gate with both arms to release her car just in time for her to back up before the train came through.

Spoelstra said she put her car in reverse but the gate got stuck on top of her car on the antenna, preventing her from backing up. A witness, Lizzy Dominguez, was behind Baur's car and took a photo of him after the rescue, posting it on social media to find and thank him. Spoelstra and Baur met again at the railroad crossing Sunday and hugged. Spoelstra says her baby grandson shares the same name as the man who saved her: Josiah.
cards.article_text: An act of bravery and compassion is bringing two strangers together on the Treasure Coast. A young man rescued a woman whose car got stuck on a railroad crossing in Hobe Sound, saving her from near disaster. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Just a few days ago, Josiah Baur and Debbie Spoelstra didn’t know each other, but now, they share a special connection. “Friday, I was leaving work, and I was heading back home. I was trying to get home for a tire appointment, funny enough, and running late for it. Train crossing went down, and I looked down on my phone, and I glimpsed up, and I saw the car stuck behind the railroad crossing,” Baur said. Spoelstra was still inside that car, stuck on the train tracks at Bridge Road and Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound. What I did is, I put my car in reverse, and apparently the gate got stuck on top of my car on the antenna. So, when I tried to reverse, it would not let me reverse. I sat there, I saw the train,” Spoelstra said. Baur, realizing she was still in the car, didn’t hesitate and jumped out of his car to help. “I threw it in park and just took off running. Try to see what side the train was on to see if it would clear her or not. But it was on her side and didn't really want to take a chance. So, I ran across and tried to push up on the thingy to release her,” Baur said. That split-second decision helped to avoid what could have been a devastating crash from a freight train. “He came just like a hero. And lifted the gate up off of my car. And I was able to reverse and get off the tracks. And as soon as he did that, within seconds, the train passed by me. So it was very scary, you know, life-changing experience for me,” Spoelstra said. “We think of heroes, I think police officers and military, not what I did. It was just a good, good thing to do,” Baur said. The two said they’ve now bonded over this unique experience, attributing it to their shared faith. “He was put in one place, I was put in one place, and it was just fate. And it was a God thing, you know, and then once I told him my grandson was Josiah, and then he was just like, ‘Oh, wow. It's definitely a God thing.’ So, I don't know. I would just say, like I said, I'm so grateful for him,” Spoelstra said. He puts us exactly where we need to be. If you're running late for something, it's probably for a reason. Just trust his plan,” Baur said. Spoelstra said she wasn’t texting or distracted while driving and was simply just taken off guard by the railroad crossing arms lowering. She wants to pass this message on to other drivers: always be careful and look both ways before crossing train tracks. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

cards.headline: Martin County deputies find deplorable conditions during Border Collie hoarding investigation on Southwest Alligator Street
cards.teaser: Paige O'Donnell, 62, faces felony animal cruelty and improper confinement charges after deputies in Tyvek suits removed at least 29 Border Collies from a Palm City home filled with feces and debris.
cards.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies served a search warrant Monday at a Palm City home in the 1200 block of Southwest Alligator Street and found at least 29 Border Collies in what authorities described as deplorable conditions. Paige O'Donnell, 62, was arrested and charged with felony animal cruelty and improper confinement. Approximately eight Border Collies had been removed from the home by Monday afternoon, with deputies and animal services officers continuing to work to safely remove the remaining dogs.

Deputies and animal services officers were required to wear Tyvek protective clothing because of extensive accumulations of feces, urine-soaked materials, boxes and other debris throughout the residence. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the dogs were running loose in the house and described the conditions as deplorable. The house was stacked with garbage and had feces over every square inch, making it difficult and time-consuming to locate and safely remove the animals. It was extremely hot inside and the home may not have had air conditioning.

O'Donnell will face at least 40 charges and is expected to make her first appearance before a judge on Tuesday. The case comes weeks after a U.S. Postal Service carrier was arrested after more than 100 dogs and cats were found in her Palm City home.

hero.headline: Florida awards $1 million to fire departments for cancer prevention equipment
hero.body:
Florida Chief Financial Officer Jimmy Ingoglia announced Monday the allocation of $1 million to fire departments across the state through programs designed to protect firefighters from cancer-causing chemicals. Ingoglia made the announcement at West Palm Beach Fire Station 1, joined by state Rep. Anne Gerwig, state Rep. Peggy Gossett-Seidman, and West Palm Beach Mayor Keith James. The funds come from the Firefighter Cancer Decontamination Grant Program, the Firefighter Assistance Grant Program, and projects appropriated in the state's fiscal 2025-2026 budget.

The program provides financial assistance to fire departments, including volunteer departments, to procure equipment, supplies, and educational training designed to mitigate exposure to hazardous, cancer-causing chemicals. Ingoglia explained that modern fires pose greater health risks than decades ago because burning structures now contain materials beyond wood and concrete that release substances absorbed through the skin, eyes, and lungs of firefighters. West Palm Beach received $19,635, Greenacres received $6,806, and Highland Beach received $5,962 from Monday's allocation. West Palm Beach Fire Chief Diana Matty said the grants fund second sets of gloves, particulate blocking hoods, on-scene cleansing wipes, and specialized washers.

The state still has $1 million available through the Firefighter Cancer Decontamination Grant Program and another $1 million available for the Firefighter Assistance Grant Program in this year's state budget. Ingoglia urged fire chiefs across Florida to apply for the remaining funds.

Ingoglia also addressed concerns about an upcoming property tax amendment vote and funding worries expressed by cities and first responders. He said county budgets have increased between 60 to 160 percent over the past six years and counties have benefited from historic property tax revenue. Ingoglia stated he believes there is room to offer property tax relief while still funding necessary items for first responders, despite anxiety from sheriffs, police chiefs, and fire chiefs about potential budget cuts and layoffs. He said the vast majority of their budgets are controlled by county commissioners or mayors and there is more than enough money available.

hero.headline: Palm City woman arrested after deputies rescue 24 Border Collies from hoarding home on SW Alligator Street
hero.body:
Martin County sheriff's deputies arrested Paige O'Donnell, 62, on Monday after rescuing 24 Border Collies from her home in the 1200 block of SW Alligator Street in Palm City. O'Donnell faces charges of felony animal cruelty and improper confinement, with Sheriff John Budensiek saying she will face at least 40 charges total, one felony and one misdemeanor for each dog rescued.

Deputies and Martin County Animal Services officers executed a search warrant at the property following an ongoing investigation. The conditions inside the home were described as deplorable, with feces covering every square inch of the house. Deputies and animal services officers were required to wear Tyvek protective clothing because of extensive accumulations of feces, urine-soaked materials, boxes and other debris throughout the residence. Authorities said it was extremely hot inside and that O'Donnell may not have had air conditioning.

The search warrant came after WPTV reporting revealed that Martin County Animal Control officers and sheriff's deputies had visited homes in the area at least 11 times since 2020, all related to concerns about dogs and their owners. After the news station began asking the sheriff's office about the house, investigators conducted days of surveillance. O'Donnell agreed last week to surrender one dog, which appeared to be malnourished, giving deputies probable cause to execute the warrant.

Budensiek said the dogs were running loose inside the house and described it as stacked with garbage. The rescued dogs were taken to the Humane Society in Martin County for care. O'Donnell is expected to make her first appearance before a judge on Tuesday. The case comes weeks after a U.S. Postal Service carrier was arrested after more than 100 dogs and cats were found in her Palm City home.

cards.headline: Hallandale Beach man arrested in Indian River County on charges of traveling to meet minors for sex
cards.teaser: Emaad Mir, 27, of Hallandale Beach was arrested Saturday in Indian River County after deputies say he drove two hours to Vero Beach to meet what he believed was an underage girl.
cards.body:
Emaad Mir, 27, of Hallandale Beach was arrested on Saturday in Indian River County on charges of traveling to meet a minor for unlawful sexual activity, transmitting harmful information to minors and unlawful use of a two-way communication device. Indian River County Sheriff's Office deputies responded to a home on Thursday, Aug. 6, where a mother reported her daughter was sexually battered by an adult man who went by the name of Adam.

The victim said she was contacted by the suspect on the messaging application TextNow and that the suspect picked her up near her residence during the early morning hours on July 31. The sheriff's office report notes that Adam allegedly had sexual contact with other underage girls who knew each other that occurred between June and July. In one instance, another female victim told deputies she attempted to purchase THC vape pens from the suspect, and when she met him and entered his vehicle, sexual contact occurred.

Deputies created a TextNow account and contacted the suspect while pretending to be the victim who attempted to purchase THC vape pens. Deputies persuaded the suspect to travel two hours to Vero Beach to meet. On Aug. 8, deputies stopped a dark blue Kia sedan near the 1300 block of 29th Avenue in Vero Beach. The victim who attempted to purchase THC vape pens was given a photo lineup and selected Mir as the person she believed was Adam. A court ordered Mir not to have contact with the victim, and he is being held in the Indian River County Jail on $1.75 million bail. Mir was previously arrested on Feb. 11, 2026, in Brevard County on allegations involving sexual activity with an underage female at Anderson Park in Rockledge. He was released from Brevard County Jail on Feb. 13 after posting $150,000 bond and has a scheduled court date in Brevard County on Aug.

cards.headline: Centennial High School student hit by car while crossing Crosstown Parkway in Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: A 16-year-old Centennial High School student was struck by a vehicle Monday morning at the intersection of Crosstown Parkway and Southwest Cameo Boulevard while attempting to cross against the pedestrian signal.
cards.body:
A 16-year-old Centennial High School student was hit by a vehicle Monday morning while attempting to cross a Port St. Lucie intersection against the pedestrian signal. The incident occurred shortly after 7 a.m. at the intersection of Crosstown Parkway and Southwest Cameo Boulevard, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.

Police say the preliminary investigation indicates the teenager attempted to cross Crosstown Parkway against the pedestrian signal, entering the roadway in front of oncoming traffic that had the right of way. The teen told investigators they believed they could make it across the street before an approaching vehicle reached them. However, the driver was unable to avoid striking the student.

The 16-year-old sustained superficial injuries but declined medical transport at the scene. The teen's guardians were notified of the incident. The vehicle involved in the crash sustained minor cosmetic damage. In March 2024, a 15-year-old student was hit by a car making a right turn onto Crosstown Parkway at Southwest Cameo Boulevard and was taken to the hospital with minor injuries.

cards.headline: Four Indian River County schools reach 90% reading proficiency milestone through Moonshot Moment program
cards.teaser: Four elementary schools in Indian River County have achieved a 90% reading proficiency goal through a community-driven literacy program called the Moonshot Moment, drawing national attention to the effort.
cards.body:
Four schools in Indian River County have reached a 90% reading proficiency goal through a community-driven literacy program called the Moonshot Moment, a program born in 2012 through The Learning Alliance. The nonprofit was co-founded by parent Liz Remington, whose son struggled with reading. When Remington first launched the effort in 2017, just 56% of third graders in the district were reading at grade level.

The nonprofit brings together schools, philanthropists and business owners to fund added resources, including reading coaches in elementary classrooms. Rosewood Magnet School principal Adam Faust said the achievement came down to the final day. Six students had to test to make the 90% threshold, and the school needed three to be at proficiency or above. Five of those students made it. At Osceola Magnet School, principal Jennifer Norris said students will return to a new campus building and a new reading challenge after the school also cleared the 90% threshold. Norris said the school is shooting for 95% this year.

The stakes behind that goal are significant. If students are reading at grade level by third grade, data show they are going to be proficient readers for the rest of their life, Norris said. Other school districts across Florida are now looking at adopting the Moonshot Moment model, a continuation of a mission that started with one parent's child and has since helped thousands of students.
